Methods for finding square roots are algorithms used to determine the principal, or non-negative, square root of a real number. Mathematically, this means finding a number that, when multiplied by itself, equals the given number. Algebraically, it involves solving the equation \(x^2 - s = 0\). Geometrically, it means finding the side length of a square with a given area. Every real number has two square roots, but we usually consider only the positive one. For most numbers, the square root is an irrational number with a never-ending decimal. Thus, we can only approximate its decimal value to a certain degree of precision. Even when dealing with perfect square integers, the method used might only provide a series of increasingly accurate approximations. Continued fractions, an alternative to decimal or binary expansions, can help. They have a special property: the square root of any non-perfect square rational number has a repeating pattern in its continued fraction representation, similar to how rational numbers have repeating decimal patterns. The most common methods are iterative, involving two steps: choosing a starting value and refining it until the desired accuracy is reached. The closer the starting value is to the actual root, the fewer iterations are needed. One of the most familiar methods is Newton's method, based on calculus. Some methods, like paper-and-pencil synthetic division or series expansion, do not require an initial guess. For integer square roots, the result is rounded or truncated to the nearest integer. The choice of method depends on the required accuracy, the effort involved, and the available tools. Methods can be grouped into those suitable for mental calculation, those requiring paper and pencil, and those implemented in computer programs. Historically, methods for finding square roots have existed since ancient times, with Heron's method from first-century Egypt being the first known algorithm. Modern methods emerged after the introduction of the Arabic numeral system to Europe. Today, almost all computing devices have fast and accurate square root functions, either as programming constructs or hardware operators.

In telecommunications networks, a node is a point where information is redistributed or where communication begins or ends. The exact definition of a node can change based on the network and the layer of protocol being used. A physical network node is an electronic device connected to the network that can send, receive, or process information. Passive distribution points, like distribution frames or patch panels, do not qualify as nodes.

Hypothyroidism, also called underactive thyroid or low thyroid, happens when the thyroid gland doesn't make enough thyroid hormone. It can cause feeling cold, tiredness, constipation, slow heart rate, depression, and weight gain. Sometimes, the front of the neck swells because of a goiter. If not treated during pregnancy, it can delay a baby's growth and brain development. Worldwide, not having enough iodine in the diet is the most common cause of hypothyroidism. In countries with enough iodine, Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the most common cause. Other causes include radiation treatment, injuries to certain glands, medications, a birth defect where the thyroid doesn’t work, or previous thyroid surgery. Doctors can diagnose hypothyroidism using blood tests that measure thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and thyroxine levels. Adding iodine to salt can prevent hypothyroidism in many people. Treating it involves taking thyroid hormones, like levothyroxine, in the right amount based on symptoms and test results. These medicines are safe during pregnancy. Iodine in the diet is important, but too much can worsen some types of hypothyroidism. Globally, about one billion people lack enough iodine, but it’s not clear how often this leads to hypothyroidism. In the U.S., hypothyroidism affects 0.3% to 0.4% of people. A milder form, subclinical hypothyroidism, is estimated to affect 4.3% to 8.5% of people. Women and older people are more likely to get it. Dogs, cats, and horses can also get hypothyroidism, but less commonly.

Spahn is part of the Health Committee of the 17th Bundestag and leads the Health and Health Policy Working Group. He is also the spokesperson for the CDU/CSU Health Parliamentary Group. In 2018, when Angela Merkel said she would not run again for CDU party leadership, Spahn decided to try to become the new leader. However, he was not chosen in the first voting round. Later, in February 2020, when Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer stepped down, Spahn decided not to run for the party leadership but to support another candidate, Armin Laschet.

Wilhelm Gustav Keitel was a German field marshal and war criminal during World War II. He served as the chief of the armed forces high command (OKW) during the Nazi era. Keitel signed orders that led to very cruel and illegal actions during the war. Keitel became head of the armed forces office at the Reich Ministry of War in 1935. After the war, he was charged with being one of the major war criminals by the International Military Tribunal in Nuremberg. He was found guilty of crimes against humanity, crimes against peace, criminal conspiracy, and war crimes. Keitel was sentenced to death and executed by hanging in 1946.

Mária Pozsonec was a Slovenian politician with Hungarian heritage. She lived from January 16, 1940, to April 3, 2017. The heat index (HI) combines air temperature and relative humidity to show how hot it feels in the shade. It's also called "felt air temperature," "apparent temperature," "real feel," or "feels like." For instance, if the temperature is 70% humid, the heat index will tell you how hot it feels. The human body cools itself by sweating. Sweat evaporates, taking heat away from the body. High humidity slows down evaporation, meaning less heat is removed. This makes you feel hotter. How you feel can vary—some people feel hotter than others due to differences in body shape, metabolism, hydration, pregnancy, menopause, or drug use. Heat index measurements come from people describing how hot they feel for a given temperature and humidity. This helps create a heat index that links temperature and humidity levels. The heat index measures conditions in the shade, but in the sun, it might show a lower temperature than what you actually feel. If you're exercising or active, the heat you feel could be even higher than the heat index suggests.

David is described in the Hebrew Bible as the third king of Israel and Judah. He became king after Ish-bosheth. In the Books of Samuel, David starts as a young shepherd and gains fame by playing music and later by killing Goliath. Saul, the king, likes David and David becomes close friends with Saul's son Jonathan. Saul becomes worried and turns against David. When Saul and Jonathan die in battle, David is made king. David conquers Jerusalem and brings the Ark of the Covenant there, establishing the kingdom. As king, David has an affair with Bathsheba, which leads him to have Uriah the Hittite killed. His son Absalom tries to take over. David flees Jerusalem but returns after Absalom's death. God doesn't let David build the temple because he has killed many people. David chooses his son Solomon to take over when he dies. People praise David as an ideal king and see him as a future messiah. Many songs are said to be written by him. Some historians think David likely existed around 1000 BCE, but there is little evidence about him. A stone from Damascus mentions "house of David." David is a key figure in Jewish, Christian, and Islamic traditions, inspiring many stories and artworks over time.

Tyrus Raymond Cobb, nicknamed the Georgia Peach, was an American baseball player who played in the major leagues. He was born in a small town in Georgia on December 18, 1886, and played for the Detroit Tigers for 22 seasons. The last six seasons, he was also the team's manager. He finished his career with the Philadelphia Athletics. Cobb was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1936 with 98.2% of the votes, the highest percentage until Tom Seaver in 1992. In 1999, Cobb was ranked third on the list of the "100 Greatest Players" by "Sporting News." He set many records during his career, including the highest career batting average (.366 or.367) and the most career batting titles (11 or 12). Cobb still holds several records, such as the most career hits (4,189 or 4,191), most career runs (2,245 or 2,246), and most career games played (3,035) as of 2019. His legacy includes a scholarship fund for Georgia students, which he financed through his investments in Coca-Cola and General Motors. However, his reputation has been damaged by accusations of racism and violence, mainly due to some discredited biographies written after his death. Cobb was known to sometimes have violent conflicts but supported the integration of black players into the major leagues and was a generous donor.

Liu Shaoqi, born on November 24, 1898, and died on November 12, 1969, was a Chinese leader who fought for his country's revolution. He was an important politician and thinker. From 1954 to 1959, Liu was the chairman of the NPC Standing Committee. He was also the first vice chairman of the Communist Party of China from 1956 to 1966. Liu became the president of the People's Republic of China, China's official head of state, from 1959 to 1968. During his presidency, he worked to rebuild China's economy. Liu was one of the most powerful men in China for 15 years, ranking third after Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai. Initially, Mao planned for Liu to take over his position. However, in the early 1960s, Liu and Mao had a disagreement. Mao then criticized and removed Liu from power in 1966 during the Cultural Revolution. Liu was no longer seen in public after 1968 and was called a "capitalist-road leader" and a traitor. Liu died under harsh treatment during the Cultural Revolution but was later forgiven by Deng Xiaoping's government in 1980 and had a national memorial service.

The Wilmington insurrection of 1898, also known as the Wilmington massacre of 1898 or the Wilmington coup of 1898, happened on November 10, 1898, in Wilmington, North Carolina. This event marked a turning point in North Carolina's post-Reconstruction politics. It led to stricter racial segregation and more African American disenfranchisement across the South. Laura Edwards wrote in "Democracy Betrayed" (2000) that what happened in Wilmington affirmed white supremacy not just in that city, but throughout the South and the nation. The event showed that invoking "whiteness" overrode the legal citizenship and equal protection that blacks were supposed to have under the Fourteenth Amendment. Originally, the white press in Wilmington called it a race riot caused by blacks. However, over time, more facts came to light, and the event is now seen as a "coup d'état," the violent overthrow of a democratically elected government by a group of white supremacists. Multiple factors led to this event. It is claimed to be the only such incident in American history, as other late Reconstruction-era violence did not result in a direct "coup" with the replacement of elected officials. The "coup" occurred after white southern Democrats planned and led a mob of 2,000 white men to overthrow the legitimately elected local Fusionist government. They expelled black and white political leaders, destroyed the property and businesses of black citizens who had built since the Civil War, including the only black newspaper in the city, and killed an estimated 60 to more than 300 people.

Chemical stability, when used in chemistry, means a system is in its lowest energy state or in chemical equilibrium with its environment. This can be a dynamic equilibrium where atoms or molecules change form, but the overall number in a particular form remains the same. This equilibrium lasts indefinitely unless the system changes. A chemical system might involve changes in the state of matter or a series of reactions. If state A has more chemical stability than state B, it means the change from A to B requires more energy, indicated by a positive Gibbs energy.

Ronald Adolphis Johnson was an American football player who played as a running back. He played college football at the University of Michigan from 1966 to 1968. In 1967, he set a school record by running for 270 yards in a game. In 1968, he became the first African-American to lead the Michigan football team. That year, he also set an NCAA record by running for 347 yards in a game. He also set Big Ten conference records with 92 points scored and 1,017 rushing yards in seven conference games. In 1968, he set Michigan records with 2,524 career rushing yards, 19 rushing touchdowns in a season, and 139.1 rushing yards per game. Johnson played in the National Football League (NFL) from 1969 to 1975. He was the first player in New York Giants history to rush for 1,000 yards in a season, doing it in 1970 and 1972. He also led the NFL in rushing attempts in both 1970 and 1972. He retired in 1976 and was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame in 1992. In 2006, he became the chairman of the National Football Foundation. Johnson was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in 2008 and passed away in 2018. His brother, Alex Johnson, was the 1970 American League batting champion.

The Ron, Ronic, or Ron–fyer languages belong to group A.4 of the West Chadic branch of the Afro-Asiatic language family. These languages are spoken in Plateau State, which is in the north-central part of Nigeria. The Ron languages have been strongly influenced by Tarok.

Eric Peter Brewer, born on April 17, 1979, is a Canadian former professional ice hockey player who played for sixteen seasons in the National Hockey League (NHL). He last played for the Toronto Maple Leafs. Brewer was an NHL All-Star and won an Olympic gold medal. Brewer started his career as a top junior ice hockey player. In 1998, he was named to the Western Hockey League (WHL) West Second All-Star Team and the Western Conference roster for the WHL All-Star Game, though he couldn't play that game because of an injury. He was drafted by the New York Islanders in the 1997 NHL Entry Draft, picked fifth overall. Brewer played for several NHL teams: the Islanders, Oilers, Blues, Lightning, Ducks, and Maple Leafs. He also captained the Blues for two years. Brewer played for the Prince George Cougars in the WHL and the Lowell Lock Monsters in the American Hockey League (AHL). In 1999, he was chosen for the Prince George Cougars' all-time team. Brewer represented Canada in eight international ice hockey events. He won three gold medals in ice hockey world championships and one in the World Cup of Hockey. He also won an Olympic gold medal at the 2002 Winter Olympics. For this achievement, Brewer was inducted into the BC Sports Hall of Fame with his teammates in 2003.

The Creation Museum is in Petersburg, Kentucky, U.S. and is run by Answers in Genesis (AIG), a Christian organization. The museum teaches a young Earth creationist view, based on a literal reading of the Bible. It opened on May 28, 2007, at a cost of $27 million, funded by private donations. The museum has a special effects theater, a planetarium, an "allosaurus" skeleton, and an insect collection. AIG, headquartered there, has about 300 employees. Staff must agree with AIG's beliefs. The museum shows humans and dinosaurs living together, says the Earth is about 6,000 years old, and doubts evolution. Scientists and educators criticize it for inaccurate science, fearing it might harm science education. Those who support other religious views, like old Earth creationism, theistic evolution, or intelligent design, say it hurts Christianity's credibility. Many Americans believe young Earth creationism, making the museum popular. Scholars note that creationist displays lack scientific connection and are not true museums.

The Canary Islands, also called "the Canaries," are a Spanish archipelago in the Atlantic Ocean, west of Morocco. They are part of Spain's southernmost autonomous community. These islands are part of Macaronesia, a region known for its unique islands. The Canary Islands are the largest and most populated group of islands in Macaronesia. The eight main islands, from largest to smallest, are Tenerife, Fuerteventura, Gran Canaria, Lanzarote, La Palma, La Gomera, El Hierro, and La Graciosa. Smaller islands like Alegranza, Isla de Lobos, Montaña Clara, Roque del Oeste, and Roque del Este are also part of the archipelago, along with some nearby rocks. Historically, these islands were called "the fortunate isles." They are the southernmost part of Spain and are the largest archipelago in Macaronesia. The islands have been seen as a bridge between Africa, North America, South America, and Europe. In 2019, the islands had about 2.15 million people living there, with the most people living in Tenerife and Gran Canaria. The Canary Islands are famous for their beaches, climate, and natural attractions, especially in places like Maspalomas in Gran Canaria, and Teide National Park and Mount Teide in Tenerife. Teide is the third tallest volcano in the world, measured from the ocean floor. The islands have a subtropical climate with hot summers and warm winters. Different areas have different levels of rain and wind from the sea. There are green areas and deserts on the islands. Because they are above a temperature layer, the high mountains are good for watching stars. Two big observatories, Teide Observatory and Roque de los Muchachos Observatory, are on Tenerife and La Palma, respectively. In 1927, the Canary Islands were split into two provinces. In 1982, they became an autonomous community. Their capital cities are Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Las Palmas de Gran Canaria. Las Palmas de Gran Canaria has been the largest city since 1768. In 1927, the capitals were shared because the previous capital, Santa Cruz de Tenerife, was alone for too long. The third largest city is San Cristóbal de La Laguna, a world heritage site on Tenerife, which also hosts the "Consejo Consultivo de Canarias," the supreme consultative body of the Canary Islands. During the time of the Spanish Empire, the Canary Islands were a main stop for Spanish ships traveling to the Americas.

yellowcake is a type of uranium powder. It is obtained from processing uranium ore. This powder is a step in uranium processing, coming after mining and before making fuel or enriching uranium. Yellowcake is made by extracting and refining the ore. The method depends on the type of ore. Yellowcake has a strong smell, doesn't dissolve in water, and contains about 80% uranium oxide. This oxide melts at around 2880°C.

The Arctic National Wildlife Refuge (ANWR or Arctic Refuge) is in northeastern Alaska, United States. It covers a large area in the Alaska North Slope region. It is the biggest national wildlife refuge in the country, just a little smaller than the Yukon Delta National Wildlife Refuge. The refuge is managed from offices in Fairbanks. ANWR has many different types of plants and animals, such as polar bears, grizzly bears, black bears, moose, caribou, wolves, eagles, lynx, wolverines, martens, beavers, and migratory birds. These animals depend on the refuge. Just across the border in Yukon, Canada, there are two national parks, Ivavik and Vuntut.

The Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) is a group that represents the music industry in the United States. It has record labels and distributors as members. The RIAA says they handle about 85% of legally sold music in the U.S. Their main office is in Washington, D.C. The RIAA was created in 1952. At first, their job was to manage copyright fees, work with trade unions, and do research about the record industry and government rules. They set early standards like the RIAA equalization curve and the formats for different record speeds. Now, the RIAA's main tasks include: Since 2001, they have spent over $6 million each year on lobbying in the U.S. They also manage the rights of sound recordings and certify gold and platinum albums and singles in the U.S.

Deer Island is a small community in Columbia County, Oregon, United States. In 2010, it had 294 people living there. Deer Island is near Columbia City, about north-northwest of it. It has a post office with the zip code 97054.

Origin of Symmetry" is the second album by the English rock band Muse. It came out on June 18, 2001, through Mushroom Records and Taste Media. The album's title and theme are based on an idea from physicist Michio Kaku's book "Hyperspace." The album was successful in the UK. It reached number three on the UK albums chart and was certified BPI Platinum. Four singles were released: "Plug in Baby," "New Born," "Bliss," and "Hyper Music"/"Feeling Good.
Craig is a city in Plymouth County, Iowa, United States. It had 89 people in 2010. Craig became a town in Plymouth County on April 26, 1911.

Beam bridges, also called stringer bridges, are simple structures supported by an abutment or pier at each end. There are no moments transferred through the supports, making them "simply supported." The simplest beam bridge could be a log, a wood plank, or a stone laid across a stream. For modern bridges, materials like steel or reinforced concrete, or both, are used. The concrete parts can be reinforced, prestressed, or post-tensioned. These bridges include girder, plate girder, and box girder types, all of which are beam bridges. You can build them with many beams side by side and a deck on top, or with main beams supporting a deck between them. The main beams can be -beams, trusses, or box girders, and can be half-through or braced at the top to create a through bridge. Since no moments are transferred, these bridges cannot handle the thrust like arch bridges can, leading to designs such as lenticular trusses and bowstring arches. Beam bridges can have multiple simply supported spans with piers, unlike continuous spans. They are often used for short distances because they need piers for support, and the farther apart the supports, the weaker the bridge. So, beam bridges typically don't span more than a certain length. However, they can still be used to cross great distances by connecting several beam bridges, creating continuous spans.

Lupita Nyong'o, born on March 1, 1983, is a Kenyan-Mexican actress and author. She was born in Mexico City, where her father, Kenyan politician Peter Anyang' Nyong'o, was teaching. Lupita moved to Kenya when she was one year old and grew up there. She studied film and theatre in the United States, earning a bachelor's degree from Hampshire College. Lupita started her career as a production assistant. In 2008, she acted in a short film called "East River." She then starred in the TV show "Shuga" from 2009 to 2012 and wrote, produced, and directed a documentary named "In My Genes" in 2009. She later studied acting at Yale School of Drama. After graduating, Lupita got a role as Patsey in the movie "12 Years a Slave" (2013). She received good reviews and won an Academy Award for best supporting actress. She was the first Kenyan and Mexican actress to win this award. In 2015, Lupita appeared on Broadway in the play "Eclipsed," for which she was nominated for a Tony Award. She also did voice work for characters in "Star Wars" and "The Jungle Book." Her other acting roles include "Black Panther" (2018) and "Us" (2019). Lupita supports historic preservation and works for women's and animal rights. She was called the most beautiful woman by People in 2014. She wrote a children's book named "Sulwe" (2019), which became a top-selling book. She also narrated the TV series "Serengeti" and was nominated for an Emmy Award. In 2020, she was listed among Africa's 50 most powerful women by Forbes.

Carlo Caffarra was born on June 1, 1938, and died on September 6, 2017. He was an Italian church leader in the Catholic Church. From 2003 to 2015, he was the Archbishop of Bologna. In 2006, Pope Benedict XVI made him a cardinal. Before that, from 1981 to 1995, he was the president of the Pontifical John Paul II Institute for Studies on Marriage and Family. From 1995 to 2003, he was the Archbishop of Ferrara-Comacchio.

Rachel Marilyn Lloyd, born Laird on January 3, 1929, and passed away on September 19, 2018, was an American politician and businesswoman. She served in the United States House of Representatives from 1975 to 1995.

Mallemort is a small town in southern France, in the Bouches-du-Rhône department. It is near the river Durance, south of the Luberon mountains. Mallemort is not on the main motorway to the south and Marseille. However, it is close to Arles, Saint-Rémy, and Salon-de-Provence.

James Stephen Fossett, born on April 22, 1944, and died on September 3, 2007, was an American businessman and adventurer. He set world records as a solo balloonist, sailor, and fixed-wing aircraft pilot. Fossett flew solo non-stop around the world in both a balloon and an aircraft. He earned his wealth from the financial services industry and held records for five non-stop trips around the Earth: as a balloonist, sailor, and aircraft pilot. He was a member of the Royal Geographical Society and the Explorers Club, and broke three of the seven global records for aircraft, all in his Virgin Atlantic GlobalFlyer. In 2002, he received the Royal Aero Club's Gold Medal, and was inducted into the National Aviation Hall of Fame in 2007. Fossett disappeared while flying a small plane over the desert between Nevada and California in September 2007. Search efforts were unsuccessful, and he was declared legally dead in February 2008. In September 2008, someone found his identification cards in the Sierra Nevada mountains, leading to the discovery of the plane wreckage. Only two of Fossett's bones, possibly scattered by animals, were found near the crash site.

Charlie Countryman, originally called The Necessary Death of Charlie Countryman, is a 2013 American-Romanian romantic drama. Fredrik Bond directed it, and Matt Drake wrote it. Shia LaBeouf, Evan Rachel Wood, and Mads Mikkelsen starred in the film. It first showed at the 2013 Sundance Film Festival on January 21, 2013. The film also screened at the 63rd Berlin International Film Festival. In the United States, it was released on November 15, 2013. In the United Kingdom, it came out on October 31, 2014.
Termen is a town in the Brig district of the Valais canton in Switzerland.

Happy Valley Shanghai is an amusement park in China. It is in Songjiang District and is about far from downtown Shanghai. The park covers an area. It opened on August 16, 2009. This is the fourth Happy Valley theme park.

In 2003, the Pacific hurricane season had no major hurricanes – storms with high intensity – for the first time since 1977. Many tropical storms formed and affected Mexico. Two notable hurricanes, Ignacio and Marty, hit Mexico, causing 2 and 12 deaths and about $1 billion in damage. Three other storms, including two hurricanes, and three more from the Atlantic also affected Mexico. The only other significant storm was Hurricane Jimena, which went close to Hawaii, the first to threaten the island in years. The season began on May 15, 2003, in the eastern Pacific, and June 1, 2003, in the central Pacific, and ended on November 30, 2003. Usually, these dates mark when most storms form in the northeastern Pacific. A total of 16 tropical storms formed, with 7 becoming hurricanes, which is typical. Overall, the damage was about $129 million, and 23 people died from the storms.

A trauma center is a hospital ready to treat people with serious injuries from accidents, like car crashes or gunshot wounds. Sometimes, a trauma center just means an emergency room, but without special care for seriously injured people. In the U.S., a hospital can become a trauma center if it meets criteria set by the American College of Surgeons and passes a review. Each state decides officially if a hospital is a trauma center. Trauma centers are grouped into levels, with level I being the best and level III the lowest (some states have up to level V). Level I centers have many special doctors and nurses, surgery equipment, and diagnostic tools. Lower level centers can treat patients first and send them to a higher-level center if needed. Running a trauma center costs a lot, especially in places like rural areas. Patient traffic can change a lot, but different methods help manage it. Trauma centers often have landing spots for helicopters. People hurt far away can get better care faster by helicopter than by ambulance to a nearby hospital. The level of trauma care can greatly affect a patient's recovery and whether they need to go to a better center.

Panphagia is a genus of sauropodomorph dinosaur described in 2009. It lived about 231 million years ago, during the Carnian age of the Late Triassic period in what is now northwestern Argentina. Fossils were found in the La Peña member of the Ischigualasto formation in the Ischigualasto-Villa Unión basin. The name "Panphagia" means "all" and "to eat" in Greek, referring to its likely omnivorous diet. Panphagia is one of the earliest known dinosaurs, and finding it is important because it might show how early sauropodomorph dinosaurs changed their eating habits.

Harry Gulkin was born on November 14, 1927, and died on July 23, 2018. He came from Montreal, Quebec, Canada. Harry Gulkin worked in films and theatre. He was also an arts director and project manager. He helped make the film "Lies My Father Told Me," which won a Golden Globe.

Stewart-Haas Racing is an American professional stock car racing team. It competes in NASCAR Cup Series, Xfinity Series, K & N Pro Series West, and iRacing Series. The team is co-owned by Tony Stewart, a three-time NASCAR Cup Series champion, and Gene Haas, founder of Haas Automation. It was founded in 2002 as Haas CNC Racing. In 2009, Tony Stewart joined the team and got 50% ownership. The team is based in Kannapolis, North Carolina, near Charlotte Motor Speedway. It has a sister team, the Haas F1 team, but operates separately for legal reasons. In the NASCAR Cup Series, Stewart-Haas Racing currently has four Ford Mustang teams: numbers 4, 10, 14, and 41. In the Xfinity Series, they have one full-time Ford Mustang team with driver Chase Briscoe. For the K & N Pro Series West, they run one Ford Mustang part-time with Aric Almirola. The Xfinity team partners with Biagi-Denbeste Racing. The team used Chevrolet engines and chassis from Hendrick Motorsports until 2016, except for a brief 2003 period when they used Pontiac. Since 2017, they've used Ford engines and built their chassis themselves. They are one of the few teams to win in all three national touring divisions.
Bernard Greenhouse was born on January 3, 1916, and died on May 13, 2011. He was an American cellist. He was also one of the people who started the Beaux Arts Trio.

Sridevi came in is an Indian Tamil drama. It stars Ananya, Nandhan, Loganadhan, Lasya Nagraj, and Meera Krishnan. This show is a remake of a Kannada serial called Lakshmi Baramma. It replaced Enga Veetu Mapillai and was on Colors Tamil from April 18, 2018, to June 28, 2019.

Ryan Zinke, born on November 1, 1961, was an American politician and businessman. He was the U.S. Secretary of the Interior during President Trump's administration from 2017 to 2019. Before that, he was a U.S. representative for Montana from 2015 to 2017. From 2009 to 2013, he served in the Montana Senate. Zinke played college football at the University of Oregon and got a degree in geology. He also has degrees in business and leadership. He was in the U.S. Navy as a SEAL from 1986 to 2008 and retired as a commander. Zinke supported using ground troops in the Middle East to fight ISIS. He did not like the Affordable Care Act and certain environmental rules. He also opposed giving state governments control over federal lands. President Trump chose Zinke to be the U.S. Secretary of the Interior. Zinke's job included making more federal lands available for oil, gas, and mineral exploration. People talked about the cost of his trips, which made some people upset. In October 2018, there was a report on a TV news program about these issues. The Department of the Interior's inspector general looked into Zinke's behavior. In December 2018, Trump said Zinke would leave his job in January 2019, with David Bernhardt taking over.
The COVID-19 pandemic was found in the Republic of the Congo in March 2020.

Ingrid of Sweden, born on March 28, 1910, and died on November 7, 2000, was queen of Denmark from 1947 to 1972. She was the wife of King Frederick IX. Born into the House of Bernadotte, Ingrid was the daughter of King Gustaf VI Adolf of Sweden and Princess Margaret of Connaught. In 1935, she married Crown Prince Frederick of Denmark and had three daughters: Margrethe, who is now the queen of Denmark, Benedikte, a princess of Sayn-Wittgenstein-Berleburg, and Anne-Marie, the former Greek queen. In 1947, her husband became king when their father died. As queen, Ingrid changed the way Danish court life was done. She got rid of many old customs and made official events more relaxed. King Frederick IX passed away in 1972, and Ingrid's daughter Margrethe became the new queen. Ingrid was also a grandmother to King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden.

Hillside Lake is a small community in Dutchess County, New York. According to the 2010 census, it had 1,084 people. It is part of the Poughkeepsie–Newburgh–Middletown, NY metropolitan area. It is also part of a larger area called the New York–Newark–Bridgeport, NY-NJ-CT-PA combined statistical area.

The Great Wave, also known as just the Wave, is a woodblock print by the Japanese artist Hokusai. It was published between 1829 and 1833 during the late Edo period. This is the first print in his series called "Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji." It is his most famous work and is often considered one of the most recognizable works of Japanese art. The image shows a very big wave threatening three boats off the coast of Sagami Bay (in Kanagawa prefecture) while Mount Fuji is visible in the background. Sometimes people think it's a tsunami, but it's more likely a large rogue wave. Like the other prints in the series, it shows the area and activities around Mount Fuji under different conditions. Berlin blue is used dramatically throughout the series.

Owls are birds from the strigiformes group, which has more than 200 species. Most owls are solitary and active at night. They have an upright posture, a big head, and sharp claws. Owls can hear and see very well. Their feathers allow them to fly silently. Not all owls fit this description; for example, the northern hawk-owl is active during the day, and the burrowing owl lives in groups. Owls mainly eat small animals like mammals, insects, and other birds. Some species catch fish. These birds live almost everywhere, except in very cold areas and some islands. Owls are divided into two families: true owls and barn-owls. A group of owls is called a "parliament."

Kenneth Gary Albert, born on February 2, 1968, is an American sportscaster. He is the son of sportscaster Marv Albert and the nephew of sportscasters Al Albert and Steve Albert. Kenneth Albert is unique because he does the play-by-play for all four major professional sports leagues in the United States and Canada: the NFL, NBA, MLB, and NHL.

Chattanooga was a pop group made up of three sisters named Mia, Ackie, and Clara Kempff from Halmstad, Sweden. They had some chart successes in the early 1980s. In 1982, they performed "Hallå Hela Pressen" at Melodifestivalen and came in fourth place. In 2004, the sisters reunited to record the song again with Nina and Kim.

The Malagasy Wikipedia is an edition of Wikipedia in the Malagasy language. It was launched in April 2004 and has articles. This makes it the 63rd largest Wikipedia by the number of articles. It has 3 administrators, 13,671 registered users, and 25 active users.
The 970s decade started on January 1, 970, and ended on December 31, 979.

A record chart, also known as a music chart, ranks songs based on certain criteria for a specific time period. Different criteria like sales, radio play, downloads, and streaming are often used together. Some charts focus on a particular music type and most are for a specific area. Charts usually cover one week, and weekly charts are used to make yearly and decade-long summaries. These weekly charts are important for measuring song success. TV and radio shows often list the top songs from these charts.
Jan Kobuszewski is a name.

Robert Deroy Windham, known as Blackjack Mulligan, was born on November 25, 1942, and passed away on April 7, 2016. He was an American professional wrestler, writer, and ex-football player. He had two wrestler sons named Barry and Kendall Windham. Mike Rotunda is his son-in-law. His daughter, Kelly, is the mother of Bray Wyatt and Bo Dallas.
Sidney Haight was born on August 21, 1847, and died on September 17, 1918. He received the Medal of Honor during the American Civil War for his actions in the Siege of Petersburg.

Antonio Tavaris Brown Sr., born on July 10, 1988, is an American football player who is currently not playing for any team. He grew up in Liberty City, Miami, and played both football and track in high school. Brown went to Miami Norland High School. He played college football at Central Michigan University. There, he was named an All-American in 2008 and 2009 as a punt returner. In 2010, the Pittsburgh Steelers picked him in the sixth round of the draft. During his rookie season, the Steelers reached Super Bowl XL but lost. In his first season, Brown had 16 catches for 167 yards in ten games. In his second NFL season, he was the first player to have over 1,000 yards receiving and returning in the same year. For this, he was chosen for the 2012 Pro Bowl as a punt returner. In 2013, he became the only receiver to have at least five catches and 50 yards in every game of an NFL season. His performance continued to be strong, leading the league in receptions and receiving yards in 2014, in receptions in 2015, in receiving yards in 2017, and in receiving touchdowns in 2018. However, his relationship with the Steelers became difficult, especially with quarterback Ben Roethlisberger. Brown asked to be traded. In 2019, he was traded to the Oakland Raiders, who made him the highest-paid receiver in the league. But his time with the Raiders was brief. He had off-the-field issues, like a fight with the team's general manager, Mike Mayock, and was released without playing in a regular-season game. Brown then signed with the New England Patriots but was released after just one game. At the time, the NFL was investigating him for sexual assault allegations.

Jan Hus, sometimes called John Hus, was a Czech theologian and philosopher. He was born in Husinec, Bohemia, in 1369 and died on July 6, 1415. He is known for reforming the church and inspiring Hussitism, which was a major influence on Protestantism. Hus was considered the second church reformer after John Wycliffe, as he lived before Martin Luther, Calvin, and Zwingli. His teachings affected the religious practices in Western Europe, leading to the creation of a reformed Bohemian denomination. He also influenced Martin Luther nearly a century later. Jan Hus came from a poor family and became a priest to escape poverty. He moved to Prague, where he earned money by singing and working in churches. He was well-behaved and very serious about his studies. After becoming a priest, Hus started preaching in Prague. He criticized many aspects of the Catholic Church, such as how they ran the church and their views on the Eucharist. When Alexander V became pope, he sided with Bohemian church officials against Hus. He excommunicated Hus, but this order was not enforced. Hus continued to preach. Later, he spoke against Alexander V’s successor, Pope John XXIII, for selling indulgences. Hus was then excommunicated again and spent two years in exile. The Council of Constance asked Hus to come and present his ideas. When he arrived, he was arrested and put in prison. He was asked to change his ideas but refused, saying, "I would not change for a chapel of gold." He was then put back in prison and burned at the stake for heresy on July 6, 1415. As he burned, Hus could be heard singing psalms. After Hus’s death, his followers, known as Hussites, refused to choose a Catholic king and defeated five papal crusades between 1420 and 1431. This led to the Hussite Wars. The Bohemian and Moravian populations stayed mostly Hussite until the 1620s. After a Protestant defeat at the Battle of the White Mountain, the Bohemian lands came under Habsburg rule and were forced to convert back to Catholicism.
Browning is a village in Schuyler County, Illinois, United States. The 2000 census showed 130 people lived there.

megaraptor, meaning "giant thief," is a type of large dinosaur from the theropod group. It lived during the late Cretaceous period, specifically in the Turonian and Coniacian ages. Fossils have been found in the Portezuelo formation in Argentina. Initially, scientists believed it was similar to a giant dromaeosaur-like coelurosaur. However, more recent studies and discoveries of related dinosaurs placed megaraptor either as a basal tyrannosauroid or a basal coelurosaur.
Los Osos is a place along the Pacific coast in San Luis Obispo County, California. It uses zip codes 93402 and 93412, and the phone area code is 805. In 2010, the population was 14,276.
Most of the 35 streams are small and don't last all year. They get water from melting snow until late April. Some are just winter streams that dry up in the summer.

The Arc de Triomphe de l'Étoile is a famous monument in Paris, France. It stands at the western end of the Champs-Élysées, at the center of Place Charles de Gaulle, formerly called Place de l'Étoile. This place is in three parts of Paris: the 16th, 17th, and 8th arrondissements. The monument honors French soldiers who fought and died in the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars. Names of victories and generals are on its insides and outsides. Beneath it lies the grave of a soldier from World War I. This monument is part of the "historic axis," a line of important places and big streets running from the Louvre courtyard to the Grande Arche de la Défense. The Arc de Triomphe was designed by Jean Chalgrin in 1806. It has statues of young French men against German warriors and shows a message of victory and patriotism. Inspired by the Arch of Titus in Rome, it is 50 meters high, 45 meters wide, and 22 meters deep. In 1919, a pilot flew his plane under it to celebrate the end of World War I. The Arc de Triomphe was the tallest triumphal arch until 1938 when Mexico City's Monumento a la Revolución became taller. In 1982, North Korea built a similar arch in Pyongyang, which is slightly taller. Near Paris, the Grande Arche in La Défense is 110 meters high, even though it's not called an Arc de Triomphe.
founex is a town in the district of nyon, which is in the canton of vaud, in Switzerland.
A carapace is the upper part of the hard outer shell in animals like crustaceans, arachnids, and turtles. In turtles and tortoises, the bottom part is called the plastron.
