Giza governorate is one of Egypt's governorates. It is in the center of the country, on the west bank of the Nile River, opposite Cairo. The capital is the city of Giza. It includes land on the left bank of the Nile Valley around Giza and part of Egypt's western desert, including Bahariya Oasis. On April 14, 2011, the 6th of October governorate joined it. The Giza governorate has the Great Sphinx and the Pyramids of Giza.

José Vítor Roque Jr., also known as Roque Júnior, was born on August 31, 1976, in Santa Rita do Sapucaí. He played as a defender in association football. Roque Júnior last played for Ituano Futebol Clube. He represented Brazil 48 times and was part of the team that won the 2002 World Cup.

In computer architecture, 64-bit integers, memory addresses, or data units are 64 bits wide. A 64-bit CPU and ALU use registers, address buses, or data buses of that size. 64-bit microcomputers use 64-bit microprocessors. From a software perspective, 64-bit computing means using code with 64-bit virtual memory addresses. However, not all 64-bit instruction sets support full 64-bit virtual memory addresses; for example, x86-64 and ARMv8 support only 48 bits of virtual address. 64-bit processors became common in supercomputers since the 1970s, like the Cray-1 in 1975, and in workstations and servers since the early 1990s, such as MIPS R4000, DEC Alpha, Sun UltraSPARC, and IBM Power3 and later Power microprocessors. In 2003, 64-bit processors were introduced to mainstream personal computers with x86-64 and PowerPC G5. ARMv8 targeting smartphones and tablets came in 2012, first in the iPhone 5s in 2013. A 64-bit register can hold 2 different values. For unsigned numbers, the range is from 0 to 18,446,744,073,709,551,615. For two's complement, it's from -9,223,372,036,854,775,808 to 9,223,372,036,854,775,807. Thus, a processor with 64-bit memory addresses can access 2 bytes (16 exabytes) of memory. Generally, a 64-bit computer architecture has 64-bit registers for data types and addresses. However, a CPU may have different sizes for external data or address buses. The term can also refer to the size of low-level data types, like 64-bit floating-point numbers.
La Chapelle is a town in the Allier region of central France.

Grono is a municipality in the Moesa region. It is in the part of the Swiss canton of Graubünden where people speak Italian. On January 1, 2017, the towns of Leggia and Verdabbio became one municipality called Grono.

La Riviera is a census-designated place in Sacramento County, California, United States. It is part of the Sacramento–Arden-Arcade–Roseville metropolitan area. The population was 10,802 in 2010, an increase from 10,273 in 2000. La Riviera is mainly a residential neighborhood situated between the American River to the north and Highway 50 to the south.

Glenn Franklin Howerton III, born on April 13, 1976, is an American actor. He was born in Japan. Glenn is known for his role as Dennis Reynolds in the TV show "It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia." He also writes for and produces this show. In another show, "A.P. Bio," he plays Jack Griffin. He had a lead role in a sitcom called "That '80s Show."

Birdbrook is a village and civil parish in Essex, England. It is about southeast of Haverhill, Suffolk. The village is 34 kilometers (21 miles) north of Chelmsford, the county town. Birdbrook is in the Braintree district and part of the Saffron Walden parliamentary constituency. It belongs to the Bumpsteads and Upper Colne parish cluster. The village is 93 meters above sea level. In 2011, it had 397 people living there. There is a pub called "The Plough" and a church named "St Augustine of Canterbury." Nearby is Moyns Park, an Elizabethan country house listed as Grade I. Legend has it that Ian Fleming wrote part of his book "From Russia, with Love" there.

The Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI) was a plan to create a missile defense system for the United States. President Ronald Reagan announced it on March 23, 1983. He wanted to protect the country from attacks by nuclear missiles. Reagan said MAD, or mutually assured destruction, was a "suicide pact" and called for scientists and engineers to develop something that would make nuclear weapons useless. In 1984, the SDI organization was set up in the U.S. Department of Defense to lead the development. Many advanced weapon ideas were studied, including lasers, particle beams, and missile systems in space and on the ground. These ideas needed sensors, command centers, and powerful computers to control. Many of these ideas were tested in the late 1980s, and some projects continued. The SDI's science and technology office, led by physicist Dr. James Isonson, mainly invested in basic research at national labs, universities, and companies. This funding helped many scientists in areas like high-energy physics and supercomputing. In 1987, the American Physical Society said the technologies needed were still decades away. This led to cuts in SDI's budget. By the late 1980s, the project focused on the "Brilliant Pebbles" idea—small orbiting missiles like air-to-air missiles. This was cheaper to develop. SDI was controversial. Some people feared it might destabilize MAD and cause another arms race. With the end of the Cold War and reduction in nuclear weapons, support for SDI faded. In 1993, the Clinton administration changed the focus to theater ballistic missiles and renamed the organization the Ballistic Missile Defense Organization (BMDO).

Michael Joseph Mansfield, born on March 16, 1903, and died on October 5, 2001, was an American politician and diplomat. He was a Democrat and served as a US Representative from 1943 to 1953. Mansfield was also a US Senator from Montana from 1953 to 1977. He was the longest-serving Senate Majority Leader, from 1961 to 1977. During his time as Majority Leader, he helped pass the Great Society programs and later criticized the Vietnam War. Mansfield was born in Brooklyn but grew up in Great Falls, Montana. During World War I, he joined the US Navy by lying about his age. After the war, he taught history and political science at the University of Montana. In 1942, he joined the House of Representatives and served on the House Committee on Foreign Affairs during World War II. In 1952, Mansfield won an election to become a US Senator, defeating the Republican incumbent. From 1957 to 1961, he was Senate Majority Whip. After Lyndon B. Johnson left the Senate to become Vice President, Mansfield became Senate Majority Leader. In the later years of the Vietnam War, he started opposing the war and supported President Nixon's plans to involve Vietnamese troops. After retiring from the Senate, Mansfield became the US Ambassador to Japan from 1977 to 1988. He was given the Presidential Medal of Freedom upon retirement. Mansfield is the longest-serving American Ambassador to Japan. After his ambassadorship, he worked as a senior advisor on East Asian affairs for Goldman Sachs.

Jacques Marquette, a Jesuit missionary, was born on June 1, 1637, and died on May 18, 1675. He is sometimes called Père Marquette or James Marquette. He was from France and America. Marquette founded the first European settlement in Michigan, called Sault Ste. Marie. Later, he founded another settlement in Michigan, named St. Ignace. In 1673, Marquette and Louis Jolliet, an explorer from Quebec City, were the first Europeans to explore and map the northern part of the Mississippi River valley.

Ruy Alexandre Guerra Coelho Pereira, born on August 22, 1931, is a film director and screenwriter from Portugal and Brazil. He was born in Lourenço Marques, which is now called Maputo. At the time, it was still a Portuguese colony.

Tim Francis, born on May 1, 1928, and passed away on January 2, 2016, was a New Zealand diplomat. He worked as the permanent representative to the United Nations from 1978 to 1982. From 1988 to 1991, he served as the ambassador to the United States. Between 1984 and 1988, he managed Tokelau.

Arthur Garfunkel, born on November 5, 1941, is an American singer, poet, and actor. He is famous for working with Paul Simon in the folk rock duo Simon & Garfunkel. As a solo artist, his biggest hits include three top 20 songs, six top 40 songs, and two UK number one hits. He also won a People's Choice Award. Garfunkel has received eight Grammy Awards, including a lifetime achievement award. Simon and Garfunkel were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1990. In 2008, Garfunkel was ranked 86th on Rolling Stone's list of the 100 greatest singers of all time.

La Bañeza is a town in the province of León, in Castile and León, Spain. In 2010, it had 11,050 people living there. It is the capital of the Tierra de La Bañeza region. During Roman times, it was part of the Astur conventus area. The town was founded in the 9th century by Count Gatón, who joined two small villages, San Pedro de Périz and Bani Eiza. In the 1890s, a marquis lived there. In 1896, a railroad arrived, leading to changes. In 1895, Queen Regent Maria Cristina of Austria gave the town city status. Important buildings include the churches of San Salvador and Santa María. The town has many celebrations, like carnival, Holy Week, and August festivities, which include a motorcycle race. This race is called the La Bañeza Grand Prix. These events make La Bañeza a great place for tourism.

The Germanic languages are part of the Indo-European language family. They are spoken by about 515 million people mainly in Europe, North America, Oceania, and southern Africa. The most widely spoken Germanic language is English, with about 2 billion speakers. All Germanic languages come from a common ancestor called Proto-Germanic, spoken in Scandinavia during the Iron Age. The West Germanic languages include English, with around 360-400 million native speakers; German, with over 100 million; and Dutch, with 24 million. Other West Germanic languages are Afrikaans (7.1 million), Low German (0.3 million with 6.7-10 million understanding it), Yiddish (1.5 million), Scots (1.5 million), Limburgish (1.3 million), and Frisian languages (0.5 million). The North Germanic languages are Danish, Norwegian, and Swedish, each with about 20 million native speakers and 5 million second language speakers. Faroese and Icelandic are more conservative with less influence from Low German. The East Germanic languages, like Gothic, Burgundian, and Vandalic, are now extinct. Proto-Germanic had unique features, such as Grimm's law. Germanic tribes moved to northern Germany and southern Denmark around the 2nd century BC.

Millry is a town in Washington County, Alabama, United States. It became a town in 1947. In 1950, official records showed it had 546 people. In 2000, it had 615 people. By 2010, the population decreased to 546.

György Sándor Ligeti (28 May 1923 – 12 June 2006) was a composer from Hungary and Austria. He is known as one of the most important avant-garde composers of the latter half of the 20th century and one of the most innovative and influential composers of his time. Born in Transylvania, Romania, he lived in Hungary before moving to Austria in 1956. In 1968, he became an Austrian citizen. In 1973, he became a professor of composition at the Hamburg Hochschule für Musik und Theater and taught there until 1989. Ligeti was not able to fully develop his avant-garde music style in Hungary due to restrictions by the government. After moving to the West in 1956, he could freely pursue his passion. He experimented with electronic music in Cologne and later developed micropolyphony, a technique used in his famous "Atmosphères." His work "Le Grand Macabre" was an "anti-anti-opera," and he later focused on polyrhythm. Ligeti is best known for his music used in film soundtracks. While he did not write any film scores, parts of his compositions were adapted for films. Stanley Kubrick’s films, especially "2001: A Space Odyssey," featured Ligeti’s work, which also included pieces by other classical composers.

Durrës is the second largest city in Albania and the capital of its county and municipality. Located on a flat plain near the southeastern coast of the Adriatic Sea, it has a Mediterranean climate. Durrës was founded by Greek colonists from Corinth and Corfu around 700 BC and called Epidamnos. Later, it was renamed Dyrrhachium. It grew important when it became part of the Roman and Byzantine Empires. The Via Egnatia, which continues the Via Appia, started from Durrës and went across the Balkan peninsula to Constantinople. In the Middle Ages, Durrës was controlled by Bulgaria, Venice, and the Ottoman Empire. After Albania became independent, Durrës was briefly the capital. Later, it was taken by Italy and Nazi Germany. During communism, Durrës grew in population and economy. The city has a large port that connects it to Italy and nearby countries. Durrës also has an important amphitheater, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site. This amphitheater could hold up to 20,000 people and is the largest in the Balkans.

"Raise Your Glass" is a song by American singer Pink. It's from her first greatest hits album, "Greatest Hits... So Far!!" (2010). Pink wrote the song with Max Martin and Karl "Shellback" Schuster, who also produced it. The song honors Pink's first ten years in music since her debut in 2000, and it's for her fans who have supported her all along. "Raise Your Glass" came out as the main song from the album on October 5, 2010, through Jive Records. It did very well, getting good reviews from music critics and being seen as a party song. In several countries, including the U.S., it reached the top ten, and in the U.S., it was Pink's third number-one hit. In 2011, it was ranked 13th on the "Top 40 Year End Chart" by Mediabase. The song was also used in a commercial for the 2011 movie "Bridesmaids" and in the trailers for "What's Your Number?" and "New Year's Eve".

During 1833 to 1836 and from 1845 until 2010, when the Kallikratis reform was implemented, prefectures were the main administrative units in Greece. These are now not used and have been mostly replaced by regional units. The United Nations calls them departments. Prefectures were like second-level government organizations, grouped into 13 regions or 10 geographical departments. They were further divided into provinces, which included many communities and municipalities. In 1994, prefectures became self-governing, and the first elections for their leaders were held. By 2010, there were 51 prefectures, with the Attica prefecture, home to over a third of Greece’s population, split into four smaller administrations. The Kallikratis reform abolished prefectures on January 1, 2011. Most prefectures were replaced by regional units within larger regions, which took over some of the prefectures' roles.
cotton is a commune in Calvados department, which is in Normandy region in northwestern France.

A listed building is one that has been put on a special list by Historic England in England, Historic Environment Scotland in Scotland, the Welsh government, and the Northern Ireland Environment Agency. In Ireland, buildings are checked for the National Inventory of Architectural Heritage, following a rule from the Granada Convention. However, in Ireland, the term used is "protected structure." Without special permission from the local planning authority, you can't demolish, extend, or change a listed building in England or Wales. In these areas, a national amenity society must be told about any work involving demolition. Some religious buildings in current use can avoid this rule if they follow their own permission system. Owners of listed buildings must sometimes repair and maintain them, or they might face legal trouble. When changes are allowed, owners often need to use specific materials or methods. Not all listed items are buildings; bridges, monuments, sculptures, and even some road crossings can be listed too. Ancient, military, or uninhabited structures like Stonehenge are usually scheduled monuments, protected by older laws. Cultural landscapes like parks and gardens are listed informally.

Ah, wilderness! It's a comedy written by Eugene O'Neill, an American playwright. It first showed on Broadway at the Guild Theatre on October 2, 1933. Unlike his other plays, this one has a happy ending and shows a happy family in America at the start of the 1900s. It's the only well-known comedy O'Neill wrote. The play did well during its first Broadway show and during the tours that followed. It's now a常见剧目。

Mark Dayton was born on January 26, 1947, and is an American politician. He served as Minnesota's 40th governor from 2011 to 2019. He was also a U.S. senator for Minnesota from 2001 to 2007 and Minnesota's state auditor from 1991 to 1995. Dayton is part of the Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party, which works with the Democratic Party. Dayton comes from Minnesota and is the great-grandson of George Dayton, who started Dayton's department store. After graduating from Yale University in 1969, Dayton taught and worked in social services in New York City and Boston. He worked as a helper for U.S. Senator Walter Mondale and Minnesota Governor Rudy Perpich in the 1970s. In 1978, Dayton became the Minnesota Economic Development Commissioner. That year, he also married Alida Rockefeller Messinger, from the Rockefeller family. Dayton tried to become a U.S. senator in 1982 but lost. He then worked in the Perpich administration until 1990 when he became Minnesota's state auditor. Dayton tried for governor in 1998 but lost to Hubert Humphrey III. He won a seat in the U.S. Senate in 2000 against Republican Rod Grams. As a senator, Dayton voted against the Iraq War and was the first to suggest creating a Department of Peace. In 2006, he did not run for re-election. In 2010, Dayton won the governorship of Minnesota, beating Republican Tom Emmer. Despite national Republican successes that year, he secured the position. He was re-elected in 2014 over Republican Jeff Johnson. Dayton chose not to run for a third term in 2018, leaving office in January 2019. As governor, he supported same-sex marriage and helped build U.S. Bank Stadium for the Minnesota Vikings.

In music theory, a theoretical key or impossible key has a key signature with at least one double-flat or double-sharp. Double-flats and double-sharps are usually used as accidentals. However, putting them in the key signature makes the music hard to read.

Samurai Champloo is a Japanese anime series. It was created by Manglobe. Shinichirō Watanabe was the director, Kazuto Nakazawa designed the characters, and Mahiro Maeda was the mechanical designer. This was Watanabe’s first time directing an anime TV series after the popular Cowboy Bebop. The show first aired on May 20, 2004, on Fuji TV and ended on March 19, 2005, after 26 episodes. Set in a version of Japan from the Edo period (1603–1868) with a mix of ancient and modern elements, the story follows three characters: Mugen, a free-spirited swordsman; Jin, a calm rōnin; and Fuu, a brave girl who asks them to help her find a samurai who smells of sunflowers. Samurai Champloo is similar to Watanabe’s other work, Cowboy Bebop. Both shows are well-received, mix different genres, have episodic stories, and use modern music. The English version was released in North America by Geneon Entertainment, then by Funimation. It was also shown in the UK, Australia, and New Zealand by different companies.

The Panhard VBL, also known as VBL, is a French 4x4 all-terrain vehicle made by Panhard. It comes in different versions. The vehicle combines the agility of the Peugeot P4 liaison car with protection against small arms fire, artillery fragments, mines, and NBC weapons. It was produced from 1985 to 2010. The vehicle has been used by the French army and other European, African, and Central American armies in various conflicts since the 1980s.

Carlito's Way is a 1993 American crime movie directed by Brian de Palma. It is based on novels by Judge Edwin Torres, specifically "After Hours." David Koepp wrote the script. The main actors include Al Pacino, Sean Penn, Penelope Ann Miller, and Luis Guzmán. The film tells the story of Carlito Brigante, played by Al Pacino. He is a Puerto Rican criminal who promises to change his life and retire in a peaceful place. However, his past catches up with him, and he gets involved in his old criminal activities again. The movie mostly follows "After Hours" but uses "Carlito's Way" as its title to avoid confusion with Martin Scorsese's 1985 film of the same name. Critics had mixed opinions about the film, and it didn't do well at the box office. However, it has since become a cult movie. Sean Penn and Penelope Ann Miller were nominated for Golden Globes for their performances. A prequel, also titled "Carlito's Way," based on the first novel, was released in 2005 directly to video.

neurosis is a type of mental disorder causing ongoing distress. It does not involve delusions or hallucinations. The term is not used by American psychiatrists anymore. It was removed from the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders" (DSM) in 1980, with the release of DSM-III. However, the term is still sometimes used. Neurosis is not the same as psychosis, which means losing contact with reality. It is also different from neuroticism, a part of personality described in the big five traits theory.

Samantha Anne Bee, born on October 25, 1969, is a comedian, writer, producer, political commentator, actress, and television host. She became famous as a correspondent on "The Daily Show with Jon Stewart," where she worked for 12 years and became the longest-serving regular correspondent. In 2015, she started her own show called "Full Frontal with Samantha Bee." Bee became a U.S. citizen in 2014, keeping her Canadian citizenship. In 2017, she was named one of the 100 most influential people in the world by Time magazine.

Coriolanus is a tragedy by William Shakespeare, likely written between 1605 and 1608. It is about the life of the Roman leader Caius Marcius Coriolanus. This is one of the last two tragedies Shakespeare wrote, along with "Antony and Cleopatra." Coriolanus was a Roman general who had success against uprisings against Rome's government. After this, he wanted to be a political leader. But his personality wasn't good for popular leadership, and he was quickly removed. He then made friends with others who helped him, but this led to his downfall.

Anil Adhikari, born on May 30, 1987, and passed away on January 14, 2017, was a rapper from Nepal. People knew him better as Yama Buddha. He was one of the most famous rappers in Nepal. Some of his popular songs include "Sathi," "Aama," "Aaudai Chhu Ma," "Yo Prasanga," and "Antya ko Suruwat." He created and hosted a popular rap battle show called "Raw Barz."

In telecommunications, dirty paper coding (DPC) is a method to send digital information effectively through a channel with known interference. It works by changing the data before sending it to cancel out the interference. DPC can reach the channel's maximum capacity without extra power and without the receiver needing to know about the interference. The term "dirty paper coding" comes from Max Costa’s idea. He compared it to writing a message on a paper with random dirt or ink stains. By carefully erasing and adding ink in the right places, the writer can still convey the same information as if the paper were clean, even though the reader doesn't know where the dirt was. In this example, the paper is the channel, the dirt is interference, the writer is the transmitter, and the reader is the receiver. At the sender, DPC is like the opposite of Wyner-Ziv coding at the receiver.

An atlas is a group of maps. Traditionally, atlases are books, but now they can be in other formats too. Maps in atlases show places and where countries are. They also include information about people, religion, money, and other facts about different areas. This information helps explain the maps and the places shown.

Humayun Ahmed (born on November 13, 1948, and died on July 19, 2012) was a writer from Bangladesh. He wrote novels, plays, screenplays, made films, wrote songs, and taught. His first novel, "Nondito Noroke," came out in 1972 and was a hit. He wrote more than 200 books, both fiction and non-fiction, which were very popular in Bangladesh. His books were the top sellers at the Ekushey Book Fair in the 1990s and 2000s. In 1981, he won the Bangla Academy Literary Award, and in 1994, he got the Ekushey Padak for his work on Bengali literature. In the early 1990s, he started making films based on his novels. He directed eight films and won six Bangladesh National Film Awards. He also had his own film company called Nuhash Chalachitra.

Defunctland is a YouTube web series that continues to run. It tells the history of closed amusement parks and rides. The show is made and hosted by Kevin Perjurer. It focuses on the history and end of theme parks, especially those from Disney, Universal, and Six Flags. It started on February 15, 2017. People praise it for its thorough research and good production quality. The channel has more than 700,000 subscribers. The success of Defunctland led to two spin-offs: Debunkedland and DefunctTV. Both premiered in 2018.

Mexican Americans are people with full or partial Mexican ancestry living in the United States. By July 2018, about 37 million people in the U.S. had some Mexican background, making up 11.3% of the population. Mexican Americans made up 61.9% of all Latinos in the U.S. Many live in the Southwest, especially in California and Texas, where over 60% of Mexican Americans reside. Mexicans are the largest group of foreign-born people in the U.S., accounting for 25% of the foreign-born population as of 2017. The U.S. has the second-largest Mexican community in the world, after Mexico itself, and includes more than 24% of the world’s Mexican-origin population. Mexican American families with Native American heritage have been in the U.S. for at least 15,000 years. Mestizo Mexican American history goes back over 400 years, to the 1598 founding of Spanish New Mexico. Many historically Hispanic populations in the Southwest eventually switched to English as their main language. About 10% of current Mexican Americans are descendants of early settlers who became U.S. citizens in 1848 through the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. Although the treaty made most Mexican Americans officially white, they faced and still face discrimination. Indigenous Mexican Americans, such as Pueblo, did not get citizenship until the 1920s. The U.S. often did not honor the property rights of formerly Mexican citizens in line with the treaty. Large-scale migration, especially after the 1910 Mexican Revolution, added to this original population. During the Great Depression, many Mexican Americans were deported, affecting up to two million people. The federal government allowed state and local governments to deport citizens without due process. About 85% of those deported were U.S. citizens, with 60% being born in the U.S. The population became more homogeneous and politically active during the New Deal and World War II, including the Bracero program. The 1965 Delano grape strike, led by mostly Filipino American farmworkers, turned into an intersectional struggle when Dolores Huerta and César Chávez joined the strikers. Their slogan "Sí, se puede" (Yes, we can) became a rallying cry for the Chicano Movement, aimed at civil rights reforms. The Chicano Walkouts in 1968 are seen as marking the more radical phase of the movement. Migration from Mexico increased in the 1980s and 1990s, peaking in the mid-2000s. In 2008, "Sí, se puede" was used in Barack Obama's campaign, highlighting the growing importance of the Mexican American vote. The Great Recession led to a significant loss of wealth among Mexican Americans, and immigration from Mexico decreased. Both parties failed to enact proper immigration reform, leading to increased polarization among an increasingly diverse population. In 2015, the U.S. admitted 157,227 Mexican immigrants, and by November 2016, 1.31 million Mexicans were waiting to immigrate legally.

Louis-Philippe I (born October 6, 1773 – died August 26, 1850) was the king of France from 1830 to 1848 and the last king. Before that, he was called Duke of Chartres. He fought in the revolutionary wars and later disagreed with the Republic because they executed King Louis XVI. In 1793, he went to Switzerland after a plan to bring back the king's rule failed. His father, Duke of Orléans, was also in trouble and was killed. Louis-Philippe stayed away from France for 21 years until the Bourbon family returned to power. In 1830, after his cousin Charles X had to stop being king, Louis-Philippe became king. His rule, known as the July Monarchy, had rich business people and bankers as important people. He was a conservative leader, especially when French statesman François Guizot was helping him from 1840 to 1848. Louis-Philippe made friends with Britain and expanded France's control in other countries, like Algeria. As France's economy got worse in 1847, people stopped liking him. He lost his job when the French Revolution of 1848 started. He spent the rest of his life in the United Kingdom. People who liked him were called Orléanists, while those who supported the Bourbon family were called Legitimists.

The Orient Express was a long-distance train service created in 1883 by a company called Compagnie Internationale des Wagons-Lits. The route and trains changed many times. In the past, different routes used the name Orient Express or similar names. The original Orient Express was just a regular international train service, but the name became famous for being mysterious and fancy. The cities Paris and Istanbul were the main stops for the scheduled service. The Orient Express offered luxury and comfort when traveling was still tough. In 1977, the train stopped going to Istanbul. The next train, running from Paris to Bucharest, then Budapest, and finally to Vienna, stopped in 2007. In 2007, a shorter train started from Strasbourg. It left Strasbourg at 10:20 PM and joined an overnight train from Amsterdam to Vienna. On December 14, 2009, the Orient Express stopped completely. A private train called Venice-Simplon Orient Express, run by Belmond, still operates. This train uses old carriages from the 1920s and 1930s and runs from London to Venice and other European cities, including parts of the original Paris to Istanbul route.

The University of Houston (UH) is a public research university in Houston, Texas. It is the main institution of the University of Houston System. Founded in 1927, UH has over 46,000 students and is one of the largest universities in Texas. Its campus covers 667 acres in southeast Houston. From 1983 to 1991, it was called University of Houston–University Park. UH is a top research university with over 282 degree programs. It has 14 academic colleges. The university offers degrees in architecture, law, optometry, and pharmacy. UH does $150 million in research each year. It has over 40 research centers and institutes. Research covers areas like superconductivity, space commercialization, biomedical sciences, energy, natural resources, and artificial intelligence. More than 9,000 degrees are awarded each year, and UH has over 260,000 alumni. The university has a big impact on the economy, adding over $3 billion annually and creating about 24,000 jobs. UH hosts many events like theater performances, concerts, and lectures. It has over 400 student organizations and 17 sports teams. Some key events include Cat's Back, Homecoming, and Frontier Fiesta. UH’s sports teams, known as the Houston Cougars, are part of the American Athletic Conference. They compete in all sports at the NCAA Division I level. The football team often plays in bowl games. The men's basketball team has made 21 NCAA tournament appearances, including five final fours. The men's golf team has won 16 national championships, the most in NCAA history.

Ikaalinen is a town in Finland and part of the Pirkkamaa region. It has about 20, 000 people and covers an area with 10% water. The nearest municipalities are Hämeenkyrö, Jämijärvi, Kankaanpää, Parkano, Sastamala, and Ylöjärvi. Ikaalinen is a Finnish-speaking town. Part of the Seitseminen National Park is in Ikaalinen. It is an old tourist place known for its spa and accordion music. The town is famous for its beautiful landscape. In recent decades, Ikaalinen became a service center with good business, education, and recreation. Today, most people (55%) work in services, and 15% in agriculture, which is important. S. Albert Kivinen, a professor, is famous for his horror stories. His most famous work is set in Ikaalinen. Ikaalinen became a municipality in 1641, a market town in 1858, and a town in 1977. Its center is near Lake Kyrösjärvi, close to highway 3. The biggest factories are UPOFloor, Georgia Pacific Paper, E Avenue, and Katsa.

In 1972, the American Broadcasting Company (ABC) created the term "after-school special." These were TV films usually shown late afternoon, meant for school-age kids, especially teenagers. ABC aired such specials four to six times a year, replacing local programming. CBS had its "CBS Afternoon Playhouse," later called "CBS Schoolbreak Special." It also broadcast "Famous Classic Tales," which showed Australian cartoons based on books. NBC offered after-school programs under "Special Treat." ABC had its own "ABC After-school Special," as well as "ABC Saturday Superstar Movie" and "ABC Weekend Special."
Coyolles is a commune in the Aisne department, which is in Hauts-de-France in northern France. Before the French Revolution, Coyolles was the center of the deanery of the Diocese of Soissons.

Bisma Karisma, born on November 27, 1990, in Bandung, is known for being a member of the boy band SM*SH. Before joining SM*SH, she was a national b-boy and played the drums, percussion, and sang. With SM*SH, she has released two albums and achieved over forty awards. Their first album sold over a million copies in six months and was awarded platinum. In mid-2014, Bisma started his solo career with the single "Lakukanlah." He wrote and composed the song himself. In 2016, Bisma was part of the TV soap opera Cinta Cenat Cenut with his SM*SH bandmates. He also became a co-producer, wrote the original soundtrack, and was one of the main actors in the show Juara.

"Troublemaker" is a song by English singer Olly Murs, released in 2012 as the first single from his album "Right Place Right Time." It features American rapper Flo Rida. The song was written by Murs, Steve Robson, Claude Kelly, and Flo Rida. It was produced by Robson. The song was first played on Capital FM radio on October 8, 2012, and could be bought on October 12 in some countries. "Troublemaker" was very successful. In the UK, it was the top song when it came out, making it Murs's fourth solo number-one hit and his first to stay at number one for more than a week. It was also the last song played at Murs's 2013 arena tour. By November 2016, it was Murs's best-selling single.
Montord is a town in the Allier region of central France.

Mohammed Aamir Hussain Khan, born on March 14, 1965, is an actor, director, filmmaker, and TV talk-show host in India. He has been active in Hindi films for over thirty years and is one of the most popular and influential actors in Indian cinema. Khan has a large global following, especially in India and China, and was named "the biggest movie star" by Newsweek. He has received many awards, including nine Filmfare Awards, four National Film Awards, and an AACTA Award. The Indian government honored him with the Padma Shri in 2003 and the Padma Bhushan in 2010. In 2017, he was given an honorary title by the Chinese government. Khan has been listed among the 500 most influential Muslims worldwide for many years. Khan began his acting career as a child in the film "Yaadon ki Baaraat" in 1973. As an adult, his first major role was in the film "Holi" in 1984. He gained recognition in the tragic romance "Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak" in 1988 and in the thriller "Raakh" in 1989, which earned him a National Film Award. In the 1990s, Khan acted in several successful films like "Dil" (1990) and "Raja Hindustani" (1996), for which he won a Filmfare Award for best actor. He also starred in "Sarfarosh" (1999). In 1999, Khan started his own production company, "Aamir Khan Productions." His first film, "Lagaan" (2001), was nominated for an Academy Award and won him a National Film Award and two more Filmfare Awards. After a four-year break, he returned with successful films like "Fanaa" (2006) and "Rang De Basanti" (2006). Khan directed and acted in "Taare Zameen Par" (2007), which was a big success. His films like "Ghajini" (2008), "3 Idiots" (2009), "Dhoom 3" (2013), "PK" (2014), and "Dangal" (2016) were very popular, often dealing with social issues. "Secret Superstar" (2017) was the highest-grossing film with a female lead. Khan won a Filmfare Award for best actor for his role in "Dangal." Khan is known for using his films to address social issues in India. He also hosts a TV show, "Satyamev Jayate," to discuss sensitive social issues. His work as a social activist earned him a place on the "Time" 100 list of most influential people. Khan was married to Reena Dutta for 15 years and then married film director Kiran Rao. He has three children, two with Dutta and one with Rao through surrogacy.

The corn snake (Pantherophis guttatus) is a type of rat snake found in North America. It catches small animals by wrapping around them. It is common in the southeastern and central United States. People often mistakenly think it is venomous, but it does not have venom and is safe for humans. It helps control rodent pests that damage crops and spread disease. Corn snakes are gentle, do not usually bite, are medium-sized, have attractive patterns, and are easy to care for. These are why they are often kept as pets. They are called corn snakes because they often live near grain stores, where they eat mice and rats that eat corn. Some say their belly scales look like corn kernels. The name “corn snake” helps people identify them.

A Brief History of Time is a popular science book about the universe. It was written by Stephen Hawking and first published in 1988. Hawking wrote it for people who know little about the universe and want to learn more. In the book, Hawking explains the structure, beginning, and future of the universe in simple terms. He talks about basic ideas like space and time, and the smallest parts that make up the universe, such as quarks. He also explains the forces that control it, like gravity. Hawking discusses big events in the universe, such as the big bang and black holes. He explains two main theories used by scientists—general relativity and quantum mechanics—to understand the universe. Finally, he talks about trying to find one big theory that can explain everything in the universe. The book became very popular and sold over 25 million copies.

Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. They change substances called substrates into different molecules known as products. Almost all chemical processes in cells need enzymes to happen quickly enough to keep life going. Enzymes help in metabolic pathways by catalyzing individual steps. The study of enzymes is called enzymology. A new field, pseudoenzyme analysis, has developed, recognizing that some enzymes have lost their ability to catalyze reactions due to changes in their amino acid sequences. Enzymes can speed up over 5,000 types of biochemical reactions. RNA molecules that act like enzymes are called ribozymes. Enzymes work very specifically due to their unique three-dimensional shape. Like other catalysts, enzymes lower the energy needed for reactions but are not used up. They don't change the final outcome of chemical reactions. Enzyme activity can be affected by other molecules. Some increase activity, while others decrease it. Many medicines and poisons work by blocking enzymes. Enzyme activity can also be reduced by extreme temperatures or changes in pH. Excessive heat can permanently change enzymes, making them lose their structure and ability to catalyze reactions. Some enzymes are used in industry. For example, they help in making antibiotics and breaking down stains in laundry detergents. Enzymes in meat tenderizers help make meat easier to chew.

The Presidio Ahú was a prison in Curitiba, a city in Paraná, Brazil. It was the first prison built in Curitiba, opening in 1905. It closed in 2006. Now, the site is used for filming movies and TV shows.
Rachel Mary Berkeley Portman, OBE, was born on December 11, 1960. She is an English composer famous for scoring films.
Hetepheres was a queen in Egypt during the fourth dynasty, around 2600 BC.

Dr. Lo Wing-lok, JP (born September 13, 1954, died May 9, 2015) was a doctor and politician in Hong Kong. He served as a legislative councillor for the medical functional constituency from 2000 to 2004. He was the vice-chairman of the Pro-Democracy League of Social Democrats but left the party in late 2007. Dr. Lo tried to become a legislative councillor again in 2004, 2008, and 2012, but he did not win. He passed away because of lung cancer in 2015.

Cumberland is a city in Cass County, Iowa, United States. It was founded in 1884. In 2010, the population was 262. Cumberland has a sister city named Massena in Iowa.

Michael P. Botticelli, born on January 2, 1958, is an American public health official. He served as the director of the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP) from March 2014 until the end of President Obama's term. He took over as acting director after Gil Kerlikowske resigned. In February 2015, he was confirmed by the United States Senate. Before working at ONDCP, he was part of the Massachusetts Department of Public Health. After finishing his role as ONDCP director, he became the executive director of the Grayken Center for Addiction Medicine at Boston Medical Center.

Paul the octopus lived from January 26, 2008, to October 26, 2010. He was used to predict football match outcomes. He became famous after accurately predicting matches during the 2010 World Cup. During his predictions, Paul's keepers gave him two boxes with food. Each box had a team's flag. He was supposed to choose the winning team by eating from the box with the flag. His keepers mostly let him predict games involving Germany's national team. Paul was right in four out of six Euro 2008 games and in all seven of Germany's 2010 World Cup matches, including Germany's win over Uruguay on July 10. He also correctly picked Spain as the 2010 World Cup winner. Overall, he made 12 correct predictions out of 14, which is about 85.7% accuracy.

Abies nordmanniana, also known as the Nordmann fir or Caucasian fir, is a fir tree native to the mountain regions south and east of the Black Sea, in Turkey, Georgia, and the Russian Caucasus. It grows between 900 and 2,200 meters in altitude on mountains with more than 1,000 mm of rain. During the Ice Age, the Nordmann fir survived in forest refugia along the eastern and southern Black Sea coast. Despite suitable current climate conditions, the tree does not grow in areas of the eastern Greater Caucasus that are more than 400 to 500 km away from the Black Sea coast.
Randall Paul Stout was an architect. He was born on May 6, 1958, and died on July 11, 2014. He worked in Los Angeles, California.

Lisbon is a small village in Claiborne Parish, Louisiana, United States. In 2010, it had 185 people. Lisbon is east of the town of Homer, which is the parish seat. In the late 1800s, there was a school called Lisbon Academy in Lisbon. T. H. Harris, who later became the state superintendent of education from 1908 to 1940, briefly studied there. Lisbon is also where John Sparks Patton was born. He worked as a member of the Louisiana Public Service Commission from 1939 to 1944 and twice tried to become state superintendent but lost to T. H. Harris. John Sparks Patton is remembered for being the first person to suggest that school textbooks should be paid for by taxpayers.

Bad Moms is a 2016 American comedy film. Jon Lucas and Scott Moore directed and wrote it. Mila Kunis, Kristen Bell, Kathryn Hahn, Jay Hernandez, Annie Mumolo, Jada Pinkett Smith, and Christina Applegate acted in it. Filming began on January 11, 2016, in New Orleans. The film had its premiere on July 19, 2016, in New York City. It was released in theaters on July 29, 2016, by STX Entertainment. Critics had mixed opinions about it, but it earned over $183 million worldwide. It was the first STX film to make $100 million domestically. A sequel called Bad Moms Christmas came out on November 1, 2017.
Serres-Sainte-Marie is a village in the Pyrénées-Atlantiques region of southwestern France.

Respiratory diseases, or lung diseases, affect the organs and tissues that help with breathing in air-breathing animals. They include problems with the trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli, pleura, pleural cavity, and the muscles and nerves that control breathing. These diseases can be mild, like a common cold or flu, or very serious, such as bacterial pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, tuberculosis, severe asthma, lung cancer, and severe acute respiratory syndrome. The study of these diseases is called pulmonology. Doctors who specialize in treating them are called pulmonologists, chest medicine specialists, respiratory medicine specialists, respirologists, or thoracic medicine specialists. Respiratory diseases can be grouped in different ways, such as by which part of the body is affected, by symptoms, or by what causes the disease.

Charles Quinton Murphy, born on July 12, 1959, and passed away on April 12, 2017, was an American actor, comedian, and writer. He was famous for writing and being on the comedy show "Chappelle's Show" on Comedy Central. He also starred in the sitcom "Black Jesus." He had an older brother named Eddie Murphy, who was also a comedian.

Hispar Pass (also known as Hispar La) is a high mountain pass in the Karakoram range in Pakistan. It is at an elevation of 5,128 meters (16,824 feet). At this pass, the Biafo Glacier (63 km long) and the Hispar Glacier (49 km long) come together. This forms the longest non-polar glacial traverse in the world, which is 100 kilometers long.
Gurdon is a city in Clark County, Arkansas, United States. The population in 2010 was 2,212.

Brighton is a village in Macoupin County, Illinois, and a small part is in Jersey County. In 2010, the village had 2,254 people. The mayor is Michael Roberts. Brighton is in the Metro-East area and is part of the St. Louis area.

MICHIO KAKU, born on January 24, 1947, is an American physicist who talks about science and writes books. He teaches theoretical physics at the City College of New York and the CUNY Graduate Center. Kaku has written popular books like "Physics of the Impossible" (2008), "Physics of the Future" (2011), and "The Future of the Mind" (2014). He also appears on radio, TV, and in films, and writes online. Kaku has hosted TV shows for the BBC, the Discovery Channel, the History Channel, and the Science Channel.

Manuel Luis Quezon y Molina, also known as MLQ, was born on August 19, 1878, and died on August 1, 1944. He was a Filipino statesman, soldier, and politician who served as the president of the Philippines from 1935 to 1944. He was the first to lead the government of the whole Philippines, after previous states. Quezon is considered the second president of the Philippines, following Emilio Aguinaldo. During his presidency, Quezon worked to help landless farmers in rural areas. He also focused on improving military defenses, reforming the government, developing Mindanao, and dealing with foreign control over Philippine trade. He proposed land reforms and fought against corruption in the government. When the war began and the Japanese threatened to invade, Quezon set up a government in exile in the United States. He died of tuberculosis in Saranac Lake, New York, and was buried at Arlington National Cemetery until the end of World War II. His remains were later moved to Manila and are now at the Quezon Memorial Circle. In 2015, the International Raoul Wallenberg Foundation awarded Quezon and the Filipino people the Wallenberg Medal posthumously. This was for helping Holocaust victims between 1937 and 1941. President Benigno Aquino III and Maria Zenaida Quezon Avanceña, Quezon's daughter, were informed of this honor.

The chloralkali process is used to make chlorine and sodium hydroxide (lye or caustic soda) from sodium chloride solutions. This process began in large scale in 1892 and produces about 35 million tons of chlorine in one year. It involves passing an electric current through a saltwater solution, resulting in chlorine, hydrogen, and sodium hydroxide. When other salts like calcium chloride or potassium chloride are used, different products are formed. Related processes can produce chlorine and sodium metal or hydrogen and chlorine from molten salt or concentrated hydrogen chloride. The process uses a lot of electricity, around 2500 kilowatt-hours per ton of sodium hydroxide. Since equal amounts of chlorine and sodium hydroxide are made, both must be used together. For each chlorine molecule produced, one hydrogen molecule is also made. Most of the hydrogen is used to make hydrochloric acid, ammonia, hydrogen peroxide, or for energy production.

James P. Molinaro, born on March 11, 1931, is an American politician. He was the former borough president of Staten Island. Molinaro first won his election as borough president on November 6, 2001, beating his opponent, Jerome X. O'Donovan, with 50% of the votes. He became president on January 1, 2002. Molinaro won his re-election for a third term on November 3, 2009, with 62.7% of the votes. His challenger, John Luisi, received 37.3% of the votes. Luisi also challenged Molinaro in 2005.

Guangdong is a coastal province in southern China, near the South China Sea. Its capital is Guangzhou. As of 2018, it had 113.46 million people and was the most populous province in China. Its area is about 150,000 square kilometers, making it the 15th largest province. Guangdong’s economy is the largest in China and the 4th largest in the world, with a GDP of $1.47 trillion in 2018. The Pearl River Delta, an important economic zone, focuses on high-tech, manufacturing, and foreign trade. Its core cities, Guangzhou and Shenzhen, are among the most populous and significant in China, and they are now major world megacities. Guangdong had the most people in China in 2005, with 79.1 million permanent residents and 31 million migrants. Its 2010 census showed 104,303,132 people, which is about 7.8% of China’s total population. The Pratas islands, part of Guangdong historically, are now controlled by Taiwan. Guangdong’s economy is very diverse. It has been leading China’s GDP since 1989. Its 2018 GDP was $1.47 trillion, larger than Spain’s. It also hosts the Canton Fair in Guangzhou, a big trade fair. Guangdong’s culture has spread to Southeast Asia and other countries through its people's movement, influencing languages, music, food, and more. Hong Kong and Macau, two special administrative regions, are also influenced by Guangdong culture, as are Chinese communities in Singapore and Malaysia.

The Tagalog Wikipedia is the Tagalog language version of Wikipedia. It was created on December 1, 2003. As of now, it has fewer articles than the Cebuano and Waray editions. The Cebuano Wikipedia has more than 20,000 articles, while the Waray Wikipedia has more than 5,000. Most of these articles were created by a bot called Lsjbot. However, the Tagalog Wikipedia has more active users compared to the Waray and Cebuano editions. It has around 1,000 active users, while the Cebuano and Waray editions have 250 and 500 active users, respectively.

In mathematical analysis, the intermediate value theorem says that if "f" is a continuous function with the interval [a, b] in its domain, then "f" will take on any value between "f(a)" and "f(b)" at some point within the interval. This theorem has two important corollaries.
Günther Maleuda was an East German politician. He lived from January 20, 1931, to July 18, 2012. From 1989 to 1990, he was the president of the People's Chamber, which was the East German parliament.
Saint-Samson is a commune in Calvados, which is in the Normandy region of Northwestern France.

The British Rail Class 22, also known as "baby warship," were diesel-hydraulic locomotives designed for the Western Region of British Railways. They were made by the North British Locomotive Company. These locomotives looked very much like the Class 21 diesel-electric locomotives. They were called "baby warship" because of their similar appearance and internal equipment to the British Rail Class D20/2 or Class 41 "warship class." The Class 22 locomotives had numbers from D6300 to D6357.

Stara Zagora is a province in south-central Bulgaria. It was formerly known as Stara Zagora Okrug. The province's biggest city is Stara Zagora, which is the sixth-largest town in the country. Stara Zagora is the center of the province's administration and industry. As of December 2009, the province had 350,925 people living in it. The province is made up of 11 municipalities. In the southeast, near Radnevo, there is a coal mine. From 1934 to 1949, Stara Zagora province included parts of what is now Kardzhali province.
The COVID-19 pandemic was found in Rwanda in March 2020.

The Kinsey Reports are two books about human sexuality: "Sexual Behavior in the Human Male" (1948) and "Sexual Behavior in the Human Female" (1953). Alfred Kinsey wrote them with help from Wardell Pomeroy, Clyde Martin, and Paul Gebhard. The books were very popular but also caused a lot of controversy. They questioned common ideas about sex and talked about topics that people didn't usually discuss. Some people doubted the methods Kinsey used to gather information. Kinsey was a zoologist at Indiana University and started the Kinsey Institute for sex, gender, and reproduction research. The data in "Sexual Behavior in the Human Male" came from interviews with around 5,300 men over 15 years. "Sexual Behavior in the Human Female" was based on interviews with about 6,000 women. Kinsey looked at how age, money, and religion affected women's sexual behavior. He compared female and male sexual activities. His findings suggested that women were less sexually active than men. Critics said Kinsey's methods were flawed. Some said the reports might have included information from child molesters. The Kinsey Institute said this was not true but admitted men who had sexual experiences with children were interviewed. Kinsey tried to protect their identities to get honest answers, considering the seriousness of their crimes. The Kinsey Institute later said the controversial data did not significantly affect the original findings. Some later researchers think Kinsey might have overestimated same-sex attraction due to problems with his sample. However, his work is seen as groundbreaking and one of the most famous studies on sex.

Ellen Louise Axson Wilson (born Axson; May 15, 1860 – August 6, 1914) was Woodrow Wilson's first wife and the mother of their three daughters. She was from the South and her father was a minister. She was born in Savannah, Georgia, but grew up in Rome, Georgia. With an interest in art, she studied at the Art Students League in New York before marrying. She continued to create art throughout her life. From 1913 to 1914, she was the First Lady of the United States after Wilson became president. During this time, she organized weddings for two of their daughters in the White House.

Hudson Hawk is a 1991 American action comedy film directed by Michael Lehmann. Bruce Willis stars as the main character and also helped write the story and the theme song. Danny Aiello, Andie MacDowell, James Coburn, David Caruso, Lorraine Toussaint, Frank Stallone, Sandra Bernhard, and Richard E. Grant appear in the film. The movie uses cartoon-like humor with lots of funny sounds to make it silly and fun to watch. The story has conspiracy theories, secret groups, and mysterious history mixed in. Hudson and his friend Tommy sing songs at the same time but separately to keep their plans in sync. Bing Crosby's "Swinging on a Star" and Paul Anka's "Side by Side" are among the songs you can hear in the movie. In the U.S., the film didn't do well, making only $17 million and getting three Razzies, including worst picture. However, it did better in other countries, making $80 million, for a total of $97 million worldwide.
Sargodha division is a part of Punjab province in Pakistan. The capital city of this division is Sargodha. In the 2017 Pakistan census, the division had a total population of 8.18 million people.
Peter Fox, born on September 3, 1971, is a German singer, songwriter, musician, and music video director. He is also a member of the German reggae and dancehall band Seeed.

The Blue Dolphins is a 1960 children's book by American author Scott O'Dell. It's about a 12-year-old girl named Karana who is alone on an island off California for many years. The story is based on a true story about a Native American girl named Juana Maria, who was alone on San Nicolas Island for 18 years during the 19th century. The book won the Newbery Medal in 1961. It was made into a movie in 1964. O'Dell wrote a sequel called Zia, which came out in 1976. A special 50th anniversary edition of The Blue Dolphins includes a new introduction by Lois Lowry, a writer who won the Newbery Medal. It also has some pages from a book about a Spanish priest named Father Gonzalez Rubio. Another version, The Blue Dolphins: The Complete Reader's Edition, was published in 2016. This version has two extra chapters that were removed before the book was first printed.
Ahmed Salah Mohamed Hosni Hassan was born on July 11, 1979. He was an Egyptian football player who played as a striker. He is now retired.

Tori Kedar Hunter (born July 18, 1975) is an American. He played center field and right field in Major League Baseball. Hunter played for the Minnesota Twins, Los Angeles Angels of Anaheim, and Detroit Tigers from 1997 to 2015. He was an all-star five times. Hunter won nine consecutive Gold Glove Awards as a center fielder. He also won the Silver Slugger Award twice.

Coventry Cathedral, also known as the Cathedral Church of St Michael, is where the Bishop of Coventry and the Diocese of Coventry work within the Church of England. It is in Coventry, West Midlands, England. The current bishop is Christopher Cocksworth, and the current dean is John Witcombe. Coventry has had three cathedrals. The first was St Mary's, a monastic building, of which only some ruins remain. The second was St Michael's, a 14th-century Gothic church that became a cathedral but was mostly destroyed during World War II. The third is the new St Michael's Cathedral, built after the old one was destroyed.

The National Assembly of Thailand (abbreviated as NAT) is the legislative branch with two parts. It meets in Sappaya-Sapasathan in Bangkok. This assembly was created in 1932 when Thailand changed from an absolute monarchy to a constitutional one. During the 2013 crisis, the Representative House was dissolved by Prime Minister Yingluck Shinawatra. She called for elections on February 2, 2014, but these were nullified by the Constitutional Court. After the 2014 coup, a new single-chamber National Legislative Assembly was formed with military backing. In 2017, a new constitution allowed the National Assembly to be re-established, but the National Legislative Assembly stayed in place until after the 2019 general election.

Vijaya Mulay was born on May 16, 1921, and passed away on May 19, 2019. She was a filmmaker, film historian, writer, and educator. She had close friendships with filmmakers like Satyajit Ray, Louis Malle, and Mrinal Sen, which gave her a special view of Indian cinema. This influenced her work. Her films have helped shape how India is seen by filmmakers around the world. Her daughter, Suhasini Mulay, is a well-known actor who won a national award. Her son-in-law is Atul Gurtu, a high-energy physicist. Vijaya Mulay is best remembered for her animated film "Ek Anek Aur Ekta," which won the National Film Award for the best educational film.
Daniel Hicks or Dan Hicks may refer to:

Ivan Hašek, born on September 6, 1963, is a former Czech football player. He played as a central midfielder. He spent 11 years with Sparta Prague, playing in over 300 official games for the club. Later, he became its manager. Hašek also played for the Czechoslovakia national team in the 1990 World Cup. He was also the president of the Czech Football Association.
Billy used to be a commune in Calvados, which is in Normandy, France. On January 1, 2017, it became part of a new commune called Valambray.
glos is a commune in Calvados, which is in Normandy, a region in northwestern France.
Egliswil is a village and municipality in the district of Lenzburg in the canton of Aargau, Switzerland.

Katiti Aboriginal Land Trust (Katiti ALT) is a land trust for an area in the southwest of Australia's Northern Territory. It's near Petermann. This trust was created in 1980 through the Katiti Land Claim. The trust is owned by Pitjantjatjara, Yankunytjatjara, and Luritja people. The land is officially called Northern Territory portion 1818. It borders Petermann Land Trust and Uluṟu–Kata Tjuṯa National Park to the north and west. To the east and south, there are two cattle stations: Curtin Springs and Mulga Park. The town of Yulara is not part of the land trust and is between the Katiti area and Uluṟu–Kata Tjuṯa National Park. The land trust is named after Katiti, which means "Bobbie's Well." It's a natural spring located south of Lake Amadeus. It was first described by Baldwin Spencer and Francis James Gillen in 1894 during their trip to Uluṟu. In 1903, Lawrence Wells' exploration team visited the spring, and Herbert Basedow marked it on his maps as "curtyteena."

Kansas is now split into 4 congressional districts. Each district has a representative in the United States House of Representatives. The number of districts in Kansas stayed the same after the 2010 census. From 2010 to 2018, all representatives from Kansas were Republicans. In 2018, a Democrat won a seat, making the delegation 3 Republicans and 1 Democrat.

The Institute for Research on Public Policy (IRPP) is an independent, bilingual, non-profit organization based in Montreal, Quebec. Its job is to improve public policy in Canada by researching, providing insights, and helping people discuss current and upcoming policy issues. It publishes reviewed research and organizes meetings with experts, academics, policymakers, and the public to discuss policies. IRPP focuses on four main areas: Canada's changing federal community, meeting Canada's innovation challenges, income inequality, and how global trade and production are affecting the Canadian economy. The IRPP was created in 1968 by Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau. It gets funding from an endowment, contributions from federal and provincial governments, and the private sector. The endowment is managed under Canadian tax laws. Anne Mclellan is the chair of the board, and Graham Fox is the president and CEO.

Air Dolomiti S.p.A. is an Italian regional airline based in Dossobuono, Villafranca di Verona, Italy. It has main operating bases at Munich Airport and Frankfurt Airport in Germany. Air Dolomiti is fully owned by Lufthansa. The airline flies to and from Munich and Frankfurt from several Italian cities. Most of the flights use the Air Dolomiti brand and are shared with Lufthansa. A few flights keep the Lufthansa brand.
David Wayne, born Wayne James McMeekan on January 30, 1914, and died on February 9, 1995, was an American actor. He performed on stage and in movies for more than 50 years.
Janine Sutto was born in France and lived in Canada. She was an actress and comedian. She was born on April 20, 1921, and died on March 28, 2017.

Antonino Rocca, born Antonino Biasetton, was born on April 13, 1921, and died on March 15, 1977. He was an Italian wrestler in Argentina. He often teamed with Miguel Pérez. After he died, he was honored and inducted into the WWF Hall of Fame in 1995 and the Wrestling Observer Newsletter Hall of Fame in 1996.

Slim Harpo, born James Isaac Moore on January 11, 1924, and known for his stage name, was an American blues musician. He was famous for playing swamp blues. Slim Harpo was very successful and one of the most popular blues artists of his time. Some of his most famous songs include "I'm a King Bee" (1957), "Rainin' in My Heart" (1961), and "Baby Scratch My Back" (1966). The last song reached the top of the R&B chart and went to No. 16 on the US pop chart. He was called Slim because "harp" is a common nickname for the blues harmonica.

The Celtic League is a group that was started in 1961. It promotes Celtic culture and identity in Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Brittany, Cornwall, and the Isle of Man. It focuses especially on the Celtic languages in these areas. The league also supports more self-governance for these regions and aims for each to be an independent country. The Celtic League is recognized by the United Nations as a non-governmental organization.

Lake Amadeus is a big salt lake in the southwest corner of the Northern Territory of Australia. It is about north of Uluru, also known as Ayers Rock. Nearby, to the northwest, is a smaller lake called Lake Neale. Lake Amadeus is part of the Amadeus Basin, which was formed from erosion from the Petermann orogeny.

Ángela María Ponce Camacho is a Spanish model and beauty pageant winner. She won Miss Universe Spain in 2018. On June 29, 2018, she made history as the first openly transgender woman to win Miss Spain. She was also the first openly transgender contestant to represent her country at Miss Universe 2018. Unfortunately, she did not advance to the finals.
Bolivia is divided into 1,374 cantons, which are below the municipality level.
