Toffen is a town in the Bern-Mittelland district of the Bern canton in Switzerland. It is about 10 kilometers south of Bern. There is a castle in Toffen called Toffen Castle. This castle is an important historical site.

Chadwell Heath is a suburban area in northeast London, England. It's located near the border of Barking and Dagenham and Redbridge. It's about west of Romford and east of Ilford, and northeast of Charing Cross. The name first appeared in the 17th century for a settlement in Dagenham, Essex. Later, it combined with a nearby hamlet in Barking (now Ilford). Chadwell Heath railway station opened in 1864, connecting the area to central London. After World War I, the area grew as a residential suburb and was part of the Becontree estate's northern boundary. Its population density increased. Chadwell Heath became part of Greater London in 1965. The area includes Chadwell Heath Academy. A local pub is named after Eva Hart, a survivor of a notable event.

McClure is a small community in Dickinson County, Virginia, United States. It is near the McClure River and Virginia State Route 63, southeast of Clintwood. McClure used to have a post office from 1919 until July 6, 2011, but it is closed now. It still has its own zip code, 24269. People say McClure was named after a pioneer who was killed by Indians.

ʻAhoʻeitu Tupou VI (born July 12, 1959) is the king of Tonga. He is the younger brother and successor to the late King George Tupou V. His brother was not married and had no children. ʻAhoʻeitu Tupou VI was officially chosen as the heir to the throne on September 27, 2006. He worked as Tonga's high commissioner in Australia and lived in Canberra. After King George Tupou V died on March 18, 2012, ʻAhoʻeitu Tupou VI became the new king. His regnal name is ʻAhoʻeitu Tupou VI.

Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle is a 2004 American stoner comedy film. It's the first movie in the Harold & Kumar series. Jon Hurwitz and Hayden Schlossberg wrote it, and Danny Leiner directed it. In the story, Harold Lee (John Cho) and Kumar Patel (Kal Penn) decide to go to White Castle after smoking marijuana. However, they have a series of funny problems along the way. The film also includes Fred Willard, Paula Garcés, Anthony Anderson, Dan Bochart, Ethan Embry, Jamie Kennedy, Bobby Lee, Christopher Meloni, Ryan Reynolds, Shaun Majumder, David Krumholtz, Eddie Kaye Thomas, Malin Åkerman, and Neil Patrick Harris, who plays a character based on himself.

Vitis, or grapevines, is a group of 79 plant species that grow as vines. These plants mostly come from the northern part of the world. Grapevines are very important because they produce grapes for eating and making wine. The study and growing of grapevines is called viticulture. Most grapevine flowers have both male and female parts and are usually pollinated by the wind. These flowers grow in bunches called inflorescences. In many grapevine species, like the "vitis vinifera," each flower that gets pollinated turns into a grape, and the bunch of flowers becomes a cluster of grapes. Although the flowers are small, the grapes are usually big and colorful, attracting birds and animals to help spread the seeds inside. In grape growing, grapevines usually only make grapes on branches that grew from buds formed the previous year. In viticulture, this is why growers cut back the previous year's growth, keeping 8 to 15 buds on longer branches or just 2 to 3 buds on shorter branches.

Eric Walter Elst, born in 1936, is a Belgian astronomer who works at the Royal Observatory of Belgium in Uccle. He has discovered many asteroids. He is one of the top 10 people who have found the most asteroids. He made these discoveries at the ESO's La Silla Observatory in northern Chile and the Rozhen Observatory in Bulgaria between 1986 and 2009. A stony asteroid, about 6 kilometers in diameter, named 3936 Elst was named after him.

Negligence is failing to be careful in a way that expected in certain situations. It's part of a legal area called tort law, where someone can be sued for being careless and causing harm. People should be careful and think about potential harm to others or property. If someone gets hurt because of negligence, they can ask for money to make up for their loss, which can be physical harm, damage to property, mental illness, or financial loss. Laws about negligence often use a five-part model: duty, breach, cause, and damages.

Voeren is a Flemish municipality in Belgium where people speak Flemish Dutch. It has services for French-speaking people. Voeren is in the province of Limburg. It borders the Netherlands to the north and the Walloon province of Liège to the south. This makes Voeren an exclave of Flanders, meaning it is geographically separate. The name Voeren comes from a small river called the Voer, which flows through the area. Voeren became an independent municipality in 1977. On January 1, 2008, it had 4,207 people living there. The area is about 8.8 square kilometers, which gives a population density of about 477 people per square kilometer. About 25% of the people living there are foreigners, mostly Dutch nationals.
goodnight goodnight or goodnight and goodnight can mean: in music: songs called "Goodnight" in taxonomy: groups named "Goodnight"

Kelowna is a city on Okanagan Lake in the Okanagan Valley of British Columbia, Canada. It is the head office of the Central Okanagan Regional District. The city's name comes from an Okanagan language word meaning "grizzly bear." Kelowna is the third-largest metropolitan area in the province (after Vancouver and Victoria), the largest inland city, and the seventh-largest city overall in British Columbia. It is the 22nd-largest city in Canada. In 2019, Kelowna had about 217,229 people in the metropolitan area and around 142,146 in the city proper. Nearby communities include West Kelowna (also called Westbank and Westside) to the west, Lake Country and Vernon to the north, Peachland to the southwest, and Summerland and Penticton to the south.

The Mil Mi-38 is a transport helicopter made by Mil Moscow Helicopter Plant. It is also being developed by Kazan Helicopters. It was created to replace the Mil Mi-8 and Mi-17. Now, it is sold for military and civilian use. The first flight was on December 22, 2003. It was certified on December 30, 2015.

Reginald Howard White (December 19, 1961 – December 26, 2004) was an American football player. He played defensive end in the NFL for 15 seasons during the 1980s and 1990s. He played college football at the University of Tennessee and was an All-American. After two seasons in the USFL with the Memphis Showboats, he joined the NFL's Philadelphia Eagles, Green Bay Packers, and Carolina Panthers. He became one of the most awarded players in NFL history. White was a two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year, 13-time Pro Bowl player, and 13-time All-Pro. He holds the second place in career sack leaders with 198 (behind Bruce Smith's 200). He was chosen for the NFL 75th Anniversary All-Time Team, the NFL 1990s All-Decade Team, and the NFL 1980s All-Decade Team. During his career, he was known for his Christian ministry as an ordained evangelical minister, earning the nickname "the Minister of Defense." He is a member of both the College Football Hall of Fame and the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

Six Flags Discovery Kingdom is an animal theme park in Vallejo, California. It is 135 acres, or 55 hectares. The park used to be called Six Flags Marine World, Marine World, The New Marine World Theme Park, and Marine World Africa USA. It has many roller coasters and fun rides. Six Flags Discovery Kingdom has been part of the Six Flags amusement park chain since 1999.

The Usual Suspects is a 1995 movie in the neo-noir mystery genre. Bryan Singer directed it and Christopher McQuarrie wrote it. The main actors are Stephen Baldwin, Gabriel Byrne, Benicio del Toro, Kevin Pollak, Chazz Palminteri, Pete Postlethwaite, and Kevin Spacey. The story focuses on Roger "Verbal" Kint, a small-time con man who survived a ship fire with just one other person. Through flashbacks, Kint tells his interrogator a complex story about how he and his friends ended up on the boat and about a mysterious crime lord called Keyser Söze. The movie was made with a $6 million budget and was first shown at the 1995 Cannes Film Festival. It was first released in a few theaters and later got more widespread release. McQuarrie won an Oscar for best original screenplay, and Spacey won for best supporting actor. The Writers Guild of America ranked the film as having the 35th greatest screenplay of all time.

Hälleforsnäs is a small village in Flen municipality, Södermanland county, Sweden. It has about 2,000 people living there. It is located 15 km (9 miles) from Flen, 32 km (20 miles) from Eskilstuna, and 40 km (25 miles) from Katrineholm. It is about 150 km (93 miles) south-west of Stockholm. Until the early 1990s, Hälleforsnäs was a busy place because of a foundry that was built in 1659 and operated for 350 years. This foundry made cannons and exported them to the Swedish army. Later, in the early 20th century, the foundry began making radiators and stoves for regular people. From 1920 to 1980, they mainly made pipes and plumbing parts. At its peak, there were over 1,000 workers at the foundry and a few hundred people working nearby. In the 1980s, Electrolux bought the foundry and started making cooker plates. But in 1990, they closed it down. Some of the workers took over the foundry, which became an art center. Today, Hälleforsnäs has become a cultural center for the whole Sörmland area. There is now a restaurant, a herbal shop during summer, and a cheese-making company called Jurss Dairy that sells award-winning cheese on site.

Văn Cao, born Nguyễn Văn Cao on November 15, 1923, and died on July 10, 1995, was a Vietnamese composer. One of his famous works is "Tiến Quân Ca," which became Vietnam's national anthem. He is often considered one of the top three important figures in modern Vietnamese music, alongside Phạm Duy and Trịnh Công Sơn. Besides being a composer, he was also known as a poet and painter.
The vice-president of Egypt is an important official in the government.

ISONOE is a retrograde irregular satellite of Jupiter. It was discovered by a team led by Scott S. Sheppard from the University of Hawaii in 2000. It has a temporary designation. ISONOE is about 3.8 kilometers in diameter. It orbits Jupiter at an average distance of 23,833,000 km and takes 751.647 days to complete one orbit. Its orbit is tilted 166° to the ecliptic (169° to Jupiter's equator) and is in a retrograde direction. The orbit's eccentricity is 0.166. ISONOE was named in October 2002 after Isonoe, a Danaïdes from Greek mythology who was a lover of Zeus (Jupiter). ISONOE is part of the Carme group, a group of irregular retrograde moons orbiting Jupiter at a distance between 23 and 24 GM with an inclination of about 165°.

Ostabat-asme, also known as Hostavalem in the Middle Ages, is a commune in the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department of France. It was a meeting point for four routes to Santiago de Compostela. Three of these routes joined there: Paris-Tours- Poitiers-Dax, Limoges, and Moissac from Central Europe; and Genoa and Lyon. The fourth route, called the "Toulouse Way," linked Central Italy with the "Languedoc region" and the "Béarn region," passing through Lescar-Oloron to Somport in Spain. From Ostabat-asme, three routes continued towards Saint-Jean-le-Vieux at 43°09'57" N, 1°11'32" W. They passed through Larceveau-Arros-Cibits, Ainhice-Mongelos, Gamarthe, Lacarre, and Iriberry. Eventually, they led to Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port and the Spanish frontier at Roncesvalles, at 42°59'23" N, 1°20'4" W. Ostabat-asme was in the former province of Lower Navarre and is named after this region.

"Too Good at Goodbyes" is a song by English singer Sam Smith. It was written by James Napier, Tor Hermansen, Mikkel Eriksen, and Smith, and produced by Napes, Steve Fitzmaurice, and Stargate. The song came out on September 8, 2017, through Capitol Records. It was the first single from Smith's second album, "The Thrill of It All," released in 2017. The song reached number one in the UK. It was also number four on the Billboard Hot 100. In other countries, it was number one in Australia, South Africa, and New Zealand. It was in the top 10 in several countries including Belgium, Canada, Denmark, France, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Sweden, and Switzerland. It was also in the top 20 in Austria, Finland, Germany, and Spain.

Hanna Grönvall was born on December 10, 1879, in Västra Sallerup, Malmöhus County, Sweden, and died on May 22, 1953. She was a Swedish Social Democrat politician and worked as a maid from 1900 to 1934. In 1933, she joined a committee to look into domestic workers' conditions. The next year, in 1934, she became the deputy leader of the Stockholm Domestic Workers' Union. She founded the Central Committee of Domestic Workers in 1936. Hanna was also a member of Stockholm Municipality's city council for the Social Democrats.

Peter Brian Hegseth, born on June 6, 1980, is an American contributor for Fox News. He served in the Army National Guard and was the executive director of two political groups: Vets for Freedom and Concerned Veterans for America. Vets for America receives funding from the Koch brothers and supports more privatization of the VA. He was thought to lead the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs during the Trump administration, but veteran groups didn't agree. In January 2017, David Shulkin got the job instead.

Troup County is in the central part of Georgia, U.S. According to the 2010 census, its population was 67,044. The county seat is Lagrange. Troup County is part of the Lagrange, GA micropolitan statistical area. It is also included in the Atlanta-Athens-Clarke County-Sandy Springs, GA combined statistical area.

A creed is a statement of shared beliefs, often used by religious communities. An example from Christianity is "Jesus is Lord," which Saint Paul wrote about. One important Christian creed is the Nicene Creed, created in 325 AD at the First Council of Nicaea. It includes beliefs about the Trinity and is widely accepted by Christian groups. Another common Christian creed is the Apostles' Creed. Some Christian groups do not follow these creeds. Muslims use the Shahada, which means "There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is his messenger." Judaism is sometimes seen as not needing a creed, but others believe in the Shema Yisrael, which says "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one."

The University of Greenland is the only university in Greenland. It is located in the capital city, Nuuk. Most classes are taught in Danish, with a few in Greenlandic. Sometimes, lectures are given in English. In 2018, there were about 205 students, mostly Greenlandic. The university has about 14 academic staff and 5 technical-administrative employees. The small student population partly results from many Greenlandic students going to universities in Denmark.

Dr. Siti Musdah Mulia is an Indonesian women's rights activist. She is the first woman to hold the position of research professor at the Indonesian Institute of Sciences, a role she still has. She also teaches about Islamic political ideas at Syarif Hidayatullah State Islamic University. Since 2007, she has led the Indonesian Conference on Religion for Peace as its chairperson. In 1997, she was the first woman to get a Ph.D. in Islamic studies from Syarif Hidayatullah Islamic State University. From 1999 to 2007, she was a top advisor for the minister of religious affairs. As part of her work, she helped create a legal proposal in 2004 to stop child marriage and allow people of different faiths to marry. However, the minister had to stop the project due to protests. From 2000 to 2005, she led the research team of the Indonesian Ulama Council. She has written several books, including "Islam Criticizes Polygamy" (2003), "Reformist Muslimah" (2004), and "Islam and the Inspiration of Gender Equity" (2005). Dr. Mulia has received important awards, such as the 2007 International Women of Courage Award, the 2009 Yap Thiam Hien Award, and the 2009 Woman of the Year Award from the Italian government.

Palaeognathae, or paleognaths, is one of two main groups of living birds, the other being neognathae. Together, they make up the group neornithes. Palaeognathae includes five flightless bird groups, called ratites, and one group that can fly, the neotropic tinamous. There are 47 tinamous species, 5 kiwi species, 3 cassowary species, 1 emu species (another emu became extinct in recent times), 2 rhea species, and 2 ostrich species. Recent studies show that paleognaths are a single group, but the idea that flightless and flying birds come from different groups is incorrect. Tinamous evolved from flightless ancestors. Three groups of extinct birds—lithornithiformes, dinornithiformes (moas), and aepyornithiformes (elephant birds)—are definitely part of palaeognathae. Some other extinct birds may also be part of this group, but scientists are not sure. The name "paleognath" comes from the ancient Greek words for "old jaws," referring to the simpler jaw structure in these birds. Despite having some basic features, paleognathae birds are not living fossils; their DNA continues to evolve at the same rate as other bird groups under similar pressures. Scientists are still debating the exact relationship and evolution of these birds.

Vermilion is a city in Ohio, near Lake Erie. It is about 35 miles west of Cleveland and 17 miles east of Sandusky. In 2010, it had 10,594 people. Part of Vermilion in Lorain County is in the Cleveland-Elyria-Mentor area. The part in Erie County is in the Sandusky micropolitan area. Both parts are in the larger Cleveland-Akron-Canton area.

In computing, a parallel port is a type of connection for attaching devices to a computer. It sends data using multiple lines at once, compared to serial ports that use just one line. This makes parallel ports larger and requires more lines in the cables and connectors. There are different types of parallel ports, but the term is most often used for the printer port or Centronics port on personal computers from the 1970s to the 2000s. It was a standard for many years and was officially standardized as IEEE 1284 in the late 1990s, defining enhanced and extended capability versions. Today, the parallel port is almost gone because USB and network printing with Ethernet or Wi-Fi are more common. Initially called the parallel printer adapter on IBM PC-compatible computers, it was mainly used for printers with IBM's eight-bit ASCII characters, but could also connect other devices. Modern printers and other devices now use different ways to connect to the computer.

Dexter in the Dark is a 2007 book by Jeff Lindsay. It is the third book in the Dexter series. The first book, Darkly Dreaming Dexter, came out in 2004 and later turned into a TV show called Dexter. The second book, Dearly Devoted Dexter, was published in 2005. Dexter in the Dark was released in the United States on September 18, 2007, and in the United Kingdom on October 3, 2007. The book was supposed to come out earlier that year. The first two chapters of Dexter in the Dark can be seen on a computer when you watch the first season DVD of the TV show.

Jorge Zavala Baquerizo was an Ecuadorian politician born on May 13, 1921, and he passed away on May 9, 2014, in Guayaquil, Ecuador, at the age of 92. He was Vice President of Ecuador from 1968 to 1970 during José María Velasco Ibarra's presidency. Zavala was also President of the National Congress from 1987 to 1988. He belonged to the Democratic Left party.

New Year marks the start of a new calendar year. It happens on January 1 in the Gregorian calendar, which is the most commonly used calendar today. In the past, in Western Europe, New Year's Day was celebrated on different dates like March 1, March 25, Easter, September 1, or December 25. After 1582, many countries switched to January 1 as New Year's Day when they adopted the Gregorian calendar. Other cultures celebrate their New Year according to their traditions or religions, sometimes also using the Gregorian calendar. Examples include Chinese New Year, Islamic New Year, the traditional Japanese New Year, and Jewish New Year. In some countries, like India, New Year is celebrated on various dates.
Francisco Fernández can be about: Francisco Fernández (person 1) Francisco Fernández (person 2)

Romain Rolland was born on January 29, 1866, and died on December 30, 1944. He was a French writer who wrote plays, novels, and essays. He also studied art history and had spiritual beliefs. In 1915, he won the Nobel Prize for Literature. He was an important supporter of Stalin in France. Rolland also had a close relationship with and influenced Sigmund Freud.
Caucasian can mean: People with light skin, typically from Europe or parts of Asia.

A railway brake is used on train cars to slow down the train, control speed going downhill, or keep the train stationary when parked. The basic idea is similar to brakes on cars, but they are more complex because they need to manage many connected cars. They must also work even when the train engine isn't running. Clasp brakes are one type of brake used on trains.

M*A*S*H is an American media franchise with novels, a film, TV shows, and other properties. It is owned by 20th Century Fox (now 20th Century Studios) and is based on Richard Hooker's semi-autobiographical fiction. The story features a group of fictional characters at the fictional "4077th M*A*S*H," a mobile army surgical hospital during the Korean War. The 1970 film and the TV series "M*A*S*H" both have a main character named Hawkeye Pierce. Later spin-offs focus on characters from the series after the war ended. Most shows mix comedy and drama, with doctors and nurses as the main characters. They find ways to laugh and have fun to cope with their work and the war. The franchise ended with the show "Trapper John, M.D." in 1986. Many people still like the series, and the movie and TV seasons are popular on DVD.

extinction means a type of living thing or a group of living things disappears completely. We usually consider a species extinct when the last individual dies. However, sometimes breeding and recovery might stop before the last one dies. Determining exactly when a species goes extinct can be hard, and we often figure it out after the event. Most species that have ever lived on Earth are now extinct. Scientists believe over 99 percent of all species, totaling more than five billion species, are no longer around. Today, we know about around 8.7 million species of eukaryotes worldwide, but the number might be much higher if we include microorganisms like bacteria. Through evolution, new species are formed when organisms adapt to their environment, and they disappear when they can't survive in changing conditions or when they face better competitors. Usually, a species lasts about 10 million years before becoming extinct. Some species, called living fossils, have barely changed for hundreds of millions of years. Mass extinctions, where many species disappear at once, are rare. However, individual extinctions are common. Recently, scientists are worried about the high rate of extinctions. Most species that go extinct are never studied. Some scientists predict that up to half of the current plant and animal species might disappear by 2100. A 2018 report suggested that erasing 300 mammal species during the human era since the late Pleistocene would take 5 to 7 million years to recover. The 2019 "Global Assessment Report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services" by IPBES found that the biomass of wild mammals has dropped by 82%, natural ecosystems have lost about half their area, and a million species are at risk of extinction—mostly due to human activities. About 25% of plant and animal species are threatened with extinction. In June 2019, one million plant and animal species were at risk of extinction. At least 571 species have been lost since 1750, likely more. The main cause of extinctions is the destruction of natural habitats by human activities, such as deforestation and turning land into farmland. A symbol (†) next to a species name usually means it is extinct.

The Boston National Historical Park shows Boston's part in the American Revolution. It became a national park on October 1, 1974. Seven out of eight sites are linked by the Freedom Trail, a walking tour in downtown Boston. All eight places are national historic landmarks. Five of the sites are not owned or run by the National Park Service. They work together through agreements made when the park was created. The National Park Service runs visitor centers in Faneuil Hall and at the Charlestown Navy Yard.

Stuart Leonard Miller (December 26, 1927 – January 4, 2015), known as the butterfly man, was a right-handed pitcher in Major League Baseball. He played for several teams: the St. Louis Cardinals (1952–56), Philadelphia Phillies (1956), New York/San Francisco Giants (1957–62), Baltimore Orioles (1963–67), and Atlanta Braves (1968). Miller had a 16-season career with a 105–103 record, 3.24 earned run average, 1164 strikeouts, and 154 saves in 704 games pitched (93 as a starter). He was an All-Star for the Giants in 1961. In 1962, Miller had his highest earned run average (ERA) since 1956, posting a 4.12 ERA in 59 games (107 innings pitched) with 5 wins and 8 losses and 19 saves. The Giants traded him to the Baltimore Orioles with Mike McCormick and John Olsino for Jimmie Coker, Jack Fisher, and Billy Hoeft after the season. Miller responded by having a strong 1963 season, leading the American League in games, games finished, and saves. He served as the Orioles' closer. His ERA was 2.24, the lowest since his rookie season. He and Leon Wagner were tied for 19th in AL MVP voting after the season. Miller finished seventh in MVP voting in 1965 with a 14-7 record, 1.89 ERA, and 24 saves. On April 30, 1967, Miller and Steve Barber combined to pitch a no-hitter for the Orioles against the Detroit Tigers, but they lost 2–1. Miller entered after Barber, who walked ten batters, gave up the tying run on a wild pitch with two outs. A ground ball to shortstop should have ended the inning for Miller, but Mark Belanger misplayed it, allowing the winning run to score. Miller was involved in a memorable moment during an All-Star game. In the ninth inning, a gust of wind caused Miller to sway, resulting in a balk, which advanced Roger Maris to second and Al Kaline to third. Later, the wind caused catcher Smoky Burgess to drop Tony Kubek's foul pop-up for an error. Miller struck out Kubek and, after Yogi Berra reached base on Don Zimmer's error, got Hoyt Wilhelm to fly out to left to end the inning. In the top of the 10th inning, Nellie Fox walked and scored all the way from first on Ken Boyer's three-base throwing error on Al Kaline's ground ball. Miller's teammates bailed him out in the bottom of the inning and made him the winning pitcher. Hank Aaron singled and scored on a double by Willie Mays, who scored the winning run on Roberto Clemente's single. On May 14, 1967, Miller gave up Mickey Mantle's 500th career home run.

Priscilla Renea Hamilton, born on September 14, 1988, is an American singer and songwriter. She is with Capitol Records. Her first album, "Jukebox," came out on December 1, 2009. She is famous for writing or co-writing popular songs like "California King Bed" by Rihanna, "Worth It" by Fifth Harmony, and "A No No" by Mariah Carey.

Mildred Ella "Babe" Didrikson Zaharias (June 26, 1911 – September 27, 1956) was an American athlete. She was very good at golf, basketball, baseball, and track and field. She won two gold medals in track and field at the 1932 Olympics. Later, she became a professional golfer and won 10 major championships. People think she was one of the greatest athletes ever.

Geoff James Nugent, born on February 14, 1977, is known as Jim Jefferies. He is an American-Australian stand-up comedian, actor, and writer. He created and starred in a TV show called "Legit" from 2013 to 2014. He also hosted a late-night show called "The Jim Jefferies Show" on Comedy Central from 2017 to 2019.

Gauri Lankesh, born on January 29, 1962, and died on September 5, 2017, was a journalist and activist from Bangalore, Karnataka. She worked as an editor for "Lankesh Patrike," a Kannada weekly newspaper started by her father, P. Lankesh. She also ran her own weekly newspaper called "Gauri Lankesh Patrike." On September 5, 2017, she was shot and killed outside her home in Rajarajeshwari Nagar. Gauri was known for criticizing right-wing Hindu extremism. She received the Anna Politkovskaya award for speaking out against right-wing Hindu extremism, advocating for women's rights, and fighting against caste-based discrimination.

In the Aztec and Nahua creation myths, there were five worlds before the current one. The Aztecs believed in four previous worlds that were destroyed by powerful gods. The present world is the fifth sun. The Aztecs saw themselves as the people of the sun. They thought they had to fight in wars to give the sun nourishment, or it would disappear. This meant offering blood and hearts to the sun to keep the universe alive.
Bank of America Tower can refer to buildings that used to be called the Bank of America Tower.
Ouanne is a town in the Yonne department, which is in Bourgogne-Franche-Comté in central France. Ouanne is also the name of a river. This river starts near the town and flows into the Loing.

Dimitar Ivanov Berbatov, born on January 30, 1981, is a former professional football player from Bulgaria. He was a striker and led the Bulgaria national team from 2006 to 2010. He is Bulgaria's all-time leading goalscorer. Berbatov was born in Blagoevgrad and started his career with Pirin, his hometown club. In 1998, he joined CSKA Sofia. In January 2001, Bayer Leverkusen signed him from Germany. He played in his first Champions League final 18 months later, as a substitute in the 2002 UEFA Champions League final, where Leverkusen lost 2-1 to Real Madrid. After five and a half years with Leverkusen, he moved to Tottenham Hotspur in July 2006, where he stayed for two years before joining Manchester United. Berbatov played in his second Champions League final in 2009, as a substitute in the 2009 final, which Manchester United won 2-0 against Barcelona. During his four seasons at Manchester United, he won two Premier League titles in 2008-2009 and 2010-2011, and also won the Premier League Golden Boot in 2010-2011. He later played for Fulham, then had spells in France with Monaco, Greece with PAOK, and India with Kerala Blasters before retiring at the end of the 2017-2018 season. Berbatov made his debut for Bulgaria on November 17, 1999, when he was 18. He played in Euro 2004, which was the only major tournament he represented his country. He captained the team from 2006 to May 2010 before retiring from international football. He scored 48 goals in 78 matches for Bulgaria. He won the Bulgarian Footballer of the Year award seven times, breaking the record set by Hristo Stoichkov.

The saying "the road to hell is paved with good intentions" means that even good ideas can lead to bad results. An alternative version is "hell is full of good ideas, but heaven is full of good actions."

Eclectic is a town in Elmore County, Alabama, United States. It became an incorporated town in 1907. According to the 2010 census, the population was 1,001 people. It is part of the Montgomery metropolitan area.

Water Stratford is a village and civil parish near the River Great Ouse in Buckinghamshire, England. It is located in the Aylesbury Vale district. Water Stratford is west of Buckingham and close to the border with Oxfordshire.

graduation is when students receive a diploma or degree. It can also include a ceremony. The day of graduation is called graduation day. The ceremony itself is sometimes called commencement, convocation, or invocation.
Love Street" is a song by the American rock band The Doors. It is on their 1968 album called "Waiting for the Sun.

This article lists the NHL teams that have played in the playoffs and won series, including Stanley Cup finals and Stanley Cup wins up to the 2019 playoffs. Teams that have never made the playoffs are listed by their first season in the league. Note: The 2004-05 NHL season is not included. Among the 31 current NHL teams, 11 have never won the Stanley Cup. The Toronto Maple Leafs have the longest drought without a Stanley Cup win, at 52 seasons. Four teams have never reached the Stanley Cup finals: the oldest is the Winnipeg Jets/Az. Coyotes franchise, at 38 seasons. The longest Stanley Cup championship drought was the New York Rangers', broken in 1994 after 53 seasons. The Toronto Maple Leafs have the current longest active drought, at 52 seasons. In 2010, the Chicago Blackhawks ended the second-longest drought at 47 seasons. This was the first of three years where one of the longest droughts was broken. The Florida Panthers have the longest active drought without winning a playoff series, at 23 seasons. The Buffalo Sabres have the longest active drought without making the playoffs, at 9 seasons. The Florida Panthers and Edmonton Oilers have the longest playoff droughts in history, at 10 seasons.

uranium-235 is an isotope of uranium found in about 0.72% of natural uranium. Unlike the main isotope, uranium-238, it can sustain a fission chain reaction. This is the only naturally occurring isotope that can do this. Uranium-235 has a very long half-life of 703.8 million years. It was discovered in 1935 by Arthur Jeffrey Dempster. When struck by slow neutrons, its fission cross section is about 584.3 barns. For fast neutrons, it's much smaller, around 1 barn. Most of the time, uranium-235 absorbs a neutron and splits into smaller parts, but some times it captures a neutron and turns into uranium-236.

Rūsiņš Mārtiņš Freivalds was a Latvian computer scientist and mathematician born on November 10, 1942, in Cēsuve. He studied at Moscow State University. Freivalds joined the Latvian Academy of Sciences in 1992. He is known for discovering Freivalds' algorithm for checking matrix products. He taught at the University of Latvia and had students like Daina Taimiņa and Andris Ambainis. Freivalds passed away from a heart attack on January 4, 2016, in Riga, at the age of 73.
Hera Hilmarsdóttir, known as Hera Hilmar, was born on December 27, 1988. She is an Icelandic actress. She began acting as a child in the 1990s. She started acting again in 2008.

A foundation, which is also a charitable foundation, is a type of nonprofit organization. Its main job is to give money and support to other charitable groups through grants. Sometimes, foundations also do charitable work directly. There are two main types: public charitable foundations, like community foundations, and private foundations, which are usually set up by an individual or a family. However, the word "foundation" can be used by organizations that don't give out public grants.

A nucleosome is the basic building block of DNA packaging in eukaryotic cells. It looks like a thread wrapped around a spool, with DNA wound around eight histone proteins. Each nucleosome includes a little less than two DNA turns and a histone octamer made of two copies each of histone proteins H2A, H2B, H3, and H4. DNA needs to be tightly packed into nucleosomes to fit inside the cell nucleus. Nucleosomes are just one part of the DNA packaging process. After nucleosome formation, DNA is further folded into more complex structures, eventually forming chromosomes. Nucleosomes can store information passed from one generation to the next through changes in histone proteins. Knowing where each nucleosome is in the DNA is important because it affects how accessible the DNA is to proteins that control gene activity. Nucleosomes were first seen in 1974 by Don and Ada Olins using an electron microscope. Roger Kornberg proposed their structure. In 1987 and 1988, Lorch et al. and Han and Grunstein showed that nucleosomes can block gene activity. Each nucleosome includes about 146 DNA base pairs wound around a histone octamer. There are stretches of DNA between nucleosomes called linker DNA. Technically, a nucleosome includes a linker region, but often it refers just to the histone core. Maps showing where nucleosomes are in the DNA are available for many organisms, including mouse liver and brain. Linker histones like H1 help pack DNA further. Without linker histones, nucleosomes look like "beads on a string" under a microscope. In sperm cells, DNA is packed differently using proteins called protamines to make it more tightly packed. Nucleosomes are found in archaea, not just eukaryotes, suggesting they are a common way to package DNA.

A gauleiter was the leader of a regional branch of the Nazi Party, similar to the head of a "gau" or "reichsgau." The word can be singular or plural, depending on the context. "Gauleiter" was the second most important Nazi Party rank, below only "Reichsleiter" and Adolf Hitler himself. During World War II, people could become a gauleiter only if directly appointed by Adolf Hitler.

Raziya al-Din, known as Razia Sultana, was a ruler of the Delhi Sultanate from 1236 to 1240. She was the first female Muslim ruler in the Indian subcontinent. Her father, Shamsuddin Iltutmish, was a Mamluk Sultan. Razia helped run Delhi when her father was away from 1231 to 1232. Her father might have thought she was good and chose her as his successor. However, he was succeeded by her half-brother Ruknuddin Firuz, whose mother planned to hurt Razia. When there was a rebellion against Ruknuddin, Razia got people to fight against his mother. She became the ruler in 1236 after Ruknuddin was removed. Some important people didn't like Razia's rule. They thought she should be just a symbol and not really in charge. They also didn't like her choosing non-Turkish people for important jobs. In April 1240, these people removed Razia from power. She married one of the people who removed her and tried to get back her throne. But in October 1240, her half-brother Muizuddin Bahram defeated her. Razia was killed shortly after.
Deer Park is a city in Hamilton County, Ohio, United States. It is a suburb of Cincinnati. In 2010, the population was 5,736.

The Jordan national under-23 football team represents Jordan in international competitions like the Olympics and Asian Games. It also plays in other under-23, under-22, and under-21 tournaments. The team is managed by the Jordan Football Association. In 2013, the Jordan Olympic team won the bronze medal in the AFC U-22 Championship in Oman.

Ganesh Chaturthi, also known as Vinayaka Chavithi, is a Hindu festival celebrating the arrival of Ganesh from Mount Kailash. People put up clay idols of Ganesh at home or in public places called pandals. The festival includes prayers, fasting, and singing. Modaka, a sweet, is offered as it is believed Ganesh likes it. The festival lasts ten days, ending with a public procession and immersion of the idols in water. About 150,000 statues are immersed annually in Mumbai. After the festival, Ganesh is thought to return to Mount Kailash with his mother Parvati. Ganesh is seen as a god of new beginnings, removing obstacles, and wisdom. This festival is observed in many parts of India, especially Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Telangana, Odisha, West Bengal, Gujarat, and Chhattisgarh. In Tamil Nadu, people celebrate it mainly at home. Ganesh Chaturthi is also celebrated in Nepal and by Hindu communities worldwide, such as in Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Malaysia, Trinidad and Tobago, Guyana, Suriname, parts of the Caribbean, Fiji, Mauritius, South Africa, the United States, and Europe. At these venues, texts are read, feasts are shared, and athletic competitions take place.

Indiana University of Pennsylvania (IUP) is a public research university in Indiana County, Pennsylvania. As of fall 2019, it had 8,279 undergraduate students and 2,079 graduate students, making a total of 10,348 students. IUP is near Pittsburgh. It is run by a local council of trustees and the Pennsylvania State System of Higher Education board. IUP has additional campuses in Punxsutawney, Northpointe, and Monroeville. The university is accredited by the Middle States Commission on Higher Education.
Vacco is a town in Mendrisio district, in Ticino canton, in Switzerland. It is the first village in the Valle di Muggio.

The 2006 Winter Paralympic Games, also called the ninth Winter Paralympics, happened in Turin, Italy from March 10 to 19, 2006. These games were the first Winter Paralympics in Italy. They were also the first Paralympics to use the new Paralympics logo.
McIntire is a city in Mitchell County, Iowa, in the United States. It had 122 people living there in 2010.

Ronald Vaughan Joyce, born on October 19, 1930, and died on January 31, 2019, was a Canadian businessman and billionaire. He co-founded the Tim Hortons doughnut chain with Tim Horton in 1964. After Tim Horton's death, Ron Joyce helped set up the Tim Hortons Children's Camps and the Tim Hortons Children's Foundation. He received many awards for his business success and charity work. In 1992, he was named a member of the Order of Canada for helping underprivileged children and youth.

The federal cabinet of Germany is the main executive body. It includes the federal chancellor and other ministers. The Basic Law of Germany (Grundgesetz) outlines how the cabinet is organized and how it is chosen and removed. Unlike in the Weimar Republic, the Bundestag can only remove the chancellor with a special vote that also chooses a new chancellor. This ensures the whole cabinet is dismissed together. The Basic Law was made to stop another dictatorship and avoid a political vacuum, which happened in the Weimar period. If the chancellor loses a simple vote of confidence, they can ask the German president to call for an early election or declare a state of emergency. This lets the cabinet use a quicker law-making process. However, the president is not forced to follow these requests. Most cabinet members are also members of the Bundestag.

Sash! is a German DJ. His third studio album, Trilenium, came out on May 22, 2000, through the X-It label. People didn't like the album as much as expected. It only reached number 13 in the British album charts.

Prince Leopold, Duke of Albany, was born on April 7, 1853, and died on March 28, 1884. He was the eighth child and youngest son of Queen Victoria and Prince Albert. Leopold was given the titles Duke of Albany, Earl of Clarence, and Baron Arklow. He had a condition called haemophilia, which caused his death at 30 years old.

Rose Joan Blondell, born on August 30, 1906, and died on December 25, 1979, was an American actress. She worked in films and TV for about 50 years. She started in vaudeville. After winning a beauty pageant, she began her movie career. Blondell became well-known for her funny, sexy roles in Warner Bros. films. She appeared in over 100 movies and TV shows. She was very active in films in the 1930s and early 1940s, starring in nine films with Glenda Farrell as gold diggers. Later in her life, she often played small, supporting roles in films and TV. She was nominated for an Academy Award for her role in "The Blue Veil" in 1951. Near the end, she was nominated for a Golden Globe for her role in "Opening Night" in 1977. She appeared in two more films: the musical "Grease" in 1978 and "The Champ" in 1979, just before her death from leukemia.

Roderick "Rody" Falesca Rene Trygvae Rijnders was from the Netherlands. He was a coxswain. Rody won a silver medal in coxed pairs at the 1968 Summer Olympics with Hadriaan van Nes and Herman Suselbeek. He also won a European bronze medal in 1965.

Bamba is a peanut butter-flavored snack made by the Osem Corporation in Kiryat Gat, Israel. Bamba is one of Israel's top snack foods. It has been sold since 1964 and its sales have not gone down. Bamba takes up 25% of Israel's snack market. Other similar snacks from other companies are Parpar, made by Telma (which is now part of Unilever since 2000), and Shush, made by Strauss-Elite.

Fruitafossor was a termite-eating mammal found only in North America during the late Jurassic period, about 150 million years ago. It was about the size of a chipmunk. Its complete skeleton was discovered on March 31, 2005, in Fruita, Colorado. Fruitafossor looked like an armadillo or an anteater and likely ate insects in a similar way to these animals today. However, other parts of its skeleton showed that Fruitafossor was not related to armadillos, anteaters, or any modern mammal group. This suggests that the special ability to feed on ants or termites evolved many times independently in mammals. Similar feeding adaptations can be seen in anteaters, numbats, aardwolves, aardvarks, pangolins, and echidnas.

Samuel Cornelius Phillips was born on January 5, 1923, and died on July 30, 2003. He was an American record producer who helped develop rock and roll in the 1950s. Phillips started Sun Records and Sun Studio in Memphis, Tennessee. At Sun Records, he worked with many famous musicians like Elvis Presley, Roy Orbison, Jerry Lee Lewis, Carl Perkins, Johnny Cash, and Howlin' Wolf. He began Presley's career in 1954. In 1969, Phillips sold Sun Records to Shelby Singleton. Phillips also invested in hotels, owning and running radio stations in Memphis, Florence, Alabama, and Lake Worth, Florida. He supported racial equality and worked to break down racial barriers in the music industry.

Aleksandar Stipčević was born on October 10, 1930, and passed away on September 1, 2015. He was a Croatian archeologist, librarian, and historian who focused on the Illyrians. His most important book, "Iliri" (meaning "The Illyrians"), was published in 1974. This book has been translated into English, Italian, and Albanian.

Dillingen is a "landkreis" (district) in Swabia, Bavaria, Germany. It borders (going clockwise from the north) the districts of Donau-Ries, Augsburg, and Günzburg, and the district of Heidenheim in Baden-Württemberg.

Amol is a city and the main town in Amol County, in the Mazandaran province of Iran. In 2006, it had 197,470 people living there, in 55,183 families. Amol is next to the Haraz River, close to the Caspian Sea and near the Alborz Mountains. It is about west of Tehran and south of the provincial capital, Sari. Amol is an old city and has been important in history. It is known as the rice capital of Iran and is a center for industry, culture, transportation, agriculture, tourism, and manufacturing. Amol is also known as the "history, science, and philosophy city," the "city that does not die," and the "hezar sangar city."

Aberfoyle is a village in Perthshire, Scotland. It is part of the Stirling council area. Aberfoyle is northwest of Glasgow. The village's name comes from the parish of Aberfoyle. In 2011, the parish had 1,065 people.

"Avatar: The Last Airbender" is an American animated TV show created by Michael Dante DiMartino and Bryan Konietzko. It started on Nickelodeon on February 21, 2005, and ended with a movie on July 19, 2008. The show has three seasons, each called a "book." Each episode is called a "chapter." The first two seasons have 20 episodes, and the third has 21. There are also two recap episodes and three "shorts." In the show's world, people can bend, or control, four elements: air, water, earth, and fire. There are four nations, one for each element. Not everyone can bend an element, and most can bend only one. But the avatar can control all four and talk to spirits. The avatar is born in one nation and reincarnates in another, following the order of air, water, earth, and fire. The story takes place 100 years after the Fire Nation starts a war against all other nations. During the war, they killed all Air Nomads. The avatar, Aang, was reincarnated as an Air Nomad. He was trapped in ice for 100 years and didn't know about the war. The story begins when Aang, an Air Nomad, is freed by Katara, a Water Nomad. Aang, Katara, and their friends, Sokka, Toph, and Zuko, have adventures as Aang tries to master all four elements and defeat the Fire Nation. Zuko, the Fire Nation's prince, is also a main character. He wants to capture Aang to regain his father's favor and his honor.

Delphi, once also known as Pytho, was a famous ancient place. People went there to ask the Pythia, the oracle, for advice on important matters. The ancient Greeks believed the center of the world was at Delphi, shown by a stone called the omphalos (meaning navel). Delphi is on the southwest side of Mount Parnassus, looking down at the coastal area to the south and the valley of Phocis. Today, it is a large archaeological site with a small town nearby. UNESCO recognizes Delphi as a World Heritage Site because it had great importance in the ancient world. Many important Greek city-states built monuments there, showing their strong connection.

Mather Tower, also known as Lincoln Tower, is a tall building in Chicago. It is located at 75 East Wacker Drive in the downtown area near the Chicago River. This building is known for its unique design, a 18-story octagonal tower on top of a 24-story rectangular part. It was the tallest building in Chicago when completed in 1928. The building is very narrow at the bottom. Its octagonal spire at the top has the smallest floor area per floor among Chicago skyscrapers. The tower was designed by Herbert Hugh Riddle for the Mather Stock Car Company, which made train cars for carrying livestock. Its design was influenced by a Chicago zoning law from 1923 that allowed tall, narrow buildings with a smaller top floor. Mather's founder, Alonzo Mather, was involved in some of the building's features, including the octagonal tower. Plans for a second, identical building on Michigan Avenue were canceled due to the Great Depression. By the 1990s, the building needed repairs. In 2000, the top cupola was removed because of safety concerns. In 2002, the tower was restored, and a new cupola was installed. The lower part of the building now houses a hotel, while the top stories are used by a Club Quarters hotel. The building became a Chicago landmark in 2001 and received a national preservation award in 2006.

In telecommunications and computer networks, multiplexing, sometimes called muxing, combines several signals into one signal for sharing on a common channel. This helps use a limited resource more efficiently. For example, many phone calls can travel through a single wire. Multiplexing started in telegraphy in the 1870s and is now used in many types of communications. In telephony, George Owen Squier developed telephone carrier multiplexing in 1910. The combined signal travels over a communication channel, like a cable. It splits the channel's capacity into separate logical channels for different signals or data streams. On the receiving end, a device called a demultiplexer, or demux, separates these original channels. Inverse multiplexing, or IMUX, works the other way. It splits one data stream into several, sends them over different channels, and then reassembles the original data stream. In computing, I/O multiplexing helps handle multiple input/output events using a single event loop and system calls like poll and select (Unix).

John Landry "Buddy" Boudreaux was a musician in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. He played saxophone and clarinet. Buddy directed and played in several bands from 1934 that toured the southern United States. His bands also attracted nationally known performers to Baton Rouge. The state-times newspaper said he was "the city's sound of big band." Buddy's bands performed with artists like Andy Williams, Bernadette Peters, Dionne Warwick, Gladys Knight and the Pips, Burt Bacharach, Johnny Mathis, The Four Tops, Bob Hope, George Burns, and Joan Rivers. He also opened shows for Tony Bennett, Tony Orlando, Louise Mandrell, The Beach Boys, and Bill Cosby. Buddy wrote a song called "My Baton Rouge" with his barber, Michael T. Abadie. In 1998, this song was declared the official city song.
CAPIF is an Argentine organization that belongs to IFPI. IFPI represents music in Argentina. CAPIF is a nonprofit group made up of big and smaller music companies.

In the fourth episode of the second season of "The Simpsons," titled "Two Cars in Every Garage and Three Eyes on Every Fish," it aired on November 1, 1990, on the Fox network. In this episode, Bart catches a fish with three eyes in a river near the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant. After checking the plant, they find many safety problems. Mr. Burns decides to run for governor to stop the plant from closing. The night before the election, Mr. Burns has a TV dinner with the Simpson family to make himself look good to voters. However, Marge sabotages his plan by serving him the head of Blinky, the three-eyed fish. The episode, written by Sam Simon and John Swartzwelder, and directed by Wes Archer, is the first of the second season. It was supposed to be the season premiere, but was replaced by "Bart Gets an F" because Bart was very popular in the early 1990s. The episode uses references from several American movies, especially "Citizen Kane," where Mr. Burns plays the character Charles Foster Kane. Mary Bailey is named after George Bailey's wife in "It's a Wonderful Life." People have said this episode is a joke about politics and protecting the environment. It won an Environmental Media Award in 1991 for being the best show with an environmental message that year. Since it first aired, the three-eyed fish Blinky has been mentioned in news stories about nuclear waste and mutations. Critics liked the episode for making fun of American politics. It got a high rating of 15.8 from Nielsen and was the top show on the Fox network when it was on air.

June Gable, born on June 5, 1945, is an American actress. She is famous for playing Estelle Leonard, Joey's agent, in the TV show "Friends." She was also nominated for a Tony Award for her work on Broadway.
James Rempe, born on November 4, 1947, in Scranton, Pennsylvania, is an American professional pool player. He was inducted into the Billiard Congress of America's Hall of Fame in 2002.

Raiford Chatman "Ossie" Davis was an American actor, director, poet, playwright, author, and civil rights activist. He was born on December 18, 1917, and died on February 4, 2005. He was married to Ruby Dee, who also was an actress, until his death. They performed together often. Both were honored by the NAACP Image Awards Hall of Fame, received the National Medal of Arts, and were given the Kennedy Center Honors. Ossie Davis was inducted into the American Theater Hall of Fame in 1994.
Helenburgh Football Club was a Scottish team from Helensburgh. They were in the Scottish Football League Third Division from 1923 to 1926.

Addison Mitchell McConnell Jr. was born on February 20, 1942. He is an American politician and serves as Kentucky's senior U.S. senator. He is also the Senate majority leader. McConnell is the second Kentuckian to be a party leader in the Senate. He is the longest-serving U.S. senator from Kentucky and the longest-serving Republican leader in the Senate. McConnell first went to the Senate in 1984 and has been re-elected five times. He was the chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee during the 1998 and 2000 elections. He became majority whip in the 108th Congress and was re-elected to this position in 2004. In 2006, he became the Senate minority leader until 2015, when Republicans gained control of the Senate, making him the majority leader. McConnell was known as a moderate Republican at the start of his career but moved to the right over time. He opposed stricter campaign finance laws, which led to the Supreme Court ruling in 2010 that partially overturned the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act (McCain-Feingold). During the Obama administration, McConnell often opposed key presidential proposals, used the filibuster frequently, and blocked many of President Obama's judicial nominees, including Merrick Garland for the Supreme Court. In the Trump administration, under McConnell's leadership, Senate Republicans set records for confirming judicial nominees, including Neil Gorsuch and Brett Kavanaugh, who were confirmed to the Supreme Court.

ReactOS is a free and open-source operating system for personal computers. It can run the same programs and device drivers as Windows Server 2003 and later versions. Some people think it could replace Windows. ReactOS has been developing since 1996. It is still missing some features and is only recommended for testing. Many Windows programs work on it, such as Adobe Reader 6.0 and OpenOffice. ReactOS is mostly written in C, but some parts, like the file explorer, are in C++. It supports parts of the Windows API and runs on AMD64 processors. ReactOS is part of the open-source software ecosystem, using and working with other projects like Wine. Wine helps Windows programs run on Unix-like systems.

Cosimo II de' Medici was the Grand Duke of Tuscany from 1609 to 1621. He was the older son of Ferdinando I de' Medici and Christina of Lorraine. For most of his twelve-year rule, he let his ministers handle the administration. He is best known for supporting Galileo Galilei, who was once his tutor.

Afrikan Tähti, known in Swedish as Den Försvunna Diamanten or Afrikas Stjärna, means "Star of Africa." It is a Finnish board game designed by Kari Mannerla in 1951. The game was first published in Helsinki, Finland, in 1951. Kari got inspired by stories of a large diamond called the Star of Africa. He created the game using a map and placed exotic locations on it. Players choose their own routes, unlike in other games. Tokens with surprises are shuffled before each game and placed on the board randomly. Robbers and horseshoes make the game exciting. Afrikan Tähti was Kari's last game. He was 19 years old and felt it was unique. He sold the game to a book publisher, Tilgmann, for a small amount of money. The publisher printed 10,000 copies. More copies were printed the following year, and the number kept increasing. Over 100,000 games were sold in seven years. It remains one of the most popular board games in Finland. It has been translated into 16 languages and is very popular in Nordic countries. In Sweden, it is called Den Försvunna Diamanten; in Norway, Den Forsvunne Diamanten; and in Denmark, Afrikas Stjerne. In Finland, over two million games were sold. In Sweden and Norway, almost one million games were sold, and in Denmark, half a million games were sold. Afrikan Tähti has sold over 4.5 million games internationally. Kari Mannerla later created another game called Inkan Aarre, which sold over 100,000 copies. Both games are now owned by Kari's five daughters.

Teruel Cathedral, also known as Catedral de Santa María de Mediavilla de Teruel, is a Catholic church in Teruel, a city in Aragon, Spain. It is dedicated to Saint Mary and is an example of Mudéjar architecture. Along with other churches in Teruel and Zaragoza, it is a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1986.

Romance is a strong feeling of love for someone, and the actions people do to show those feelings. The "Wiley Blackwell Encyclopedia of Family Studies" says that romantic love, which is based on mutual attraction between two people, can change how families and marriages are formed. This means that romantic love can create a bond between two people. Romantic love was first used widely in Western countries after 1800. It is seen as a necessary part of starting a close relationship and the basis for a family. According to "Collins Dictionary," romantic love involves a strong feeling and idealization of another person, who is seen as having special qualities, such as beauty or virtue. This makes the relationship more important than other things, including practical matters. While romantic love is often linked to sexual attraction, it can exist without expecting physical contact. Historically, the word "romance" comes from medieval ideas of chivalry, found in stories called chivalric romances.

Paiçandu is a city in Paraná, a state in southern Brazil. It was founded in 1948 and became an independent city on November 19, 1960. In 2015, its population was 39,291. The city covers an area of 171.4 km².
Ælfweard was born around 902 and died on August 2, 924. He was the second son of Edward the Elder, who was married to Ælfflæd for the second time.

An inventor is someone who creates or discovers new methods, forms, devices, or useful ideas. The word "inventor" comes from the Latin word "invenire," which means "to find." Patents exist to help inventors by giving them temporary exclusive rights to their inventions if the inventions are new, not obvious, and useful. While inventing often involves science and engineering, inventors don't have to be engineers or scientists.
dastilbe was a type of prehistoric bony fish. It is now extinct. It lived in the Aptian period.

Netball is a ball game played by two teams of seven players. It's mainly popular in Commonwealth countries, especially in schools, and mostly played by women. Over 20 million people play netball in more than 80 countries. Major leagues include the Netball Superleague in Great Britain, Suncorp Super Netball in Australia, and the ANZ Premiership in New Zealand. Four big international competitions are the World Netball Championships, Commonwealth Games, and annual Quad Series and Fast5 Series. In 1995, netball was recognized by the International Olympic Committee but hasn't been played at the Olympics. Games are played on a rectangular court with goal rings at each end. Teams try to score by passing the ball and shooting it through the goal ring. Each player has a specific position and can hold the ball for only three seconds before shooting or passing. The winning team scores the most goals. Netball games last 60 minutes. Variations increase the game's pace and appeal. Netball was developed from early basketball versions in England in the 1890s. By 1960, rules were standardized, and the International Federation of Netball and Women's Basketball (now called the International Netball Federation) was formed. As of 2019, the federation includes more than 70 national teams from five global regions.
There is an art museum in Kyoto, Japan. It is also known as MOMAK, which stands for Museum of Modern Art, Kyoto.

The Škoda Fabia is a small car made by the Czech company Škoda Auto since 1999. It replaced the Škoda Felicia, which stopped being made in 2001. When it first came out, the Fabia was available in hatchback, estate (called Fabia Combi), and saloon (called Fabia Sedan) versions. Since 2007, only the hatchback and estate models are made. The Fabia was introduced in its third version in 2015.

The national flag of Anguilla, a British overseas territory, has a blue background with the Union Jack in the top left corner. There are three dolphins in a circle on the right side. These dolphins stand for friendship, wisdom, and strength. The white background represents peace, while the blue symbolizes the sea and also stands for faith, youth, and hope. Anguilla has used three flags. The first was a red flag with the name "Anguilla" in yellow and two mermaids in a blue circle. Some versions had the name in purple and some didn’t have the name. People didn’t like this flag and it was replaced with a dolphin flag during Anguilla's brief period of independence. This dolphin flag is still commonly seen. It was white with a blue band at the bottom and three golden dolphins above it. In 1990, Anguilla adopted the blue ensign. This flag is used on land and by government-operated vessels at sea. For civilian use, Anguilla uses the regular red ensign, which is common throughout the British Empire. Anguilla hasn't created its own version of the red ensign yet. On land, the dolphin flag is often used as a general civilian flag, either instead of or along with the blue ensign. The governor uses the Union Jack with the Anguilla coat of arms. The coat of arms features three dolphins, symbolizing friendship, wisdom, and strength.

Badfinger was a Welsh/English rock band formed in Swansea. They were active from the 1960s to the 1980s. Their main members were Pete Ham, Mike Gibbins, Tom Evans, and Joey Molland. They were known for their influence on 1970s power pop music. The band started as a group called The Iveys in 1961. In 1968, they were signed by Apple Records, the Beatles' label. They changed their name to Badfinger because of a Beatles song's working title. From 1968 to 1973, Badfinger made five albums and toured a lot. They had four big hits between 1970 and 1972. Their song "Without You" was later a hit for other singers too. After Apple Records closed in 1973, Badfinger faced many problems. Pete Ham took his life in 1975. The rest of the band tried to recover but had more issues. In 1983, Tom Evans also died by suicide.
Challis is the biggest city in Custer County, Idaho, United States. It is the county seat. In 2010, the population was 1,081, which was more than in 2000, when it was 909.

In physics, chemistry, and electronic engineering, an electron hole is the absence of an electron in an atom or atomic lattice. It's not a particle but a quasiparticle, unlike the positron, which is the opposite of an electron. Because atoms and atomic lattices are usually balanced between positive and negative charges, a missing electron creates a positive charge where the hole is. In metals or semiconductors, holes can move like electrons and behave like positive charges. They are crucial in devices like transistors, diodes, and integrated circuits. When an electron moves to a higher state, it leaves a hole behind. This concept is used in techniques like Auger electron spectroscopy and in explaining how electrons move in crystals. In electronic band structure, electrons near the top of a band have a negative effective mass, but considering a positive charge with positive mass makes it easier to understand.

Bob Kelly Abreu, born on March 11, 1974, is a former professional baseball player from Venezuela. People call him "El Comedulce" and "La Leche." He played in Major League Baseball for the Houston Astros, Philadelphia Phillies, New York Yankees, Los Angeles Angels of Anaheim, Los Angeles Dodgers, and New York Mets. Abreu is a two-time All-Star. He won a Rawlings Gold Glove Award and a Silver Slugger Award. He has played in the most games in a season twice, hit the most doubles, and triples. Through 2014, he was leading active players in the most doubles (565), walks (1,456), and outfield assists (136). He also scored the most runs (1,441), stole bases (400), had the fifth most extra-base hits (911), the seventh highest on-base percentage (.396), and the tenth most runs batted in (1,363).

Kishi was known for his harsh rule over Manchukuo, a puppet state in northeast China. He was called "devil of Shōwa." After World War II, Kishi was imprisoned for three years as a suspect in Class A war crimes. However, the U.S. government released him, considering him the best leader for post-war Japan, with support from the U.S. In the 1950s, Kishi helped strengthen the conservative parties in Japan, against threats from the Japan Socialist Party. He is credited with helping start the "1955 system," a period where the Liberal Democratic Party was the main political party in Japan.

Antonín Leopold Dvořák, born on September 8, 1841, and died on May 1, 1904, was a Czech composer. He was one of the first to gain worldwide recognition. Inspired by Bedřich Smetana, Dvořák used Moravian and Bohemian folk rhythms in his music. He was skilled from a young age, started playing violin at six, and his works were first performed in Prague in 1872. In 1873, his works were more successful. He submitted his symphony for a prize in Germany but didn't win; the manuscript was lost until found many years later. In 1874, he won the Austrian State Prize for Composition, which Johannes Brahms and other jurors appreciated. Brahms recommended Dvořák to his publisher, and this led to the "Slavonic Dances," which were very popular. In 1880, his "Stabat Mater" was performed in Prague and later in London, gaining him an international reputation. Dvořák made nine trips to England, often conducting his works. He wrote the "Dumky Trio" in 1890–91. In 1892, he moved to the United States and became director of the National Conservatory of Music in New York City. There, he composed his most famous works, including the "New World Symphony" and the "Cello Concerto," and the "American String Quartet." Despite financial issues and homesickness, he returned to Bohemia in 1895. Dvořák wrote nine operas in Czech, with "Rusalka" being the most successful. He also composed popular pieces like the "Humoresque" and "Songs My Mother Taught Me." He is considered one of the most versatile composers of his time.

The Imja Khola is a river in Nepal that flows into the Dudh Kosi. It comes from the slopes of Mount Everest. The Khumbu Glacier melts into the Lobujya River, which then becomes the Imja Khola. The Imja Khola flows southward until it meets the Dudh Kosi at a place called Tengboche. Water from the Imja Glacier flows through the Dingboche Valley into the Imja Khola.

Video camera tubes used cathode ray tubes to capture images in early television cameras. These were used before CCD sensors were introduced in the 1980s. Different types of tubes were used from the early 1930s to the 1980s. In these tubes, a cathode ray scanned the image. The brightness of the image affected the current. The ray was very small compared to the image, allowing 483 horizontal scan lines in NTSC format or 576 lines in PAL format.

"Sunday Bloody Sunday" is a song by the Irish rock band U2. It comes first on their 1983 album "War" and was released as the third single on March 21, 1983, in the Netherlands and West Germany. The song has a strong drumbeat and loud guitar, but also has a melodic sound. One of U2's most political songs, it talks about the violence in Northern Ireland, especially about a sad day in 1972 when British soldiers hurt peaceful protesters in Derry. This song, along with "New Year's Day," helped U2 become more popular. People thought highly of the song when it was first released. It has become a favorite at U2 concerts. Initially, some found the song controversial, but lead singer Bono explained its message about stopping violence for many years. Today, it is seen as one of U2's most important songs. Many people say it is one of the best protest songs. Several artists have covered it, and "Rolling Stone" ranked it as the 272nd best song of all time.

Fort Scott is a city in Bourbon County, Kansas, United States. It is south of Kansas City and near the Marmaton River. In 2010, it had 8,087 people. Fort Scott has a national historic site and a national cemetery. The city is named after General Winfield Scott.
Ernie is a boy's name. It is often a shorter version of Ernest. This name can be used for a boy.
Moutiers-sur-le-Lay is a commune in Vendée, which is in the Pays de la Loire region of western France.

Eli Lilly and Company is an American drug company based in Indianapolis, Indiana. They have offices in 18 countries and sell their products in about 125 countries. The company was started in 1876 by Eli Lilly, a chemist who fought in the American Civil War. Eli Lilly is known for producing the first mass-produced polio vaccine by Jonas Salk and insulin. They were among the first to create human insulin using DNA, making products like Humulin and Humalog. They also made the first approved insulin similar product in the US, called Basaglar. Eli Lilly makes psychiatric medications, including Prozac, Dolophine, Cymbalta, and Zyprexa. Some say they also made LSD for a secret CIA program in the past. In 2019, Eli Lilly was ranked 123rd on the Fortune 500 list and 221st on the Forbes Global 2000 list. They are also one of the best employers in America. Eli Lilly is a member of major pharmaceutical groups and is the biggest company and charitable donor in Indiana as of 1997.

The penalty shootout is a way to decide a winner in sports matches that end in a tie. The rules for penalty shootouts can differ, but they usually involve players taking turns to kick a ball at the goal, with only the goalkeeper defending. If the scores are still tied after this, players continue taking shots one at a time, with the team that scores a goal the other team doesn't match wins. This process may continue until everyone has kicked, or extra kicks may be taken until a winner is decided, which is also called "sudden death."

Kavala, or "Kavála," is a city in northern Greece. It is the main seaport in eastern Macedonia and the capital of the Kavala regional unit. Kavala is located on the bay of Kavala, near the island of Thasos. It is also on the Egnatia Motorway. From Kavala, you can drive to Thessaloniki in about one and a half hours, to Drama in about forty minutes, and to Xanthi in the east. Kavala is about 150 kilometers west of Alexandroupoli. Kavala is an important economic center in northern Greece. It is a hub for commerce, tourism, fishing, and oil-related activities. It used to be known for trading tobacco.

Morissen was a former municipality in the Surselva district of the Swiss canton of Graubünden. On January 1, 2013, Morissen and seven other municipalities—Cumbel, Degen, Lumbrein, Suraua, Vignogn, Vella, and Vrin—merged to form the new municipality of Lumnezia.
Marcy is a commune in Aisne, which is in Hauts-de-France in northern France.

Hans Modrow, born on January 27, 1928, is a German politician. He is famous as the last communist leader of East Germany. During the peaceful revolution, he became the acting leader of the country in late 1989 and early 1990, trying to stop Germany from uniting. After the fall of communism and the unification of Germany, Modrow was found guilty of election cheating and lying by the Dresden court in 1995. He was in charge of the election process. Modrow was the president of the Party of Democratic Socialism from 1990 until 2007. Since 2007, he has been the president of the council of elders of the Left Party.

How to Murder Your Wife is a 1965 American black comedy film. It was made by United Artists. George Axelrod produced it, and Richard Quine directed it. Jack Lemmon, Virna Lisi, and Terry-Thomas starred in the film. Richard Quine directed Jack Lemmon in other movies too, such as "My Sister Eileen," "It Happened to Jane," "Operation Mad Ball," "The Notorious Landlady," and "Bell, Book and Candle." The film had comic strip art by Mel Keefer. He drew comic strips like "Perry Mason," "Mac Divot," and "Rick O'shay." Alex Toth created a teaser comic strip in Keefer's style. It was published in The Hollywood Reporter and several newspapers for ten days before the film's movie theater release.
Hiroshi Umemura, born on February 22, 1972, is a Japanese mixed martial artist. He competed in bantamweight and featherweight divisions.

Lynne Carol, born Josephine Caroline Gertrude Mary Faith Harber on June 29, 1914, and died on June 30, 1990, was an actress from Wales. She was usually considered English. She acted mainly in TV series and telemovies. She was famous for playing Martha Longhurst in the soap opera "Coronation Street." Martha Longhurst was a busybody character, and Lynne Carol played her in the second episode in 1960 until 1964, when the character was killed off.
Newark is a city in Texas, in Tarrant and Wise counties. The population was 1,005 in 2010.

In math, the lowest common denominator (LCD) is the smallest number that can be evenly divided by the denominators of a group of fractions. It helps make adding, subtracting, and comparing fractions easier.

A prefix is an affix placed before a word's main part, or stem. When added to the start of a word, it creates a new word. For example, adding "un-" to "happy" makes "unhappy." In language studies, a prefix is also called a preformative because it changes the form of the word. Prefixes can be inflectional or derivational. Inflectional prefixes change a word's form but keep the same meaning and category, like in sentences. Derivational prefixes create new words with different meanings and sometimes categories. Prefixes, like other affixes, are usually bound morphemes. In English, there are no inflectional prefixes; instead, suffixes are used for that purpose. The word "prefix" comes from the stem "fix" (meaning "attach") and the prefix "pre-" (meaning "before"), both from Latin roots.

The Lamborghini Huracán is a sports car made by Lamborghini, an Italian company. It replaced the Gallardo, which had a V10 engine. The Huracán first showed to the world at the 2014 Geneva Auto Show and started selling in the second quarter of 2014. Its name means "hurricane" in Spanish. The Huracán has 610 metric horsepower and four-wheel drive. "LP" in its name LP 610-4 stands for "longitudinale posteriore," which refers to the engine being positioned longitudinally at the mid-rear of the car.

Sewanee is a city in Gwinnett County, Georgia. In 2010, it had about 15,355 people. By 2019, the population grew to around 20,907. From 1979 to 2001, the Atlanta Falcons played their home games in Sewanee. The city was ranked as one of the top 10 best places to live by "Money" in 2007. In 2012, "Kiplinger" said Sewanee was the third best place in America for raising families. In 2013, "Family Circle" named Sewanee one of the 10 best towns for families in the country. In 2018, "Niche" rated Sewanee first for the best public schools in Georgia. Sewanee shares its zip code (30024) with parts of Forsyth and Fulton counties, and people there use this zip code when mailing.
Sajid Nawaz Khan was born on March 25, 1975. He is a Pakistani politician who served in the National Assembly of Pakistan from June 2013 to May 2018.

Action Comics is an American comic book series that introduced Superman, one of the first major superheroes. The publisher was originally called National Allied Publications and later became National Comics Publications and National Periodical Publications before changing to DC Comics. The first series ran from 1938 to 2011, being one of the longest-running comic books with numbered issues. In 2011, a second volume of Action Comics started with issue #1 and ran until 2016. In August 2016, Action Comics returned to its original numbering with issue #957.

Keitele is a large lake in central Finland. It covers 493.59 square kilometers and is the 9th largest lake in the country. The lake is split into three parts: Ylä-, Keski-, and Ala-Keitele, with Keski-Keitele being the largest. The water is clear and in good condition. The towns of Äänekoski and Viitasaari are near the lake. The northern part is called Ylä-Keitele. A big part of Ylä-Keitele is protected due to its clear water. In 1904, a famous Finnish painter, Akseli Gallen-Kallela, painted the lake. This was his third and most detailed painting of it, which he showed in Helsinki that year. The painting, with his Swedish name, is now in the National Gallery in London. The lake is also mentioned in a book called "A Corpse in the Koryo" by James Church.
The Centre Étienne Desmarteau is a multi-purpose complex in Montreal, Quebec, Canada. It has two ice rinks.
