The Gaslight Anthem was an American rock band from New Brunswick, New Jersey. They were formed in 2006. The band members are Brian Fallon (lead vocals, rhythm guitar), Alex Rosamilia (lead guitar, backing vocals), Alex Levine (bass guitar, backing vocals), and Benny Horowitz (drums, percussion). They released their first album, "Sink or Swim," in May 2007. Their second album, "The '59 Sound," came out in August 2008. Their third album, "American Slang," was released in June 2010. The fourth album, "Handwritten," was released in July 2012, through Mercury Records. The song "45" from "Handwritten" was their most successful single. Their fifth album, "Get Hurt," was released on August 12, 2014, through Island Records. In July 2015, the band took a break after their European tour ended at Reading Festival on August 30. They briefly reunited in 2018 to celebrate the 10th anniversary of "The '59 Sound" before taking another break.
Giron or girón can mean: A place called Giron An area named girón

Arctic Monkeys are an English rock band formed in Sheffield in 2002. The band has four members: Alex Turner (vocals, guitar, keyboards), Jamie Cook (guitar, keyboards), Nick O'Malley (bass guitar, vocals), and Matt Heilder (drums, vocals). Andy Nicholson (bass guitar, vocals) was part of the band until 2006. They have released six studio albums: "Whatever People Say I Am, That's What I'm Not" (2006), "Favourite Worst Nightmare" (2007), "Humbug" (2009), "Suck It and See" (2011), "AM" (2013), and "Tranquility Base Hotel & Casino" (2018). They also have one live album, "At the Apollo" (2008). Their first album sold very quickly, and in 2013, Rolling Stone ranked it the 30th-greatest debut album. The band won seven Brit Awards, including Best British Group and Best British Album three times. They were nominated for five Grammy Awards and won the Mercury Prize in 2006 for their first album. They also got nominated for the prize in 2007, 2013, and 2018. Arctic Monkeys played at Glastonbury Festival twice, in 2007 and 2013. They were seen as one of the first bands to become well-known through the internet, which changed how new bands are promoted and marketed.

Matthew Tyler Oakley, born on March 22, 1989, is an American YouTuber, actor, activist, and author. Much of his activism focuses on LGBTQ+ youth, LGBTQ rights, and issues like health care, education, and preventing suicide among LGBTQ youth. Oakley makes videos about queer politics, pop culture, and humor. He started making videos in 2007. His first video, "Raindrops," had over 517,715 views by March 22, 2020. His channel has over 682 million views and reached over 8 million subscribers at its peak. He was part of the YouTube channel "5awesomegays" from 2008 to 2011, producing the Friday video for over three years. In 2014, he was featured in a TV report called "Generation Like." Socialblade, a website that rates YouTube accounts, ranked his channel highly in November 2017. He also had over 5.9 million followers on Twitter and 5.8 million on Instagram. From March to October 2013, he co-hosted "Top That!" with Becca Frucht for POPSUGAR. In 2013 to 2014, he voiced Mr. McNeely in five episodes of the web series "The Most Popular Girls in School." He has many followers on Facebook and Tumblr. In 2015, he wrote a book of humorous essays called "Binge." He hosted "The Tyler Oakley Show" on Ellen DeGeneres's platform. In 2017, he was named one of Forbes' "30 Under 30." In March 2020, he said he was a landlord, which caused some criticism.

Jacob Tremblay, born on October 5, 2006, is a Canadian actor. He became famous for playing Jack Newsome in the movie "Room" in 2015. For this role, he won awards for his performance, including the Critics' Choice Movie Award for best young actor and the Canadian Screen Award for best actor. He was also nominated for a Screen Actors Guild Award. In 2017, he played August Pullman, a boy with Treacher Collins syndrome, in the movie "Wonder." In 2019, he starred in the comedy "Good Boys."

Dr. Hannibal Lecter is a character in books by Thomas Harris. He is a famous psychiatrist in Baltimore, but he also catches and eats people. After he is caught, he helps the FBI find other killers. He first appears in "Red Dragon" in 1981. In later books, he becomes a main character. In "Hannibal Rising," he is a main character who was a bad boy when he was young. In movies, Brian Cox played Dr. Lecter in "Manhunter" in 1986. Anthony Hopkins won an Oscar for playing Lecter in "The Silence of the Lambs" in 1991. He played Lecter again in "Hannibal" in 2001 and in a movie based on "Red Dragon" in 2002. In the TV show "Hannibal," Mads Mikkelsen played Lecter. Mikkelsen won an award for his acting. Dr. Lecter is seen as a great bad guy in movies and TV. He was chosen as the greatest villain in American movies in 2003. He was also one of the top 100 characters in movies and TV from 1990 to 2010. In 2019, he was ranked as the 18th greatest villain in TV history.

The president of the Spanish senate is called the speaker of the Spanish senate. This is the upper house of Spain's cortes generales. After the monarch (head of state), the prime minister (head of government), and the president of the congress of deputies (speaker of the lower house), it is the fourth most important position in the country. The speaker is chosen by and from the existing senators. If the speaker cannot do their job, a vice president of the senate takes over. Although the president of the congress shares some responsibilities, the constitution gives more power to the president of the congress due to the uneven arrangement of Spain's two-chamber system. This makes the president of the congress the leader of the cortes, and the president of the senate works in the background. The current role was created by the 1978 constitution. However, the position has been around for almost 200 years, starting in 1834 when it was known as the president of the house of peers. In the current term of the cortes generales, Pilar Llop holds this office. She represents Madrid for the socialist party.

Miikka Sakari Kiprusoff, nicknamed Kipper, was born on October 26, 1976. He is a former Finnish ice hockey goalie who played for the Calgary Flames and San Jose Sharks in the NHL. Kiprusoff was chosen by the San Jose Sharks in the 1995 NHL draft. He also played for TPS in the Finnish SM-liiga and for Aik IF and Timrå IK in the Swedish Elitserien. Kiprusoff represented Finland in international competitions, winning silver medals at the 1999 and 2001 Ice Hockey World Championships. He helped the Finnish team reach second place at the 2004 World Cup of Hockey and won a bronze medal at the 2010 Winter Olympics in Vancouver, Canada. Kiprusoff started his professional career with TPS in 1994. He led them to the SM-liiga championship in 1999, being named the best goaltender and best player of the playoffs. In 1999, he moved to North America and played in the American Hockey League (AHL) for two seasons. He then joined the San Jose Sharks and was often a backup. In 2003, he was traded to the Calgary Flames, where he became the starting goalie. He set a modern NHL record with a low goals against average of 1.69, helping the Flames reach the 2004 Stanley Cup Final. In 2006, he won the Vezina Trophy for being the best goalie in the NHL and the William M. Jennings Trophy for giving up the fewest goals in the league. He played in his first NHL All-Star game in 2007 and holds the Flames' franchise records for wins and shutouts.

Docetism is a belief in early Christianity. It says that Jesus only appeared to be human; his human form was just an illusion. The word "dokētaí," meaning "illusionists," was first used by Bishop Serapion of Antioch in a letter around 197-203 AD. He found this belief in the Gospel of Peter during a visit to a Christian community in Rhosus and later said it was a forgery. The idea of Docetism came from doubts about what "the Word was made flesh" meant in the Gospel of John. In 325, the First Council of Nicaea clearly rejected Docetism. This belief is seen as wrong by many Christian churches, including the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, and some Protestant groups.

The list of Atlantic hurricanes from the 18th century includes all known tropical storms from 1700 to 1799. Not all data for each storm are available. However, some parts of the coastline had enough people to record hurricane occurrences.

Paktika is one of Afghanistan's 34 provinces. It is in the eastern part of the country. Paktika is part of a larger area called Loya Paktia. The province has about 413,800 people, mostly Pashtuns. Sharana is the capital town. Uргун is the most populous city.

Stephen Lewis, born on December 17, 1926, and died on August 12, 2015, was an English actor, comedian, director, screenwriter, and playwright. He was best known for playing Inspector Cyril "Blakey" Blake on "The Buses" and Clem "Smiler" Hemmingway in "Last of the Summer Wine." He also played Harry Lambert in "Oh, Doctor Beeching!" Besides these, he appeared in many other stage and film roles.

In chemistry, a leaving group is a part of a molecule that leaves during a reaction by sharing electrons. This can happen with anions, cations, or neutral molecules. For it to work, the leaving group must be able to handle extra electrons. Common examples of leaving groups include halides like chlorine (Cl), bromine (Br), and iodine (I), as well as sulfonate esters like tosylate (TsO). Fluorine (F) can also leave in a nerve agent called sarin gas. Water and ammonia are other common neutral molecule leaving groups. Sometimes, a positively charged cation, like hydrogen (H), can also leave during a reaction. These are called electrofuges.

Alfred Lothar Wegener, born on November 1, 1880, and died in 1930, was a German scientist who studied the polar regions, geophysics, and meteorology. He is best known today for proposing the theory of continental drift in 1912. Wegener suggested that the continents were moving slowly over the Earth's surface. His idea was controversial and not widely accepted by other geologists at the time. However, later discoveries, like palaeomagnetism, supported his theory and helped develop the modern idea of plate tectonics. Wegener also went on several trips to Greenland to study air movements before jet streams were known. During these trips, they took many weather observations and were the first to spend a winter in the middle of Greenland's ice and the first to take ice samples from a moving glacier in the Arctic.
Paul Konrad Müller, born on March 11, 1923, in Neuchâtel, is a Swiss actor. He mostly appeared in Italian films. He acted in European movies for 51 years.

Northport is a historic maritime village on Long Island's north shore, New York. The area was first called Great Cow Harbour by English settlers in the 17th century. In 1837, it was officially renamed Northport. In 1894, the community became an incorporated village to have local governance. Northport is famous for its Victorian-era village center. The old streetcar line, which used to transport people to the East Northport train station, still has trolley rails visible. The village main street goes from the village green to the former hamlet of Vernon Valley, now part of East Northport. As of 2010, Northport had about 7,401 people and is part of the Northport-East Northport School District.

Togiola Talalelei A. Tulafono, born on February 28, 1947, is an American Samoan politician and lawyer. He served as the 56th governor of American Samoa and is a Democrat. Tulafono was the lieutenant governor before becoming governor. He became acting governor on January 3, 1997. Governor Tauese Pita Fitia Sunia died on March 26, 2003, and Tulafono took over as governor on April 7, 2003. Tulafono won a full four-year term in the 2004 governor election and was re-elected in 2008. He did not run for governor in 2012 because he was term-limited. In 2014, Tulafono tried to be a representative for American Samoa but did not win.

Baked beans are a dish that usually has white beans. These beans are boiled briefly first and then baked slowly in a sauce at a low temperature. In the US, this is how baked beans are typically made without canned beans. In the UK, they might bake or stew the beans in a sauce. Canned baked beans are not baked; they are cooked using steam. This dish comes from Native American food and was adopted by English settlers in New England in the 1600s. Over time, it spread to other parts of the US and Canada. In New England, various local beans are sometimes used. In the past, Native Americans sweetened them with maple syrup, but English settlers started using brown sugar. Later, molasses became popular as a sweetener to avoid taxes. In Boston, they use molasses and salt pork in the sauce, which gave the city the nickname "Beantown." Today, baked beans are often served with barbecue food or at picnics. They can be eaten hot or cold, straight from the can. In the 1890s, canned baked beans were first mass-produced by H. J. Heinz. They became very popular in the UK, where they are a common part of a traditional breakfast.

Caliban is the second-largest retrograde irregular moon of Uranus. It was found on September 6, 1997, by Brett J. Gladman, Philip D. Nicholson, Joseph A. Burns, and John J. Kavelaars using the 200-inch Hale telescope. At the time, it was also called S/1997 U 1 with Sycorax. Later, it was named Uranus Xvi and got its name from a character in William Shakespeare's play "The Tempest."

Valente Rodriguez, born on February 14, 1964, is an American actor. He is famous for playing the character Ernie Cárdenas in the TV show "George Lopez." He also acted as César in "Happily Divorced." He appeared in episodes of shows like "Yes, Dear," "Mad About You," and "ER." He also had a role as Marco in the movie "Suckers" in 2001.

Ryan Prosser, born on July 10, 1988, is a professional rugby player. He plays as a hooker. In June 2008, he played for Wales in the under-20 Junior World Cup. He got engaged to Hayley Thomas on January 2, 2018. He is also friends with actor Fin Samad. In January 2010, he joined the Cornish Pirates from Bristol.

The flag of Germany has three equal horizontal bands of black, red, and gold. It was first used as the national flag in 1919 during the Weimar Republic until 1933. Before that, Germany had two main color traditions: black-red-gold and black-white-red. Black-red-gold represented the 1848 revolutions, the Weimar Republic, and the Federal Republic since 1949. Black-white-red was used in the North German Confederation from 1867 to 1871 and later in the German Empire until 1918. After World War II, black-red-gold became the official flag of the Federal Republic of Germany. This flag is protected by law, and defaming it can result in a fine or up to five years in prison.

The conservation movement, also called nature conservation, aims to protect animals, plants, and their habitats for the future. Evidence-based conservation uses scientific information to make conservation more effective. Early conservation efforts focused on managing fisheries and wildlife, protecting water, soil, and forests in a sustainable way. Today, conservation also aims to preserve biodiversity. Some people see conservation as part of a larger environmental movement, but others think they differ in ideas and actions. In the United States, conservation is mainly about preserving natural resources for humans to use sustainably. Outside the U.S., conservation includes environmentalism.

A hose is a flexible tube used to carry liquids from one place to another. Sometimes it is called a "pipe," but a pipe is usually rigid, while a hose is flexible. Hoses are also sometimes referred to as "tubing." Hoses are typically cylindrical in shape. Hose design depends on its use and performance needs. Common factors include size, pressure strength, weight, length, whether it's straight or coiled, and its ability to handle certain chemicals. The materials used for hoses depend on the environment and pressure required. Common materials are nylon, polyurethane, polyethylene, PVC, or synthetic or natural rubber. In recent years, special types of polyethylene (like LDPE and LLDPE) are also used. Other materials include PTFE (Teflon), stainless steel, and other metals.
Bell is a town in the Mayen-Koblenz district, which is in Rhineland-Palatinate, a state in western Germany.

Matthew Quincy "Matt" Daddario was born on October 1, 1987. He is an American actor. Matt is famous for playing Alec Lightwood in the TV show "Shadowhunters" from 2016 to 2019. He has a sister named Alexandra Daddario, who is also an actress.

betrayal happens when someone breaks a promise or trust, causing problems in a relationship between people, organizations, or individuals. Betrayal often means supporting a rival group or going against previously agreed-upon rules. A person who betrays others is called a traitor. Betrayal is used in stories, movies, and TV shows as a surprise plot twist.
Francisco Ibáñez Talavera was born on March 15, 1936. He is a Spanish comic book artist and writer.

Blythburgh is a small village and civil parish in East Suffolk, England. It is west of Southwold and southeast of Halesworth, located by the River Blyth. The A12 road goes through the village, splitting it in two. In 2011, the village had 297 people. It also has nearby hamlets called Bulcamp and Hinton. Blythburgh is famous for its church, Holy Trinity, often called the Cathedral of the Marshes. The church has been lit up at night since the 1960s, helping travelers see it on the A12 road. There's also a priory in the village. It was built by monks in the 12th century and closed in 1537, leaving ruins. Blythburgh is part of the Suffolk Coast and Heaths Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. It's near the Suffolk Heritage Coast, close to marshes and mudflats by the River Blyth. During World War II, these areas were flooded in 1940 as part of Britain's defenses.

Appenzeller cheese is a hard cheese made from cow's milk. It is produced in the Appenzell region of northeast Switzerland, specifically in the cantons of Appenzell Innerrhoden and Appenzell Ausserrhoden. During curing, the cheese wheels are treated with a herbal brine, which can include wine or cider. This brine helps flavor and preserve the cheese while promoting the formation of a rind. Appenzeller cheese has a history of at least 700 years. It was first mentioned in a document from 1282. However, the exact manufacturing process back then was different from today. Today, around 75 dairies make Appenzeller cheese, each with its own recipe for the brine wash. Most of these recipes are kept secret. The cheese has a straw-colored appearance, with small holes inside and a golden rind outside. It has a strong smell and a nutty or fruity taste that can range from mild to tangy, depending on how long it is aged. There are three types of Appenzeller cheese sold.

Keiunta Denard Span was born on February 27, 1984. He was an American professional baseball player. Span played as a center fielder in Major League Baseball (MLB) for the Minnesota Twins, Washington Nationals, San Francisco Giants, Tampa Bay Rays, and Seattle Mariners. He batted and threw left-handed. At his best, Span was famous as one of the top leadoff hitters because he had a very good on-base percentage.

The Toronto Maple Leafs, also known as the Leafs, are a professional ice hockey team in Toronto. They play in the National Hockey League (NHL) in the Atlantic Division. The team is owned by Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment, Ltd., and Larry Tanenbaum is the chairman. They broadcast games with BCE Inc. and Rogers Communications. The Leafs started playing at the Mutual Street Arena for 14 seasons before moving to Maple Leaf Gardens in 1931. In 1999, they moved to their current home, Scotiabank Arena, previously called the Air Canada Centre. The Toronto Maple Leafs were founded in 1917 as the Toronto Arenas and became the Toronto St. Patricks in 1919. In 1927, under new ownership, they were renamed the Maple Leafs. They are part of the "Original Six," one of six NHL teams that have survived since the 1920s. The Maple Leafs have won 13 Stanley Cup championships, second only to the Montreal Canadiens' 24. They had two dynasties, from 1947 to 1951, and from 1962 to 1967. Their longest championship gap was 51 seasons, ending in 1967. The Leafs have rivalries with the Boston Bruins, Detroit Red Wings, Montreal Canadiens, and Ottawa Senators. They have retired 13 player numbers and inducted several people into the Hockey Hall of Fame. The team is linked with two minor league teams: the Toronto Marlies and the Newfoundland Growlers.

Gangwon-do is a province in South Korea. Its capital is Chuncheon. To the east, it borders the Sea of Japan. To the west, it neighbors Gyeonggi province. To the south, it borders North Gyeongsang and North Chungcheong provinces. Its northern border is the military demarcation line, separating it from North Korea's Kangwŏn province. Before Korea divided in 1945, Gangwon and Kangwŏn were one province. Pyeongchang county hosted the 2018 Winter Olympics and Winter Paralympics. Gangwon will host the 2024 Winter Youth Olympics.
Unterschächen is a municipality in the canton of Uri in Switzerland. It is located in the Upper Schächental.

Benjamin Franklin, born on January 17, 1706, was a famous American who did many things. He was a writer, printer, thinker, politician, Freemason, postmaster, scientist, inventor, funny person, and civic leader. He helped make the United States and was one of the founding fathers. As a scientist, Franklin made important discoveries about electricity. As an inventor, he created things like the lightning rod and bifocals. He also helped start many groups, like the library, Philadelphia's first fire company, and the University of Pennsylvania. Franklin was known as the "first American" for his early work in bringing together the colonies. He was America's first ambassador to France. He showed what America could be with practical values like thrift and hard work, and the ideas of the Enlightenment. At 23, Franklin became a successful newspaper editor and printer in Philadelphia, publishing the "Pennsylvania Gazette." He also wrote "Poor Richard's Almanack," a book he wrote using a fake name. Franklin helped get rid of a hated tax called the Stamp Act. He was good at diplomacy and helped America get support from France during the American Revolution. He was the first United States postmaster general after the war. Franklin worked on community and government issues, both in Pennsylvania and on a national level. From 1785 to 1788, he was the governor of Pennsylvania. He owned slaves at first but later spoke against slavery and worked to educate and integrate African Americans in American society. Franklin is remembered for his many achievements in science and politics, and as one of America's most important founding fathers. He is honored in many ways, like being on the $100 bill, and his name appears on towns, schools, and other places.

Salvador Vilar Braamcamp Sobral, born on December 28, 1989, is a Portuguese singer. He won the Eurovision Song Contest in 2017 with the song "Amar pelos Dois." His sister, Luísa Sobral, wrote and composed the song. By winning, he gave Portugal its first-ever victory in the contest, ending a 53-year winless streak for the country. Sobral and his song set a new Eurovision record for the highest score, with a total of 758 points, from both the jury and the televote.
Île-d’Eau is a commune in Vendée, which is in the Pays de la Loire region of western France.

Anna Kavan, born Helen Emily Woods on April 10, 1901, and died on December 5, 1968, was a British writer and painter. She wrote novels and short stories. At first, she used the name Helen Ferguson when publishing. In 1939, she started using the name Anna Kavan both for her writing and legally.

Hamont-Achel is a municipality in the Belgian province of Limburg. It was created in 1977 by combining the city of Hamont and the village of Achel. On January 1, 2006, Hamont-Achel had 13,770 people living there. The area of the municipality is 43. 66 square kilometers, which means there are about 315 people for each square kilometer. Hamont-Achel has a Trappist abbey called Achel, part of which is a brewery named De Achelse Kluis. This is one of the 11 Trappist breweries in the world. A professional tennis player named Elise Mertens (ranked 35th in the WTA in 2017) lives in Hamont-Achel.

The October 2015 election for Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives happened on October 29, 2015, during the 114th Congress. John Boehner, the current Speaker, was leaving his position on October 30. This was the first time a Speaker resigned during a term since 1989. The election was the 124th since the position was created in 1789. Republican Paul Ryan won, getting 236 votes. Nancy Pelosi, the minority leader, got 184 votes. Others got 12 votes. To win, you needed 217 votes. Ryan was the youngest Speaker since James G. Blaine in 1869. After the vote, Ryan spoke as the new Speaker-elect and was sworn in by John Conyers. Boehner was Speaker from January 5, 2011. He faced disputes with the Freedom Caucus. On September 25, 2015, he said he would resign. Several Republicans wanted the job. Kevin McCarthy was seen as the favorite but dropped out. Then, Ryan was chosen. After getting support, he joined the race. Ryan won the conference vote on October 28 and was elected the next day.

Mccomb is a city in Pike County, Mississippi, United States. It is roughly south of Jackson. In 2010, the city's population was 12,790. Mccomb is the main city in the Mccomb, Mississippi micropolitan statistical area.

The Phoenix Dwarf is a dwarf irregular galaxy. It was found in 1976 by Hans-Emil Schuster and Richard Martin West. At first, it was mistaken for a globular cluster. Today, it is about 1.44 million light-years away from Earth. It got its name because it is part of the Phoenix constellation.

Vauxhall Gardens is a public park in Kennington, London, England, by the River Thames. From 1785 to 1859, it was a pleasure garden and a top spot for public fun in London. It was originally called New Spring Gardens and opened before 1660, as noted by Samuel Pepys in 1662. The garden had trees, shrubs, and pretty paths. Entry was free at first, but food and drinks were sold. People could reach it by boat until the Vauxhall Bridge was built in the 1810s. As London grew, the area became part of the city. In 1785, the name changed to Vauxhall Gardens, and you had to pay to enter. It was very popular, with paths where people would meet. You could see tightrope walkers, hot-air balloons, concerts, and fireworks. There was a fancy "Turkish Tent" and a round building called the "Rotunda" that was a big attraction. A statue of George Frideric Handel was later moved to Westminster Abbey. In 1817, a big re-enactment of the Battle of Waterloo was held with 1,000 soldiers. The gardens closed in 1840 due to money problems but reopened in 1841. Ownership changed in 1842, and it closed for good in 1859. The land was later used for other buildings, but part of the original site was turned back into a park. It's now called Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens and is managed by the London Borough of Lambeth. You can see a tile design of the gardens at Vauxhall tube station.
Hans-Peter, also known as Hansi, Müller was born on July 27, 1957, in Stuttgart. He was a German football player who played as a midfielder.

Promenade concerts were musical performances in London's pleasure gardens during the 18th and 19th centuries. People walked around while listening to the music. The word comes from French, meaning "to walk." Today, the term "promenade concert" often refers to the Proms, a summer classical music series started in 1895 by Robert Newman and conductor Henry Wood.

Stanley Norman Cohen was born on June 30, 1935, in Perth Amboy, New Jersey, United States. He is an American geneticist and holds the Kwoh-Ting Li professorship at Stanford University School of Medicine. Cohen and Herbert Boyer were the first to move genes from one living thing to another. This was a big discovery for genetic engineering. Many products, like human growth hormone and the hepatitis B vaccine, were developed from their work. Microbiologist Hugh McDevitt says, "Cohen's DNA cloning technology has helped scientists in almost every area." He adds, "Without it, biomedicine and biotechnology would look very different today."

Knuts Skujenieks, born on September 5, 1936, in Riga, is a Latvian poet, journalist, and translator of fifteen European languages. He grew up near Bauska in Zemgale, southern Latvia. Skujenieks studied at the University of Latvia in Riga and at the Maxim Gorky Literature Institute in Moscow. In 1962, he was convicted for anti-Soviet activities and served seven years in a prison camp in Mordovia, Russia. Despite being a prolific poet, his first poetry collection wasn't published until 1978. The poems he wrote during his time in prison were published in 1990. Skujenieks' poetry has been translated into many European languages. His books have been published in Sweden and Ukraine. In 2008, he won the Baltic Assembly Prize for Literature. Director Ivars Tontegode is making a documentary about Skujenieks' life called "The Deviant/Nepareizais."

The second inauguration of Andrew Jackson as the president of the United States happened on March 4, 1833, in the U.S. Capitol's house chamber. This marked Jackson's second four-year term, and it was the only four-year term for Martin Van Buren as vice president. When Jackson and Van Buren arrived at the Capitol, John Peter Van Ness, the mayor of Washington, and city council members greeted them. They were escorted to the house chamber before taking their oaths. At noon, Chief Justice John Marshall swore Jackson and Van Buren in. Unlike the previous inauguration, which was in the east portico, this one was inside due to the snow and cold weather. Many important people attended, including Supreme Court judges, the House speaker, the Senate president, senators, foreign ministers, and members of the House. Jackson took his seat and, after a pause, stood to be sworn in as president. Martin Van Buren was on his left, and Andrew Jackson Donelson, Jackson's private secretary, was on his right. This was the last time Chief Justice John Marshall swore in a president. After taking his oath, Jackson gave a speech. He said he was honored to be re-elected and would work to improve people's lives. He also said the U.S. was not at war with any countries and stressed the importance of a strong, united union. Following his speech, there were two inaugural balls: one at Central Masonic Hall and another at Carusi's. Despite Jackson being a Democrat, Boston Republicans honored him with 50-gun salutes in the morning and afternoon on inauguration day.

Rayon is a man-made fiber created from natural sources like wood and plants turned into cellulose. There are different types of rayon that can feel and look like natural fibers such as silk, wool, cotton, and linen. Rayon is a cellulose fiber, meaning it has the same structure as cellulose. Some rayon types, especially those that feel like silk, are called artificial silk. Rayon is used to make clothes and other fabrics. Viscose is another name for rayon.
Beaulencourt is a commune in the Pas-de-Calais department, which is in the Hauts-de-France region of northern France.

The ARIA charts, styled as ARIA Charts since November 2018, are the main music sales charts in Australia. They are released weekly by the Australian Recording Industry Association. The charts show the top-selling songs and albums in different music genres in Australia. ARIA became Australia's official music chart in June 1988, replacing the Kent Music Report, which was used from 1974 to 1988.

Eurovision: Europe Shine a Light was a live TV show. It was organized by the European Broadcasting Union and produced by Dutch broadcasters. The show replaced the Eurovision Song Contest 2020, which was supposed to be in Rotterdam but was canceled because of the coronavirus. The program was broadcast live from Hilversum, Netherlands, on May 16, 2020, and lasted about two hours. Chantal Janzen, Edsilia Rombley, and Jan Smit hosted it. They were originally chosen to host the Eurovision Song Contest 2020 before it was cancelled.
St. Francis is a city in Clay County, Arkansas, United States. It is located near the St. Francis River. The city's population was 250 in the 2010 census.

The Academy Awards for best dance direction were given from 1935 to 1937. Then, it was stopped.
Monsignor Bernardino Piñera Carvallo lived from September 22, 1915, to June 21, 2020. He was a bishop in the Catholic Church from Chile.

Jean-Martin Charcot, born on November 29, 1825, and died on August 16, 1893, was a French doctor who studied the nervous system. He is famous for his work on hypnosis and hysteria, especially with his patient Louise Augustine Gleizes. Known as "the founder of modern neurology," his name is linked to at least 15 medical terms, such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and Charcot disease. Charcot is considered "the father of French neurology and one of the world's pioneers in neurology." His research significantly impacted the fields of neurology and psychology. Modern psychiatry owes much to Charcot and his students. He was "the leading neurologist in late 19th-century France" and was called "the Napoleon of the neuroses."
Gigondas is a commune in the Vaucluse department, in the Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur region, in southeastern France.

Sylvia Robinson, born on May 29, 1935, and passed away on September 29, 2011, was an American singer, musician, record producer, and label executive. She had two hit R&B songs: "Love Is Strange" with Mickey & Sylvia in 1957, and "Pillow Talk" as a solo artist in 1973. Later, she founded and led Sugar Hill Records, a hip hop label. Robinson is known for her role in promoting two important hip hop songs: "Rapper's Delight" by The Sugarhill Gang in 1979, and "The Message" by Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five in 1982. Because of her contributions, she was called "the mother of hip-hop." In 2000, she received a Pioneer Award at the 11th Annual Rhythm and Blues Awards gala for her singing career and founding Sugarhill Records.

Jw-jones, born on July 15, 1980, is a Canadian blues guitarist, singer, songwriter, and band leader. He has won awards, including being a Juno Award nominee in 2015, and winning the International Blues Challenge for "Best Self-Produced CD" in 2017 for his album 'High Temperature.' Jones signed his first recording contract with Crosscut Records in Germany in 2000, releasing seven CDs in Europe. He was the first artist signed to the NorthernBlues Music label in Toronto, releasing six of his recordings with them. He has also worked with Ruf Records in the USA and Blind Pig Records. Jones has released nine studio albums and one live album. He has played music in 23 countries across four continents and continues to tour. Jw-jones lives in Ottawa, Ontario, and performs at blues festivals, theaters, and clubs in Canada, the USA, Europe, the UK, Russia, Australia, and Brazil. On June 19, 2014, he received the Forty Under 40 award from the Ottawa Business Journal/Ottawa Chamber of Commerce, recognizing his business achievements, professional skills, and community involvement.

The Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (RADA) is a drama school in London that teaches acting for film, TV, and theatre. It is in the Bloomsbury area, near the University of London's Senate House. RADA is part of a group of drama schools. Founded in 1904 by Herbert Beerbohm Tree, it moved to Gower Street in 1905. In 1920, it got a special royal permission and built a new theatre on Malet Street in 1921. The theatre opened with Prince Edward's help. The school got some money from the government in 1924. Today, RADA has five theatres and a cinema. It offers basic, college, and advanced courses. RADA's education is checked by King's College London. Edward Kemp is the current head of the school. Kenneth Branagh is the president, taking over from Richard Attenborough who died in 2014. The school is supported by Queen Elizabeth II.
The following is a list of notable deaths in April 2014. Each day's entries are arranged alphabetically by last name. A typical entry includes the following information in this order:

Jules Henri Poincaré, born on April 29, 1854, and died on July 17, 1912, was a French mathematician, physicist, engineer, and philosopher of science. He is known as a polymath and is often called "the last universalist" because he was skilled in all areas of mathematics during his lifetime. Poincaré made important contributions to pure and applied mathematics, physics, and celestial mechanics. His research on the three-body problem led him to discover chaos in deterministic systems, which is now a key part of chaos theory. He is also considered one of the founders of topology. Poincaré focused on the invariance of physical laws under different transformations, presenting the Lorentz transformations in their modern form. He also discovered additional relativistic velocity transformations and wrote about them in a letter to Hendrik Lorentz in 1905. This work helped in formulating the theory of special relativity. In 1905, Poincaré suggested that gravitational waves exist and travel at the speed of light, as required by the Lorentz transformations. The Poincaré group, used in physics and mathematics, is named after him. Early in the 20th century, he proposed the Poincaré conjecture, which became one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics. It was solved by Grigori Perelman in 2002–2003.

The vertical bar is a symbol used in math, computing, and typography. It has different names depending on its use: sheffer stroke in logic, verti-bar, vbar, stick, vertical line, vertical slash, bar, pike, or pipe. It is sometimes called a broken bar too.

Wellin is a municipality in Belgium, located in the province of Luxembourg. On January 1, 2007, it covered 67.52 square kilometers and had 2,958 people living there. This means there were about 44 people per square kilometer. Wellin includes the following smaller areas: Wellin, Chanly, Halma, Lomprez, and Sohier. Other towns nearby are Barzin, Froidlieu, Fays-Famenne, and Neupont.

Common wheat, also called bread wheat, is a type of cultivated wheat. Nearly all the wheat grown around the world is common wheat. It is the most widely grown crop and brings in the most money as a cereal.

Genealogy is the study of families and their history. Genealogists use interviews, documents, and other records to find out about family connections and create family trees or write stories about families. Family history includes more than just family connections; it also covers family and community stories. Genealogical work can be shown as a family tree or a family history. A family tree usually focuses on descendants of one person, while a family history often looks at the ancestors of one person, but these terms are often used together. Family histories can include personal stories and family traditions. People study family history for different reasons, such as understanding their place in history, preserving family stories, and telling accurate stories. Genealogy research is also done for academic and legal purposes.

Lynwood is a city in Los Angeles County, California. In 2010, it had about 69,772 people, slightly fewer than 69,845 in 2000. Lynwood is near South Gate and Compton, in the southern part of the Los Angeles basin. It became a city in 1921. It was named after Lynn Wood Sessions, who was the wife of Charles Sessions, a local dairyman. The nearby railroad siding and later Pacific Electric Railway station were also named after the dairy.

Churchill College is part of the University of Cambridge in England. It mainly teaches science, engineering, and technology but also has art and humanities classes. In 1958, a trust was set up with Winston Churchill as its chairman to build and fund the college as a memorial to him. It opened in 1960 with royal approval. The college is located on the outskirts of Cambridge, near the university's main new development area, which now has the Centre for Mathematical Sciences. It is the largest college in terms of grounds. Churchill was the first all-male college to accept women, and in 1972, it admitted its first women students. By 1987, all other male colleges had followed. The college is known for being less formal than other Cambridge colleges and admits more students from state schools. Its motto is "forward," taken from Winston Churchill's first speech as prime minister.
Puget can mean: Puget
Trachselwald is a municipality in the Emmental district of the Swiss canton of Bern.

Flensburg (in Danish: "Flensborg"; in Low Saxon: "Flensborg"; in North Frisian: "Flansborj"; in South Jutlandic: "Flensborre") is a town in northern Schleswig-Holstein, Germany. It is the center of the Southern Schleswig region. After Kiel and Lübeck, Flensburg is the third largest town in Schleswig-Holstein. In May 1945, Flensburg was the place where the last government of Nazi Germany, known as the Flensburg government led by Karl Dönitz, was based. This government lasted only one week, from May 1 to May 8, when Hitler was said to have died. It ended when German armies surrendered and Allied troops occupied the town. The Flensburg government was officially dissolved on May 23. The nearest big towns are Kiel to the south and Odense in Denmark to the northeast. Flensburg's city center is close to the Danish border. In geometry, a line segment is a part of a line that starts and ends at two different points. It includes all the points between those two points. A closed line segment includes both starting and ending points, while an open line segment does not include either point. A half-open line segment includes just one of the points. Examples of line segments are the sides of shapes like triangles or squares. If the endpoints are next to each other in a polygon or polyhedron, the line segment is an edge. Otherwise, it is a diagonal. If both endpoints are on a curve, like a circle, the line segment is called a chord.

James Edward Westcott was born on January 20, 1922, and died on March 29, 2019. He was an American photographer. During the Manhattan Project and the Cold War, he worked for the U.S. government in Oak Ridge, Tennessee. As one of the few people allowed to have a camera in that area during the Manhattan Project, he took many photos. These photos became the main record of building and running the Oak Ridge factories and of everyday life for civilians in the closed community of Oak Ridge.
Virginia is a city in Cass County, Illinois, United States. In 2010, it had 1,611 people. Virginia is also the county seat of Cass County.

Madonna Louise Ciccone, born on August 16, 1958, is an American singer, songwriter, actress, author, and record executive. Known as the "queen of pop" since the 1980s, she is considered one of the most influential figures in popular culture. Madonna is famous for constantly changing her style and showing versatility in music and visual presentation. She has challenged traditional music boundaries and controlled every part of her career. Her work, which includes themes like society, politics, sex, and religion, has been both praised and criticized. Born and raised in Michigan, Madonna moved to New York City in 1978 to become a dancer. After performing in rock bands like Breakfast Club and Emmy, she signed with Sire Records in 1982 and released her first album in 1983. Some of her popular albums are "Like a Virgin" (1984), "True Blue" (1986), "Ray of Light" (1998), and "Confessions on a Dance Floor" (2005). Many of her songs topped the charts, including "Like a Virgin," "Vogue," and "Hung Up." Madonna starred in movies like "Desperately Seeking Susan" (1985), "Dick Tracy" (1990), "A League of Their Own" (1992), and "Evita" (1996). While "Evita" won her a Golden Globe for best actress, other films were not well-received. As a businesswoman, she started a company called Maverick, which included a record label. She also created fashion brands, wrote children's books, started health clubs, and made films. Madonna has donated to charities, founding the Ray of Light Foundation in 1998 and raising money for Malawi in 2006. With over 300 million records sold worldwide, she is recognized as the best-selling female music artist by Guinness World Records. According to Billboard, Madonna is the top solo artist in terms of chart-topping singles. She has the most number-one singles by a female artist in several countries and is the highest-grossing solo touring artist, earning over $1.4 billion. In 2008, she was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. VH1 ranked her as the greatest woman in music, and Rolling Stone named her one of the greatest artists and songwriters of all time.

Love & Basketball is a 2000 American movie about romance and basketball. It stars Sanaa Lathan and Omar Epps. The story is about Quincy McCall, played by Omar Epps, and Monica Wright, played by Sanaa Lathan. They are neighbors in Los Angeles and play basketball. They fall in love. The movie was released on April 21, 2000, in the United States. Critics liked the film.
The duped journalist is a 1914 Hungarian silent film. Alexander Korda and Gyula Zilahi directed it.

"Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS" and "Super Smash Bros. for Wii U" are like other games in the "Super Smash Bros." series. In these games, players use different moves to make their opponents weak and knock them out of the playing area. These games mix characters, items, music, and stages from various Nintendo games and some other games made by different companies. The games started making in 2012 and were officially announced at E3 in 2013. The gameplay was made to be in between the faster, more competitive "Super Smash Bros. Melee" and the slower, more fun "Super Smash Bros. Brawl". New features in the games include up to eight players fighting at once on the Wii U version, support for Nintendo's amiibo, using custom Miis as characters, downloadable content like new characters and stages, and customizable special moves. Some features from previous games, like the story mode in "Brawl", were removed. Critics liked how the game elements were improved, but had some complaints about online play issues. Both versions did well in sales. By December 2017, the 3DS version had sold over nine million copies worldwide, and the Wii U version had sold over five million. After these games, "Super Smash Bros. Ultimate" came out for the Nintendo Switch in 2018.
Beverly Hills is a city in McLennan County, Texas, United States. In 2010, it had 1,995 people. The city is near Waco and is part of the Waco metropolitan area.

Pir Sultan Abdal lived around 1480 to 1550. He was a Turkish Alevi poet. His simple and clear words, rich imagination, and beautiful poems made him popular among Turkish people. He wrote about important topics like God, Islam, Prophet Muhammad, Imam Ali, and the twelve Imams. He also wrote about resistance, love, and peace. He was against strong rulers and had problems with the Ottoman government because of his rebellious ideas.
Frances Winfield was an American writer and speaker.
Guttet-Feschel is a municipality in the Leuk district of Valais in Switzerland. It was created by joining the towns of Guttet and Feschel in 2000.
Carol Greitzer was born on January 3, 1925. She is an American politician. Carol served in the New York City Council from 1969 to 1991. She was the first president of Naral Pro-Choice America.
Midland City is a town in Dale County, Alabama, United States. The population in 2010 was 2,344. It became a town in 1890. It is part of the Ozark micropolitan area.

Marian Jurczyk, born on October 16, 1935, and died on December 30, 2014, was a Polish politician and activist for the Solidarity trade union. He served as a senator in the Polish Senate from 1997 to 2000 and was the mayor of Szczecin from November 18, 1998, to January 24, 2000. He was again elected mayor on November 21, 2002, and held the position until December 4, 2006. Many of his achievements were criticized. He was blamed for paying over 10 million zlotys as compensation for canceling a land deal. He was also criticized for not having a formal education and making many mistakes. For example, he forgot the name of the deputy he had just nominated and quoted Jesus incorrectly in a speech to the council. Because of these criticisms, people called for his recall. On March 23, 2004, enough signatures were collected to start a recall process. A recall referendum was held on May 23, 2004. However, not enough people voted, with only 19% of voters participating. Despite the low turnout, 92% of those who did vote supported recalling the mayor.

Irvington is a town in Lancaster County, Virginia, United States. It had 432 people in the 2010 census. Irvington is on a peninsula called the Northern Neck. It is part of a historic district. A school called Chesapeake Academy was there from 1889 to 1907. One of the students from this school was Claybrook Cottingham. He later became an assistant principal there. In his career, he was also the president of Louisiana College in Pineville and Louisiana Tech University in Ruston.

Rafael Alkorta Martínez, born on September 16, 1968, is a Spanish former football player. He mainly played as a central defender. Currently, he works as the sporting director for Athletic Bilbao. During his 17-year professional career, Alkorta played for Athletic Bilbao and Real Madrid. He played in 370 La Liga matches and scored 8 goals. He won three trophies with Real Madrid. Alkorta also played for the Spanish national team in three World Cups in the 1990s.

Topfreedom is a movement that wants changes in laws. It aims to let women go topless in public places where men can be bare-chested. This is to make things fair for both genders. The movement wants to remove laws that stop women from showing their chests in public. Additionally, they support letting mothers feed their babies in public without covering up.
Leandro Damián Marcelo Grimi, born on February 9, 1985, is an Argentine football player. He plays as a left back for Club Atlético Huracán.

Ryland Heights is a city in Kenton County, Kentucky, United States. According to the 2010 census, the population was 1,022. In 2000, the population was 799. It is part of the Cincinnati metropolitan area.

The Gibson Les Paul is a solid body electric guitar first sold by Gibson in 1952. It was designed by Gibson's president Ted McCarty, factory manager John Huis, and their team with Les Paul's help. It usually has a solid mahogany body with a carved maple top, a mahogany neck, a rosewood fretboard, two pickups with volume and tone controls, and a stoptail bridge. Some versions have a gold finish and two p-90 pickups. In 1957, humbucking pickups were added, and in 1958, sunburst finishes were introduced. The sunburst 1958-1960 Les Paul became famous, but sales were low. In 1961, it was redesigned into the Gibson SG. In 1968, the single-cutaway version was reintroduced. Many versions of the Les Paul have been made since. Along with the Fender Telecaster and Stratocaster, it was one of the first mass-produced electric solid-body guitars. Les Paul guitars are versatile and have been used in many types of music, such as rock, country, pop, soul, blues, jazz, reggae, punk, and heavy metal.

Ioannis Veryvakis was a Greek army officer. He became a full general. Veryvakis held important positions, including Chief of the Hellenic Army General Staff and Chief of the Hellenic National Defence General Staff. He was born on November 3, 1930, and passed away on June 19, 2019.

Anna Jókai (Hungarian: "Jókai Anna") was an author, poet, and teacher from Hungary. She started writing in 1974. In the 1980s, she was part of a movement to free Hungary. From 1990 to 1992, she led the Hungarian Writers' Union.

Hans Schneider was born on January 24, 1927, in Vienna, Austria, and died on October 28, 2014. He was a mathematician and taught at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. He was the first president of the International Matrix Group from 1987 to 1990 and its successor, the International Linear Algebra Society, from 1990 to 1996. The society set up the Hans Schneider Prize in 1993. Schneider was one of the creators of the journal "Linear Algebra and Its Applications" from 1968 to 1972 and then served as its editor from 1972 to 2012. He was also an advisor for the "Electronic Journal of Linear Algebra." He earned his Ph.D. in 1952 from the University of Edinburgh, with Alexander Craig Aitken as his advisor. Schneider taught at Queen's University Belfast until 1959, then moved to the University of Wisconsin, where he retired in 1993. He wrote more than 160 research papers on topics like Perron Frobenius theory and inertia theory. For his experiences between 1938 and 1940, see the Kindertransport site. Schneider died of cancer at the age of 87. His grandson, Kurt Hugo Schneider, is a YouTube musician/producer.

Lohengrin is a character in German Arthurian stories. He is the son of Parzival and a knight of the Holy Grail. Lohengrin comes in a boat pulled by swans to save a princess, but she cannot ask his name. This story first appeared in Wolfram von Eschenbach's "Parzival." Later, it was expanded in two other stories. In 1848, Richard Wagner wrote an opera called "Lohengrin" based on this legend.

Barbour County is in north-central West Virginia, USA. In 2010, it had 16,589 people. The county seat is Philippi, which was founded in 1844. Both the county and the city are named after Philip Pendleton Barbour (1783-1841), a former U.S. congressman from Virginia and an associate justice of the U.S. Supreme Court. Barbour County was created in 1843 when the area was still part of Virginia. In 1871, a small part was given to Tucker County. The Battle of Philippi, known as the "Philippi Races," happened in Barbour County on June 3, 1861. This was one of the first battles of the American Civil War. Alderson Broaddus University, a Baptist school, is in the county. The university's Physician Assistant program is one of the oldest and best in the world.

African continent is the second largest and second most populous in the world, after Asia. It covers about 30.3 million square kilometers, which is about 6% of Earth's total surface and 20% of its land. With around 1 billion people, it has about 16% of the world's population. Africa's average population is young, with a median age of 19.7 in 2012, compared to 30.4 worldwide. Despite having many natural resources, Africa is the least wealthy continent per person. This might be because of past European colonization. However, recent economic growth and a young, large population make it important for global business. Africa borders the Mediterranean Sea to the north, the Red Sea to the northeast, the Indian Ocean to the southeast, and the Atlantic Ocean to the west. Madagascar and other islands are also part of it. It has 54 fully recognized countries, eight territories, and two self-governing regions with limited recognition. Algeria is the largest country by area, and Nigeria has the most people. African countries work together through the African Union, headquartered in Addis Ababa. Africa has many climates and a lot of different animals. Climate change and environmental issues like desertification, deforestation, and water shortages are big problems there. Africa is widely believed to be where humans first came from, and where hominids, the group of great apes, evolved. Early human species, like Homo sapiens, first appeared in Africa. Ancient civilizations, such as ancient Egypt and Phoenicia, emerged in North Africa. Over the past 400 years, European influence has grown in Africa, starting with the slave trade in the 16th century. European colonization in the late 19th century led to most current African countries gaining independence in the 20th century.

Human cloning is creating a copy of a person who is genetically identical. It usually means making copies of human cells and tissues artificially, not the natural birth of identical twins. People are worried about cloning humans. Laws about cloning have been made in some countries. There are two main types of human cloning: one for medicine, and one to have a cloned person. The cloning for medicine involves using cloned cells to help treat illnesses or do transplants. Scientists are working on this but it's not used in hospitals yet. Two ways they are researching are somatic-cell nuclear transfer and pluripotent stem cell induction. Cloning to have a person involves making an entire human copy, not just cells or tissues.
Dorothea Sally Eilers was an actress from the United States. She was born on December 11, 1908, and died on January 5, 1978.

A satellite state is a country that appears independent but is strongly influenced or controlled by another, usually more powerful, country. The term comes from comparing these states to moons orbiting a planet. It was mainly used for countries in Central and Eastern Europe during the Cold War, like those in the Warsaw Pact, and for Mongolia and Tannu Tuva between 1924 and 1990. For Central and Eastern European countries, this term suggests they were under Soviet control. In some cases, it also referred to other countries like North Korea (around 1950-1953) and Cuba (after joining Comecon in 1972). The term is used less often for other countries outside the Soviet sphere. In Soviet times, the term also applied to states influenced by Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy, and Imperial Japan. The phrase "satellite state" has been used in English since at least 1916. During conflicts or tense periods, satellite states can act as a buffer between the controlling country and its enemies. The term "satellite state" is one of several that describe a state's alleged dependence on another. Other terms include "puppet state" and "neo-colony." Generally, "satellite state" suggests strong ideological and military ties, while "puppet state" indicates political and military dependence, and "neo-colony" implies heavy economic dependence. A state may fit into more than one category depending on which type of dependence is emphasized.

The car-free movement is a broad, informal, and growing network of people and groups. These include social activists, urban planners, and transportation experts. They share a belief that cars and other motorized vehicles are too dominant in most cities. The movement's goal is to reduce or eliminate the use of motorized vehicles. They do this by changing roads and parking spaces for other uses. They also rebuild cities so that most places are close enough for walking, cycling, or using public transport, personal transporters, or mobility services.
George Peter Alexander Healy was an American painter who lived from July 15, 1813, to June 24, 1894. He painted many portraits and was very popular. He painted important people of his time.

Fort Wayne is a city in Indiana, the U.S., and is the biggest city in the Allen County. It is in northeastern Indiana, close to the Ohio and Michigan borders. With 253,691 people in 2010, it is the second-largest city in Indiana after Indianapolis, and the 75th-largest in the United States. Fort Wayne is the main city in the Fort Wayne Metropolitan Area, which includes Allen, Wells, and Whitley counties, with 419,453 people in 2011. It is a cultural and economic center in northeastern Indiana. Fort Wayne was founded by the U.S. Army in 1794, named after General Anthony Wayne. The city grew at the rivers where traders met pioneers. It was officially laid out in 1823 and expanded when the Wabash and Erie Canal and railroads were built. Once a big manufacturing town in the Rust Belt, Fort Wayne now focuses on distribution, transportation, healthcare, professional services, leisure, and finance. It also has many jobs in the defense industry and healthcare. Fort Wayne won the All-America City award in 1982, 1998, and 2009, and got a City Livability Award from the U.S. Conference of Mayors in 1999.

Matthias Lukas Ginter was born on January 19, 1994. He is a German football player. He plays as a center back. He plays for Borussia Mönchengladbach in the Bundesliga. He also plays for the Germany national team.

J. Whyatt Mondesire was a reporter for "The Philadelphia Inquirer" when he started his career. He was the owner of the "Philadelphia Sun" newspaper when he died. He also served as the president of the Philadelphia branch of the NAACP for more than ten years.
A consumer is a person or group who buys goods, products, or services to use for personal, social, family, or household needs. They do not buy these things to start a business.
