Publius (or Gaius) Cornelius Tacitus lived from the first to the second century AD. He was a Roman historian and politician. Tacitus is considered one of the best Roman historians by modern scholars. He wrote during what is known as the Silver Age of Latin literature. His writing is known for being clear and concise. Tacitus wrote two major works: the "Annals" and the "Histories." These works cover the Roman Empire from 14 AD to 70 AD, focusing on the reigns of emperors Tiberius, Claudius, Nero, and those of the Year of the Four Emperors in 69 AD. There are missing parts in his writings, particularly a four-book gap in the "Annals." Besides his major works, Tacitus also wrote about oratory, Germania, and his father-in-law, Agricola, who was a general responsible for the Roman conquest of Britain.

Pratval was a former municipality in the Hinterrhein district of the Swiss canton of Graubünden. On January 1, 2015, Pratval merged with the municipalities of Almens, Paspels, Rodels, and Tomils to form the new municipality of Domleschg.

Kaoru Moto was born on April 25, 1917, and died on August 26, 1992. He served in the United States Army. After he died, he was given a very important award—the Medal of Honor. This award was given for his brave actions during World War II.
In the 1957-58 season, the Dutch Eerste Divisie had 32 teams. These teams were split into two groups. Willem II and SHS won the championship.

Cameron Barker was born on April 4, 1986. He is a Canadian professional ice hockey player who currently has no team. He recently played for the Ilves Tampere in Finland. Barker was chosen third in the 2004 NHL draft by the Chicago Blackhawks. He played for the Blackhawks for four years before being traded to the Minnesota Wild in 2010. Barker also played for Canada's national team and won two gold medals in the World Junior Championships in 2005 and 2006. People often think the Blackhawks made a poor choice when they selected him.

Karnali Zone was one of the fourteen zones in Nepal's mid-western region. Its headquarters were in Jumla. Karnali was one of Nepal's poorest and most remote areas, hard to reach by road. Airports were in all districts except Kalikot, which was linked to Jumla airport by seasonal roads. Karnali was Nepal's largest zone and had two national parks. Shey Phoksundo National Park, which includes the deepest lake in Nepal, was the biggest park. It covers 3,555 km² and is famous for snow leopards. Rara National Park, known as the "Pearl of Nepal," surrounds Rara Lake, which is the country's largest at 10.2 km². In 2015, Karnali Zone was divided into five districts, which are now called Karnali Pradesh.

Grandval is a town in the Jura Bernois area of the canton of Bern in Switzerland. It is in the French-speaking part of the Bernese Jura. Grandval used to be called "Granfel" or "Granfelden" in German, but people no longer use these names.

Mario Altmann, born on November 4, 1986, is an Austrian ice hockey player. He currently plays for EHC Black Wings Linz in the Austrian Hockey League (EBEL). Altmann previously played for EC VSV for five seasons. On April 16, 2015, he signed a one-year contract with EHC Black Wings Linz, an Austrian team. Altmann has been on the Austria men's national ice hockey team for a long time. He played in the 2009, 2011, and 2014 IIHF World Championships and also competed in the 2014 Winter Olympics.

Cee Lo Green's "Magic Moment" is his first Christmas album and his fourth overall studio album. It came out on October 29, 2012, in the UK. The US version was released on October 30, 2012, by Elektra Records. Two of his songs, "Mary, Did You Know?" and "What Christmas Means to Me," reached number 22 and 23 on the US R&B charts on December 22, 2012. In 2012, the album sold 181,000 copies in the US. This is Cee Lo Green's first solo Christmas album without a parental advisory label.
Jimmy Morales, born James Ernesto Morales Cabrera on March 18, 1969, is a Guatemalan politician, actor, and comedian. He was the 50th president of Guatemala from 2016 to 2020.

The Yukon River is a big river in northwestern North America. It starts in British Columbia, Canada, and flows through the Canadian Yukon Territory, named after the river. In Alaska, the United States, the river runs for a long distance and empties into the Bering Sea at the Yukon–Kuskokwim Delta. The river is 3,200 kilometers long and has an average flow of 227,000 feet per second. Its total drainage area is 321,500 square miles, with 126,300 square miles in Canada. This area is bigger than the states of Texas or Alberta. The Yukon River is the longest in Alaska and Yukon and was a key route during the 1896–1903 Klondike Gold Rush. A part of the river in Yukon, called "The Thirty Mile" section, is a national heritage river. Paddle-wheel boats used to travel on the river until the 1950s when the Klondike Highway was built. After the United States bought Alaska in 1867, the Alaska Commercial Company set up posts along the river. The Yukon River has faced pollution from military sites, dumps, and wastewater, but it is not listed as an impaired watershed. The river's water quality is good for turbidity, metals, and dissolved oxygen, better than other Arctic rivers. The Yukon River Inter-Tribal Watershed Council, made up of 70 tribes and nations, works to make the river drinkable again by checking government data.

Rancho Palos Verdes, also called RPV or Palos Verdes, is a coastal city in Los Angeles County, California. It sits on the bluffs of the Palos Verdes Peninsula and neighbors other cities, like Palos Verdes Estates, Rolling Hills, and Rolling Hills Estates. This city is famous for its amazing views of the Pacific Ocean, Santa Catalina Island, and Los Angeles. It also has highly-rated schools, many horse and hiking trails, and very expensive homes.

Ratnasambhava means "jewel-born." He is one of five meditation buddhas in Vajrayana or tantric Buddhism. Ratnasambhava helps with developing equanimity and equality. In Buddhist thought, he is linked to overcoming greed and pride. His partner is Mamaki, and he rides a horse or a pair of lions.

Swatch introduced Internet Time, or.beat time, in 1998. This is a new way of telling time. Instead of hours and minutes, the day is divided into 1,000 parts called.beats. Each.beat lasts 86.4 seconds, which is just over 1 minute and 26 seconds. To write the time, you use a 3-digit number out of 1,000 after midnight. For example, 248.beats would be just over 5 hours and 57 minutes after midnight. Swatch Internet Time doesn't have time zones. Instead, a new time scale called Biel Mean Time (BMT) is used. BMT is based on Swatch's headquarters in Biel, Switzerland, and is the same as Central European Time, West Africa Time, and UTC+01. Swatch Internet Time doesn't change for daylight saving time like regular time in Switzerland and many other countries does.

The covalent radius, "r," measures the size of an atom that forms part of a covalent bond. It is typically measured in picometres (pm) or angstroms (Å), where 1 Å equals 100 pm. In theory, the sum of the two covalent radii should equal the covalent bond length between two atoms, "r" (ab) = "r" (a) + "r" (b). For single, double, and triple bonds, different radii can be used, but these are just for practical purposes. These relationships aren't exact because an atom's size varies based on its chemical environment. For different types of bonds, ionic factors might be involved. Often, polar covalent bonds are shorter than expected based on the sum of covalent radii. Covalent radii in tables are usually average or idealized values, but they still provide useful information. Bond lengths "r" (ab) are determined using X-ray diffraction (and less commonly, neutron diffraction on molecular crystals). Rotational spectroscopy can also provide very accurate bond lengths. For homonuclear bonds (same atoms bonded together), Linus Pauling suggested the covalent radius is half the single-bond length in the element, like "r" (H-H in H) = 74.14 pm, so "r" (H) = 37.07 pm. In practice, an average value from various covalent compounds is usually used, with small differences. Sanderson has recently published non-polar covalent radii for main-group elements. However, large collections of bond lengths, which are more transferable, from the Cambridge Crystallographic Database have made covalent radii less necessary in many cases.

Osvaldo Bayer was an Argentine writer and journalist. He lived in Buenos Aires. In 1974, during Isabel Perón's presidency, he went to live in Linz am Rhein, Germany. This was during a time of dictatorship in Argentina, from 1976 to 1983.

The December 2010 North American blizzard was a big snowstorm. It happened from December 5 to December 29, 2010, in parts of the United States and Canada. From January 4 to January 15, it was called "Windstorm Benjamin" in Europe. This was the first big winter storm of the 2010-2011 season and the fifth blizzard in 2010. The storm hit many cities in the northeast, including Norfolk, Philadelphia, Newark, New York City, Hartford, Providence, and Boston. It brought lots of snow to these areas.
Carol Cleveland, born on January 13, 1942, is an actress and comedian from Britain and the United States. She is especially famous for her work with Monty Python.
Sandslån is a small place in Kramfors municipality, Västernorrland county, Sweden. In 2010, it had 272 people living there.

Muscular dystrophy (MD) is a group of muscle diseases that make skeletal muscles weaken and break down over time. The conditions differ in which muscles are affected, how weak they become, how quickly they get worse, and when symptoms start. Many people eventually cannot walk. Some types also cause problems in other organs. There are about 30 genetic disorders in the muscular dystrophy group, usually divided into nine main types. The most common type, Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), usually affects boys starting around age four. Other types include Becker muscular dystrophy, facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy, limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, and myotonic dystrophy. These conditions are caused by gene mutations that affect muscle protein production. Mutations can come from parents or happen during early development. Some types are inherited, while others are passed on in different ways. Diagnosis often involves blood tests and genetic testing. There is no cure for muscular dystrophy. Treatments like physical therapy, braces, and corrective surgery can help some symptoms. People with weak breathing muscles may need assisted ventilation. Medications include steroids to slow muscle breakdown, anticonvulsants to control seizures and some muscle activity, and immunosuppressants to delay damage to dying muscle cells. The outcome depends on the specific type of disorder. Duchenne muscular dystrophy, which is about half of all cases, affects about one in 5,000 boys at birth. The term "dystrophy" comes from Greek words meaning "difficult" and "nourish." Gene therapy as a treatment is still being studied.

In Norse mythology, Sigyn is a goddess and Loki's wife. She is mentioned in the "Poetic Edda" and the "Prose Edda." In the "Poetic Edda," only a little is known about her, mainly that she helped Loki during his captivity. In the "Prose Edda," she again helps Loki in his time as a prisoner. She also appears in some kennings and is called a goddess twice. Some people think she is shown on the Gosforth Cross. Sigyn has been the subject of theories and cultural references.
Bluebells, or bluebelle, can also be called bluebells.

Rain is a town in the Donau-Ries district of Bavaria, Germany. It is located near the confluence of the Lech and Danube rivers, about 11 kilometers east of Donauwörth. Rain is on the B16 road and has a railway that connects Ulm and Regensburg. The town was first mentioned in 1257 in a document from the Niederschönenfeld monastery. Rain was probably founded between 1248 and 1294. It was created for economic and strategic reasons, protecting Bavaria from the northwest and collecting tolls from a bridge over the Lech river. During the Thirty Years War, the Battle of Rain took place on April 15, 1632. The Swedish army of Gustavus Adolphus won against the Catholic League army led by Johann Tserclaes von Tilly, who died in Ingolstadt from an infection. A monument to von Tilly was erected in front of Rain's Rococo town hall in 1914. Rain has an old Catholic church with late Gothic paintings from around 1480, the Schwabian Gate, a historic hospital with an All Saints' chapel, and an old castle. The town also has three museums: the Lachner Brothers Museum, the Homeland Museum, and the Jean-Duprai Museum. Four Lachner brothers, composers from the 19th century, were born in Rain. Other notable people from Rain include lawyer and astronomer Johann Bayer, humanist Georg Tannstetter, and pianist Michael Raucheisen. Rain is the headquarters of the Dehner chain of garden centers, employing 1,100 people. Other industries in Rain include a sugar refinery with 240 to 280 employees. Rain is also twinned with Tougan, the capital of the Sourou province in Burkina Faso.
Heinrich Ludwig Futterer was born on October 14, 1931, and died on February 10, 2019. He was a German athlete who mainly ran sprint events.

Viktor Fedorovych Yanukovych, born on July 9, 1950, was a Ukrainian politician. He became the fourth president of Ukraine in 2010. He lost his job during the 2014 Ukrainian revolution and now lives in Russia. Yanukovych worked as the governor of Donetsk, an eastern Ukrainian province, from 1997 to 2002. He was Ukraine's prime minister twice, first from November 21, 2002, to December 7, 2004, and again from December 28, 2004, to January 5, 2005, under President Leonid Kuchma. In 2004, Yanukovych ran for president. He went to the second round of voting but was later declared the winner. However, there were claims of cheating and voter threats, leading to protests and the so-called Orange Revolution. The Ukrainian court voided the election and ordered a re-run. Yanukovych lost the re-run to Viktor Yushchenko. He served as prime minister again from August 4, 2006, to December 18, 2007, under President Yushchenko. In 2010, Yanukovych was elected president against Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko. International observers said the election was fair. In November 2013, Yanukovych refused to sign an agreement with the European Union and chose to get a Russian loan instead. This decision sparked protests, with people occupying Kyiv's Independence Square, an event known as Euromaidan. In January 2014, clashes at Independence Square and other places turned violent. Yanukovych left Kyiv for Kharkiv and eventually went to Russia. On February 22, the Ukrainian parliament removed him from his position. They set May 25 as the date for a new election and issued a warrant for his arrest. Yanukovych declared himself the legitimate president. In 2015, Ukraine's parliament removed his title of president. In 2019, he was sentenced in absentia to 13 years in prison for high treason.
To catch a killer is a 1992 TV movie. Eric Till directed it. Brian Dennehy and Michael Riley acted in it. The story is real and about catching the American serial killer John Wayne Gacy.

The Schwarzschild radius, sometimes called the gravitational radius, is a special measurement. It appears in a solution to Einstein's field equations and defines the event horizon of a Schwarzschild black hole. This radius is related to any amount of mass. Karl Schwarzschild, a German astronomer, figured out this solution in 1916. The Schwarzschild radius is calculated using this formula: Sch. r = (2 × g × m) / c² Here, "g" is the gravitational constant, "m" is the mass of the object, and "c" is the speed of light.
This is a list of important people who were born, raised, or live in Florida.

João Teixeira de Faria, also known as João de Deus, was born on June 24, 1942. He is from Brazil and claims to be a medium and psychic surgeon. People also say he is a convicted sex offender. He worked in Abadiânia, Brazil, at Casa de Dom Inácio de Loyola, a spiritual healing center. He appeared on CNN, ABC News, and the Oprah Winfrey Show. James Randi and Joe Nickell said his healing methods were just carnival tricks. There is no proof that his patients got real benefits—most likely it was just the placebo effect. In 2018, after over 600 accusations of sexual abuse, he went to the police. In December 2019, he was sentenced to 19 years and 4 months in prison for raping four women. In January 2020, he was sentenced to an extra 40 years for raping five women. This was his third conviction, and the total sentence is 63 years and 4 months.
Oxford is a town in Maine, United States. It had 4,110 people in 2010. Oxford has a race track, a yearly fair, and a casino. The town also includes a place called Welchville.

In 235 BC, it was a year in the pre-Julian Roman calendar. At that time, it was called the year of the consulship of Torquatus and Bulbus, or sometimes the 519th year since the founding of Rome (ab urbe condita). People have used the year 235 BC since the early medieval period. This is when anno domini (AD) became the common way to name years in Europe.

Princess Amelia of the United Kingdom was born on August 7, 1783, and died on November 2, 1810. She was the fifteenth and last child, and the sixth daughter of King George III and his wife, Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz. Princess Amelia was their first daughter to pass away and the third child to die.
Gianni Morandi, born on December 11, 1944, is an Italian singer, actor, and entertainer.
San Carlos is a community in Hidalgo County, Texas. It had 3,130 people according to the 2010 census. San Carlos is part of the McAllen-Edinburg-Mission area. It is located northeast of McAllen.

The pedal steel guitar is a type of steel guitar with pedals and knee levers. These allow players to change the pitch of certain strings, making it possible to play more varied and complex music than before. Like other steel guitars, it can produce sliding notes and deep vibrato, similar to the human voice. It is most often used in American country music. In the 1950s, pedals and knee levers were added to steel guitars. This made it easier to play a major scale without moving the bar. Players could also push the pedals while playing chords, causing the notes to slide or bend into harmony with others. This created a unique sound first used in country and western music. The steel guitar sound began in Hawaii in the 19th century and became popular in the United States by the early 20th century. This led to the development of new instruments played horizontally, like the lap steel and resonator guitar. In 1934, the electric guitar pickup was invented, allowing steel guitars to be heard as well as other instruments. Amplification led to the creation of the electrified lap steel, then the console steel, and finally the pedal steel guitar. Playing the pedal steel guitar requires special skills, as players need to use both hands, feet, and knees at the same time. Only the American reed organ has similar demands. Key inventors include Buddy Emmons, Bud Isaacs, Zane Beck, and Paul Bigsby. The instrument is used not only in American country music but also in sacred music in the eastern and southern United States, jazz, and Nigerian music.

Twiztid is an American horrorcore duo from Detroit, Michigan. They started in 1997 and are made up of Jamie Spaniolo and Paul Methric, who use the stage names Jamie Madrox and Monoxide. Spaniolo and Methric used to be in a group called House of Krazees, which broke up in 1997. They made their first album in 1997. Twiztid worked with a record label called Psychopathic Records from 1997 until December 12, 2012, when they left. After that, they created their own label, Majik Ninja Entertainment, in 2014. Twiztid makes horrorcore rap and has released 12 studio albums, 12 EPs, 10 compilation albums, and 1 mixtape.
Gabriel Pereira de Castro (1571-1632) was a Portuguese priest, lawyer, and poet.

Crystal Palace Football Club is based in Selhurst, South London, England. They play in the Premier League, the top level of English football. The club was officially founded in 1905, but claims to be a continuation of an amateur club established in 1861 by the same Crystal Palace company. This makes Crystal Palace one of the oldest professional football clubs in the world. Both the amateur and professional clubs were founded at the Crystal Palace exhibition building and played there until 1915 when they had to leave due to the First World War. In 1924, the club moved to Selhurst Park, where they play today. The amateur club was one of the original members of the Football Association in 1863 and competed in the first FA Cup in 1871–72, reaching the semi-finals. They disappeared from records after the 1875–76 FA Cup. Crystal Palace became a professional club in 1905 and applied to join the Football League but were rejected, instead playing in the Southern League. They joined the Football League in 1920 and have mostly competed in the top two tiers of English football since. They have only dropped to the third tier once, from 1974 to 1977. Crystal Palace had a successful period in the late 1980s and early 1990s, finishing third in the league in the 1990–91 season. They were FA Cup finalists twice, losing to Manchester United in 1990 and 2016. The club's kit colors changed from claret and blue to red and blue vertical stripes in 1973. Crystal Palace has a long rivalry with Brighton & Hove Albion, and also with Millwall and Charlton Athletic, fellow South London clubs.
A gag is a tool made to stop someone from talking. It can also stand for "gag," which is an acronym.

The great seal of Connecticut has been its coat of arms since May 1784. It shows three grapevines. There is also a ribbon below with the Latin motto: "He who transplanted sustains." In the border, it says "Seal of the State of Connecticut."

Gomillion vs. Lightfoot, 364 U.S. 339 (1960), was a major court case. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that an electoral district with unfair boundaries, created to stop black people from voting, broke the Fifteenth Amendment.

Richard Falk, born on November 13, 1930, is a professor at Princeton University. He specializes in international law. He has written or co-written 20 books and edited or co-edited 20 more. In 2008, the United Nations Human Rights Council appointed him to a six-year job. His job was to look at human rights in the Palestinian territories since 1967.

Horace Silver Martin Tavares Silver (September 2, 1928 – June 18, 2014) was an American jazz pianist, composer, and arranger, especially known for his hard bop style. He started playing piano and tenor saxophone in Connecticut schools. In 1950, his piano trio joined Stan Getz. Silver moved to New York City, where he became well-known for his bluesy playing and composing. His work with Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers drew more attention to his music. They recorded "Horace Silver and the Jazz Messengers," which included his first hit song, "The Preacher." Silver formed his own quintet in 1956, with a typical group of tenor saxophone, trumpet, piano, bass, and drums. Their performances and recordings for Blue Note Records made Silver more popular. His most successful album was "Song for My Father," recorded with his quintet in 1963 and 1964. In the early 1970s, Silver stopped his group to spend time with his wife and focus on composing. He added lyrics to his music and became interested in spiritualism. This often led to unsuccessful releases like the "The United States of Mind" series. Silver left Blue Note in 1978, started his own record label, and reduced his tours in the 1980s, relying on income from his compositions. In 1993, Silver returned to major record labels and released five albums before withdrawing from public view due to health issues. As a player, Silver moved from bebop to hard bop by emphasizing melodies. His compositions had catchy tunes and sometimes included dissonant harmonies. Many of his songs, like "Doodlin'," "Peace," and "Sister Sadie," became jazz standards still played today. Silver's work influenced other pianists and composers and helped young jazz musicians for over four decades.

Leo Keith Thorsness was born on February 14, 1932, and died on May 2, 2017. He was a colonel in the United States Air Force. Thorsness got a very high award called the Medal of Honor for what he did during the Vietnam War. He was given this award for a brave flight on April 19, 1967. Two weeks later, he was shot down and became a prisoner of war in North Vietnam for six years. After his time in the military, Thorsness served one term in the Washington State Senate.
Saint-Vigor-des-Mézerets was a town in Calvados, in Normandy, France. On January 1, 2017, it became part of a new town called Terres de Druance.

Rex Taylor Reed was born on October 2, 1938. He is an American film critic and has acted occasionally. Rex Reed was also a co-host on the TV show "At the Movies." He writes a column called "On the Town with Rex Reed" for "The New York Observer."

Consumer confidence measures how optimistic people feel about the economy and their finances. When they feel confident, they tend to spend more. High consumer confidence means more purchases. Low confidence leads to more saving and less spending. Consumer confidence changes month by month, showing their views on jobs and the economy. It usually rises during economic growth and falls during contraction. In the U.S., consumer confidence often follows the stock market, but with a delay.

Lawrenceville is a city in Lawrence County, Illinois, United States. It's in the southeast part of Illinois, near Vincennes, Indiana. The city has about 4,348 people. Lawrenceville is also the county seat. The Lawrenceville high school basketball team, called the Indians, won the state championship in 1972, 1974, 1982, and 1983. They didn't lose a single game in those years. The coach was Ron Felling. After coaching in Lawrenceville, Felling became an assistant coach at Indiana University.

Sheikh Ahmed Ismail Hassan Yassin (1937-2004) was a Palestinian imam and politician. He founded Hamas, an Islamic Palestinian group that provides charity and services but also did attacks on civilians. Hamas was seen as good because it helped with hospitals, schools, and libraries. It was also seen as bad because it did attacks, and was called a terrorist group by many countries. Yassin was paralyzed from a sports accident when he was 12 and nearly blind. He used a wheelchair. He was killed by an Israeli helicopter missile after morning prayers. His death, which also killed his guards and nine others, was very criticized. About 200,000 Palestinians attended his funeral.

Alfred Gomolka was a German politician who lived from July 21, 1942, to March 24, 2020. He worked in the European Parliament for Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. He also became the minister president of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

In Norse mythology, the megingjörð, meaning "power-belt" in Old Norse, is a belt worn by the god Thor. The Old Norse word "megin" means power or strength, and "gjörð" means belt. According to the "Prose Edda," the belt is one of Thor's three main possessions, along with his hammer Mjölnir and iron gloves Járngreipr. When worn, it doubles Thor's strength. In the 10th-century poem "Þórsdrápa," which was written by the poet Eilífr Goðrúnarson, mentions Thor's power-belt. A line from the poem reads: "He who benefits from the mighty belt," referring to Thor's magical belt or girdle of strength, the megingjörð. In "Gylfaginning," the first part of Snorri Sturluson's "Prose Edda," it says that when dawn came, Thor went out, standing close to where he lay in the forest, and he was not small. He fell asleep and grew very strong. Then Thor realized what had happened during the night. He put on his belt of strength, and his divine strength increased. He then woke up quickly and stood up. It is said that Thor became very strong, and he was able to use his hammer to fight.

John Francis Welch Jr. was born on November 19, 1935, and died on March 1, 2020. He was an American business leader, chemical engineer, and writer. Welch was the chairman and CEO of General Electric (GE) from 1981 to 2001. When he left GE, he got a large payment of $417 million, which was the biggest such payment in business history. In 2006, Welch's wealth was about $720 million.

Soy milk, also called soya milk or soymilk, is a drink made from soybeans. To make it, you soak and grind soybeans, boil the mixture, and then filter out the remaining bits. It has a mixture of oil, water, and protein, and it's similar to a by-product of making tofu. Soy milk came from East Asia and became popular in Europe and North America in the latter part of the 20th century, especially as methods were developed to make it taste more like regular milk. People use soy milk instead of dairy milk for various reasons, such as being vegan, lactose intolerant, or for environmental and health reasons.

Terneuzen is a city and municipality in southwestern Netherlands, in Zeeland province. It is in the middle of Zeelandic Flanders. With more than 55,000 people, it is the largest municipality in Zeeland.

"March on, Bahamaland" is the national anthem of the Bahamas. Timothy Gibson wrote both the music and the lyrics. The country chose this as its national anthem in 1973, after gaining independence from the United Kingdom. Before that, they used "God Save the Queen" as their royal anthem.

The Queanbeyan River is a constant stream in the Molonglo catchment area of the Murray–Darling Basin. It is in New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory in Australia. The river is long and covers a catchment area. The Queanbeyan River and the Cotter River provide clean water for Canberra and Queanbeyan. Their water quality is protected by federal laws. It is thought the local Aboriginal Ngarigo people used a word that sounded like "Queanbeyan" to mean "clearwater."

Hannah Dominique E. John-Kamen, born on September 7, 1989, is an English actress. She is famous for playing Yalena "Dutch" Yardeen in the TV show "Killjoys." She also acted as Orlena in "Game of Thrones," F'nale Zandor in "Ready Player One," Ava Starr/Ghost in "Ant-Man and the Wasp," and the main character in "The Stranger," a Netflix mystery series.

William Shakespeare belonged to the King's Men for most of his career. This company was called the Lord Chamberlain's Men during Queen Elizabeth I's time. In 1603, when King James I became the new ruler, they changed their name to the King's Men. King James supported this acting company. On May 19, 1603, a royal letter named the players: Lawrence Fletcher, William Shakespeare, Richard Burbage, Augustine Phillips, John Heminges, Henry Condell, William Sly, Robert Armin, and Richard Cowley. These nine men became grooms of the chamber. On March 15, 1604, each of these nine men received four and a half yards of red cloth for a coronation procession.

The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic in the Philippines is part of a global pandemic caused by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). The first case in the Philippines was found on January 30, 2020, involving a 38-year-old Chinese woman in Metro Manila. The country's first confirmed death from the disease occurred on February 1, from a 44-year-old Chinese man. After no cases for over a month, the Philippines confirmed its first local transmission on March 7. Since then, the virus has spread to all 17 regions of the country. Socio-economic status has been linked to the number of cases. As of August 21, 2020, there were 182,365 confirmed cases in the Philippines, with 114,519 recoveries and 2,940 deaths. The Philippines has the highest number of confirmed cases in Southeast Asia, ahead of Indonesia and Singapore, ranking 9th in Asia and 22nd in the world. The largest single-day increase in cases was on August 10, with 6,958 new cases. In the early months of the pandemic, the Philippines had lower testing capacity compared to its Southeast Asian neighbors. Testing was sometimes done outside the country due to a lack of testing kits, leading to controversies involving government officials. By January 2020, the Research Institute for Tropical Medicine (RITM) in Metro Manila started testing operations and became the country's first subnational laboratory. Since then, several laboratories have been accredited by the Department of Health (DOH). As of August 19, the Philippines had 109 subnational laboratories capable of detecting the virus, having conducted a total of 2,193,448 tests from over 2,051,983 unique individuals.
Cheshire is a county in England. It can also mean:

Cardboard is a general term for strong paper products that are thicker and more durable than regular paper. These products can be foldable, rigid, and resistant to impacts. They range from thick sheets called paperboard to corrugated fiberboard, which has multiple layers. Although "cardboard" is commonly used in English and French, it is not precise enough in commerce and industry. Instead, professionals use more specific terms.

Kalmar BTK is a table tennis club in Kalmar, Sweden. It was founded on June 14, 1960. The club won the Swedish national men's team championship in 1996, 1999, 2000, and 2002. Jan-Ove Waldner played for the club from 1996 to 2006.

Westville is a village in Georgetown Township, Vermilion County, Illinois, United States. It is part of the Danville, Illinois, metropolitan area. In 2010, the population was 3,202. In 2018, it was 2,990.

Borno, also called Borno State, is a state in northeastern Nigeria. Its main city is Maiduguri. The state was created in 1976 from a larger northeastern state. Until 1991, it included what is now Yobe State. Borno's slogan is "Home of Peace." Borno is where the Kanuri people and other groups live. Borno has been the center of Boko Haram's attacks since 2009. In 2009, fighting between Boko Haram and government forces drew attention. The founder of Boko Haram, Mohammed Yusuf, was reportedly captured, and later claimed to have died after trying to escape. In 2019, the state governor, Babagana Umara Zulum, started a plan. He hired 10,000 people, called "hunters with magic powers," to help defeat the attackers.

In the U.S., a "Terry" stop lets police briefly detain someone based on a guess that they might be involved in a crime. This guess needs to be reasonable, but not as strong as the proof needed for an arrest. When police stop someone walking, it's called a stop and frisk. When they stop a car, it's a traffic stop. Sometimes, police might stop a car for small reasons to check for bigger crimes; this is a pretextual stop. Police stops on a bus follow different rules. A single officer stopping one person is called a tactical definition. But if a police department or city widely uses this tactic, it can damage trust between police and the community, leading to accusations of racial profiling. The Supreme Court has given many rulings on how policing fits with the Fourth Amendment. However, Congress hasn't set a standard for police behavior. Some states have made laws and cities have passed rules about this. Unless noted otherwise, this article will mainly discuss these issues at the national level. Local and state laws might differ, but this is rare.
Hartberg-Fürstenfeld is a district in Styria, Austria. It began on January 1, 2013, after the districts of Hartberg and Fürstenfeld joined together.

"Frenzy" is a 1972 British thriller film directed by Alfred Hitchcock. It is his last important film in a long career. The screenplay was written by Anthony Shaffer and based on a 1966 novel by Arthur La Bern. The main actors are Jon Finch, Alec McCowen, and Barry Foster. Other actors include Billie Whitelaw, Anna Massey, Barbara Leigh-Hunt, Bernard Cribbins, and Vivien Merchant. Ron Goodwin composed the music. The story is about a serial killer in London and an ex-Royal Air Force (RAF) serviceman who is accused. In an early scene, there is a mention of two real London murders: the Christie murders in the early 1950s and the Jack the Ripper murders in 1888. To prepare for his role, Barry Foster studied books about Neville Heath, an English serial killer who often pretended to be an RAF officer. This was Hitchcock's third and final film made in Britain after he moved to Hollywood in 1939. The other two were "Under Capricorn" in 1949 and "Stage Fright" in 1950. The last British film he made before moving to America was "Jamaica Inn" in 1939. The film was shown at the 1972 Cannes Film Festival, but did not compete in the main event.

Saline, also called saline solution, is a mixture of salt in water. It has many uses in medicine. When applied to the skin, it helps clean wounds, remove contact lenses, and treat dry eyes. Given through a vein, it treats dehydration from illnesses like gastroenteritis and diabetic ketoacidosis. Saline is also used to dilute other medicines before injection. Large amounts of saline can cause fluid buildup, swelling, acid levels to increase, and high blood sodium. For people with low blood sodium, using too much saline can lead to a condition called osmotic demyelination syndrome. Saline is part of a group called crystalloid medications. The most common type is a 0.9% solution, known as normal saline. Sometimes, other concentrations are used. Saline has a slightly acidic pH level, mainly because of dissolved carbon dioxide. Saline was first used in medicine around 1831. It is an essential medicine for health systems and is on the World Health Organization's list of essential medicines. In developing countries, a liter of normal saline costs about $0.60 to $4.20. In 2017, sodium, the main ingredient in saline, was the 225th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with over two million prescriptions.

Inversnaid, in Scottish Gaelic "inbhir snàthaid," is a small rural community on the east side of Loch Lomond in Scotland. It's near the north end of the loch. Inversnaid has a pier and a hotel. The West Highland Way passes through the area. A small ferry runs from Inversnaid to Inveruglas on the opposite side of the loch. It also stops at Tarbet. Another ferry, operating seasonally, connects Ardlui and Ardleish, which are close to Inversnaid. To get to Inversnaid by road, you must go from Aberfoyle. Near Inversnaid is a cave called Rob Roy's Cave, which is said to have been used by Rob Roy MacGregor. The cave is hard to reach, but you can see where it is from Loch Lomond, where there is white paint marking its location.

Oona Castilla Chaplin, born on June 4, 1986, is a Spanish-British actress. She played Talisa Maegyr in the TV series "Game of Thrones," Kitty Trevelyan in "The Crimson Field," and Zilpha Geary in "Taboo." She is part of the Chaplin family. Her mother is actress Geraldine Chaplin. Her father is Charlie Chaplin's grandson. Oona is the great-granddaughter of American playwright Eugene O'Neill. She was named after her maternal grandmother, Oona O'Neill, who was Charlie Chaplin's wife.

Andry Nirina Rajoelina, born on May 30, 1974, is a Malagasy politician and businessman. He is currently the president of Madagascar. Rajoelina began his career in the private sector. First, he organized events on the island, like live concerts. Then, he invested in advertising businesses, including Injet, billboards, and print media. He also worked in media, owning Viva TV and radio. From December 2007 to February 2009, he was the mayor of Antananarivo. From March 21, 2009, to January 25, 2014, he served as the president of the High Transitional Authority of Madagascar. After the 2013 general elections, he stopped being the president of the High Transitional Authority but remained the head of the majority party, MAPAR. In 2018, he won the presidential election. He was inaugurated as president on January 19, 2019.

René Angélil was born on January 16, 1942, and died on January 14, 2016. He was from Canada and worked as a musical producer, talent manager, and singer. From 1981 to 2014, he managed Céline Dion. They were also husband and wife from 1994 until his death in 2016.

Alfred Pleasonton was born on July 7, 1824, and died on February 17, 1897. He was a United States army officer and served as a major general in the Union cavalry during the American Civil War. Pleasonton led the cavalry corps of the Army of the Potomac during the Gettysburg campaign. He commanded in the largest cavalry battle of the war, called Brandy Station. In 1864, he moved to the Trans-Mississippi theater and defeated Confederate General Sterling Price in two important battles, including the Battle of Mine Creek, the second largest cavalry battle of the war. This defeat effectively ended the war in Missouri. He was the son of Stephen Pleasonton and the younger brother of Augustus Pleasonton.

The Metre Convention, also known as the Treaty of the Metre, is an international agreement signed in Paris on May 20, 1875. Representatives from 17 countries, including Argentina, Austria-Hungary, Belgium, Brazil, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Peru, Portugal, Russia, Spain, Sweden and Norway, Switzerland, the Ottoman Empire, the United States, and Venezuela, signed it. This treaty created the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM), an organization under the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) and the International Committee for Weights and Measures (CIPM). The BIPM coordinates global measurements and the metric system. The treaty also set up a system for countries to work together on measurement issues. Only countries can be full members, but the CGPM created a special status in 1999 for states and economic entities. They can join through their national metrology institutes. Being a member costs money, and countries can be removed if they don't pay. Initially, the convention focused on mass and length. In 1921, during the 6th CGPM meeting, it was expanded to include other areas of physics. In 1960, at the 11th CGPM meeting, the system of units was renamed the International System of Units (SI).

The king's gambit is a chess opening where white gives up a pawn to distract the black e-pawn. If black takes the pawn, white has two main strategies. One is to play d4 and bxf4, gaining the pawn back and controlling the center. The other is to play nf3 and bc4, followed by 0-0. This creates an open f-file, allowing white to attack the black pawn on f7. Black might have to make weak moves like... g5 or place pieces oddly to keep the pawn. A downside is that white's king becomes weaker, making it vulnerable to... qh4+. If black has a pawn on f4, white can't usually respond with g3. If the king has to move, it can't castle either. The king's gambit is very old. It was studied by 17th-century Italian player Giulio Cesare Polerio and mentioned in an early chess book from 1497. It was one of the most popular openings until the late 19th century. Today, it's less common in professional games but still popular among amateurs.

In military tactics, a strongpoint is a crucial part of a defensive position. It anchors the overall defense line and is usually a hard place to take over or go around. Strongpoints can be redoubts, bunkers, pillboxes, trenches, or fortresses, either alone or together. A good strongpoint is in a strategic location, like high ground, that blocks the enemy's path, such as commanding lines of communication. In history, Thermopylae is an example where ancient Greeks stopped a much larger Persian army. Monte Cassino, during World War II, anchored the winter line in Italy.

A hedgehog is a spiny mammal in the family Erinaceidae. There are 17 species of hedgehogs in five groups, found in parts of Europe, Asia, and Africa, and in New Zealand by human introduction. Hedgehogs are not native to Australia and are not native to the Americas, except for an extinct species in North America. Hedgehogs are related to shrews and possibly to gymnures. They have stayed very similar for about 15 million years. Like early mammals, hedgehogs are mostly active at night. Their spines look like those of porcupines and echidnas, which are different animals.

Kembangan MRT station is an above-ground Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) station on the East West Line in Bedok, Singapore. It is located where Sims Ave East meets Jalan Kembangan. Part of the station is directly above the Siglap Canal. The name "Kembangan" means "expansion" in Malay.

The Industrial and Mining Water Research Unit (IMWARU) is part of the School of Chemical and Metallurgical Engineering at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg. IMWARU does research and helps supervise master's and PhD students at the university. It also gives advice to businesses.

Madison County is in Arkansas, a state in the U.S. In 2010, it had 15, 717 people. The county seat is Huntsville. Madison County was created on September 30, 1836, and named after James Madison, the fourth president of the United States. It is part of Northwest Arkansas.

Mary Fallin, born on December 9, 1954, is an American politician. She was the 27th governor of Oklahoma from 2011 to 2019. Fallin, a Republican, was elected governor in 2010 and won re-election in 2014. Fallin began her political career in 1990 when she was elected to the Oklahoma House of Representatives. She served two terms from 1990 to 1995. In 1994, she became the 14th lieutenant governor of Oklahoma and held this position from 1995 to 2007, serving three terms under two different governors. In 2007, Fallin ran for Congress. After winning, she served two terms in the U.S. House of Representatives until 2011. In 2010, Fallin ran for governor. She won the Republican primary with 54% of the vote and the general election against the Democratic nominee, Lieutenant Governor Jari Askins, with 60% of the vote. She was re-elected in 2014, defeating Oklahoma State Representative Joe Dorman. Fallin’s time as governor was difficult. She faced many controversies, accusations, and low approval ratings. A 2018 poll found her to be the least popular governor in the country, with only 17% approval and 75% disapproval. Term limits stopped her from running for another term, and Kevin Stitt was elected to replace her.

"Baby Don't Forget My Number" is a song by the German dance-pop group Milli Vanilli. It came out in December 1988 as the second single from their album "Girl You Know It's True." This song was their first to reach number one on the Billboard Hot 100 chart in 1989. In 1992, Weird Al Yankovic made a funny version of this song and another called "Blame It on the Rain" into "The Plumbing Song" for his album "Off the Deep End." The single was also certified gold in the USA by the RIAA.

Echinoderms are marine animals belonging to the phylum Echinodermata, named after the Greek words for "hedgehog" and "skin" because they often look like hedgehogs. They are known for their radial symmetry, often with five parts. Examples include starfish, sea urchins, sand dollars, sea cucumbers, and sea lilies. Found in all ocean depths, echinoderms make up about 7,000 living species, the second-largest group of deuterostomes after chordates, which include vertebrates. Unlike many other animals, echinoderms do not live in freshwater or on land. The earliest known echinoderms appeared during the Cambrian period. Some Cambrian echinoderms had external gills for filter feeding, similar to other animals. Echinoderms are important in both ecology and geology. They are abundant in the deep sea and shallower waters, can reproduce asexually and regenerate body parts, and their fossilized skeletons help determine geological environments. They were widely used in regenerative research during the 19th and 20th centuries, and some scientists believe their evolution contributed to the Mesozoic Marine Revolution.

Ahattı Atun was a former prime minister of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus. He served from 1994 to 1996. Born in 1935 in Famagusta, Atun graduated as an engineer-architect from Istanbul Technical University in 1959. He studied urban planning at Manchester and Nottingham universities. In 1961 to 1975, Atun had various public roles. In 1963, he became the regional director of Limassol-Paphos planning. In 1967, he was the head of the planning and construction department. In 1975, he became the undersecretary of housing. Atun was elected to the National Unity Party and served as a member of parliament for Nicosia in the 1976, 1981, 1985, and 1990 general elections. He held several ministerial positions, including minister of settlement and rehabilitation, minister of economy and finance, and minister of national education, culture, youth, and sports. He was also the secretary general of the National Unity Party. In 1983, Atun was a member of the constituent assembly and minister of settlement in the first republican government. From 1985 to 1993, he was the speaker of the assembly of the republic. In 1992, he became the president of the Democratic Party, formed after a movement he led with 9 MPs within the National Unity Party. Atun was elected to parliament from the Democratic Party in 1993 and served as prime minister from August 16, 1996, until October 4, 1996. He later did not participate in the parliament. He is the honorary president of the Democratic Party and speaks English and a little Greek. He is married with two children. His aunt is the 3rd president of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, Derviş Eroğlu.

Scorpion is Drake's fifth album. It came out on June 29, 2018. Drake made it with his record labels, Cash Money, Republic, and Young Money. The album has 25 songs. The first part is mainly hip hop, and the second part is r & b and pop. Drake produced it with his friend 40 and his manager Oliver. The album includes songs by Jay-Z and Ty Dolla Sign, and there are also songs about Michael Jackson and Static Major who are no longer alive. Drake talks about fame, relationships, and his success in music. The album's music mixes different styles like soul, ambience, slow jam, r & b, pop, and trap. Drake's singles from the album were "God's Plan," "Nice for What," "I'm Upset," "Don't Matter to Me," "In My Feelings," "Nonstop," and "Mob Ties." They all did well, reaching the top 20 in the US. Three of them, "God's Plan," "Nice for What," and "In My Feelings," were number one hits. Scorpion set records for the most streams on Spotify and Apple Music on its first day. Critics didn't love the album, but it sold very well. It topped the US Billboard 200 charts, selling 732,000 album-equivalent units, with 160,000 from actual sales. As of January 2019, it was five times platinum in the US. Scorpion was nominated for five Grammys, including Album of the Year, and "God's Plan" won Best Rap Song. Drake also won the Billboard 200 Album of the Year at the 2019 Billboard Music Awards.

Exology Chapter 1: The Lost Planet is the first live album by EXO. EXO is a boy band from South Korea. It was released on December 22, 2014, by SM Entertainment. The album has two CDs with 36 songs in total. One CD has 18 songs. It includes individual tracks from each member and remixes of some of their songs. There are two versions of the album: a normal version and a special version.

An ofrenda is a collection of objects put on a special display during the Day of the Dead celebration in Mexico. This display, which can be large and detailed, is made to welcome a person who has died.
Chidester is a city in Ouachita County, Arkansas, United States. The population was 335 in 2000. It is part of the Camden micropolitan statistical area.
The company decided to cut costs by reducing the number of employees. This will help save money.

Guatemala is one of 22 departments. The capital is Guatemala City, which is also the national capital. This department includes Guatemala City and its suburbs. It covers an area and had 3,015,081 people in the 2018 census.
Hardancourt is a commune in the Vosges department, which is in Grand Est, in northeastern France.

William Grant "Bill" Moggridge, who lived from June 25, 1943, to September 8, 2012, was a British designer, writer, and teacher. He helped start a design company called IDEO and was the director of the Cooper-Hewitt, National Design Museum in New York. Moggridge was one of the first to focus on designing things that fit people's needs. He also helped make interaction design a recognized area of design. Moggridge is credited with creating the term "interaction design." He designed the first laptop computer, called the Grid Compass. He received awards for his lifetime achievements in design and the Prince Philip Designers Prize. Moggridge once said, "The common thread in everything I have done is my interest in people and how they interact with objects."

Lady Susan is a short novel by Jane Austen. It was written around 1794 but not published until 1871. This early complete work, which Jane Austen never tried to publish, tells about the plans of the main character.

The Vickers Viscount is a British medium-range turboprop airliner. It was first flown in 1948 by Vickers-Armstrongs. It entered service in 1953 and was the first turboprop-powered airliner. People liked it because it had a comfortable cabin, reduced vibration and noise, and big windows. Many were built and it was very successful, with 445 Viscounts made for customers around the world, including in North America.

The Blossoms are an American girl group from California. In the 1960s, they were most known for Darlene Love, Fanita James, and Jean King. They made their own music but were famous for singing background vocals on many big 1960s hits. The Blossoms were like the Sweet Inspirations on the West Coast and the Andantes for Motown.

TESOL International Association, formerly known as Teachers of English to Speakers of Other Languages, is the biggest group for teachers of English as a second or foreign language. It was created in 1966 and is based in Alexandria, Virginia, in the United States. By 2018, it had about 10, 113 members worldwide and was connected to 109 language education organizations, with more than half based outside the U.S. The group had around 44, 000 members in total, including those from affiliated organizations. TESOL publishes two respected academic journals called "TESOL Quarterly" and "TESOL Journal." In the summer, it organizes professional development seminars called "TESOL Academies" across the United States. It also holds an annual convention.

Neptune Beach is a beach city in Duval County, Florida, east of Jacksonville. In 1968, most communities in Duval County joined Jacksonville. However, Neptune Beach, along with Jacksonville Beach, Atlantic Beach, and Baldwin, stayed mostly independent. These towns have their own local government. Residents vote in Jacksonville's mayor election and are represented on the Jacksonville city council. As of the 2010 census, the population was 7,037. Neptune Beach is part of the Jacksonville Beaches area.

The Plymouth Fury was a car made by Plymouth from 1955 to 1989. It first appeared in 1956 as part of the Plymouth Belvedere series but became its own series in 1959. The Fury was a full-size car from 1959 to 1961, then mid-size from 1962 to 1964. It was full-size again from 1965 to 1974 and mid-size from 1975 to 1978. From 1975 to 1977, it was sold with the full-size Plymouth Gran Fury. In 1978, the Fury was the largest Plymouth. By 1979, there were no large Plymouths. The Gran Fury was introduced in 1980, followed by the Fury with the M-body in 1982. The last V8, rear-wheel drive Plymouth Fury was made on December 23, 1988, in Kenosha, Wisconsin. Unlike Dodge, Plymouth did not see a return of large, V8 rear-wheel drive sedans. The last Plymouth rolled off the Belvedere assembly line in 2001.

Franzobel is the pen name of an Austrian writer named Franz Stefan Griebl. He was born on March 1, 1967, in Vöcklabruck. In 1997, he won the Wolfgang Weyrauch Prize. In 1998, he received the Kassel Literary Prize. He has won many other literary awards. In 2017, he got the Nicolas Born Prize and was a finalist for the German Book Prize for his novel "Das Floß der Medusa." He now lives in Vienna.

County Westmeath is a county in Ireland. It is in the province of Leinster and part of the Midlands region. It used to be part of a historic kingdom called Meath, which meant 'middle'. The county's name comes from the word "mide," which means "middle," because the kingdom was in the center of Ireland. The administrative body for Westmeath is the Westmeath County Council, and the main town is Mullingar. According to the 2016 census, the county had 88,770 people.

Graves' disease, also called toxic diffuse goiter, is an autoimmune disorder that impacts the thyroid. It often leads to hyperthyroidism, which is the most common cause of an overactive thyroid. People with Graves' disease might have a bigger thyroid gland. Symptoms of hyperthyroidism can include feeling irritable, having weak muscles, trouble sleeping, a fast heartbeat, feeling too warm, diarrhea, and losing weight unintentionally. Other signs can be thickened skin on the shins and bulging eyes, known as Graves' ophthalmopathy. About 25 to 80% of people with this condition develop eye problems. The exact cause is not clear, but it involves genetic and environmental factors. You are more likely to get it if your family member has it. If one twin is affected, there’s a 30% chance the other will too. Stress, infection, giving birth, or having other autoimmune diseases like type 1 diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis can trigger the onset. Smoking raises the risk and may worsen eye issues. Graves' disease happens when your body makes antibodies called TSI that make your thyroid produce too much thyroid hormone. Doctors can diagnose it based on symptoms and blood tests. Blood tests often show high T3 and T4 levels, low TSH, increased radioiodine uptake, and TSI antibodies. Treatment options include radioiodine therapy, medicines, and surgery. Radioiodine therapy involves taking iodine-131, which destroys the thyroid over weeks to months, leading to hypothyroidism treated with thyroid hormone pills. Beta blockers can help control symptoms, and antithyroid medicines like methimazole can provide temporary relief. Surgery removes the thyroid. Eye problems may need special treatment. About 0.5% of men and 3% of women develop Graves' disease. Women are about 7.5 times more likely to get it than men. It commonly starts between 40 and 60, but can appear at any age. In the U.S., it causes about 50 to 80% of hyperthyroid cases. The condition was first described by Irish surgeon Robert Graves in 1835, with earlier descriptions existing as well.

Earl Wilbur Sutherland Jr. was born on November 19, 1915, in Burlingame, Kansas. He was an American pharmacologist and biochemist. Sutherland won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1971. He received the prize for his discoveries about how hormones work, especially epinephrine, through something called second messengers. These messengers are cyclic AMP, also known as cyclic AMP.
Gevelsberg is a town in Ennepe-Ruhr-Kreis district, which is in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany.

Francisco Waldir Pires de Souza was a Brazilian politician born on October 21, 1926, and died on June 22, 2018. He worked as the Minister of Defence under President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. However, he was fired due to poor job performance and inaction during Brazil's aviation crisis from 2006 to 2007. At that time, some people in Brazil thought he was becoming less capable. Nelson Jobim, who was a former president of the Supreme Court, took his place. Souza was also in charge of a mission to Haiti. This mission, known as MINUSTAH, caused problems in Haiti after a police chief took power by force and removed President Jean-Bertrand Aristide.

Patrick James Riley, born on March 20, 1945, is an American basketball executive. He was also a coach and player in the NBA. Riley has been the Miami Heat's team president since 1995 and coached the team twice (1995-2003, 2005-2008). As a player, Riley was part of the Lakers' championship team in 1972. He is considered one of the greatest NBA coaches of all time. Riley led five championship teams, including four during the Lakers' Showtime era in the 1980s and one with the Heat in 2006. He was named NBA Coach of the Year three times, in 1989-90, 1992-93, and 1996-97, coaching the Lakers, New York Knicks, and Heat, respectively. Riley was the head coach of the NBA All-Star game team nine times. He coached the Western conference team eight times (1982, 1983, 1985-1990, all as the Lakers' head coach) and once coached the Eastern team (1993, as the Knicks' head coach). He is the first North American sports figure to win championships as a player, assistant coach, head coach, and executive. In 1996, Riley was named one of the 10 greatest NBA coaches in history. He won the 2012 and 2013 NBA championships as the Miami Heat's team president. He received the Chuck Daly Lifetime Achievement Award from the NBA Coaches Association on June 20, 2012.

Bloomsburg is a town in Columbia County, Pennsylvania, United States. It is located southwest of Wilkes-Barre along the Susquehanna River. Bloomsburg is the county seat of Columbia County and the only Pennsylvania municipality incorporated as a "town." In 2010, Bloomsburg had 14,855 people, with an estimated population of 13,811 in 2019. Bloomsburg is part of the Bloomsburg-Berwick, PA micropolitan area, which includes Columbia and Montour Counties. This area had 85,562 people in the 2010 census.
Walala Tjapaltjarri (born Walala Tjapangati) is an Australian Aboriginal artist.

The United States has many types of laws, with the most important being the United States Constitution. This constitution sets up the federal government and includes important freedoms. Federal laws include acts of Congress, treaties, rules from the executive branch, and court decisions. The United States Code is a collection of these federal laws. Federal laws and treaties, as long as they follow the Constitution, can override state laws in the 50 states and territories. However, federal power is limited. In the United States, states and the federal government have their own powers. States can give their citizens more rights as long as they do not break federal rules. Most of the laws that affect daily life, like contracts, property, and criminal laws, are state laws that can differ from state to state. Except for Louisiana, U.S. laws are mostly based on the common law system from English law, which was in place when America declared independence. American law has changed a lot from its English origins, both in content and how it works, and has included new ideas from civil law.

Meresankh I, who loved life, was a wife of an ancient Egyptian king and the mother of King Sneferu. She might have been married to King Huni, the last king of the 3rd dynasty. Her name is on a piece of the Palermo Stone, and there might be a place named after her estate in the tomb of Pehernefer in Saqqara. She and her son Sneferu are mentioned together in writings found in the Pyramid Temple at Meidum. These writings date back to the time of King Tuthmosis III, who ruled during the 18th dynasty. The text says a special message, called a "hetep di nesu" text, was written for King Sneferu and Queen Meresankh.

Gerald Göttig was a German politician who lived from June 9, 1923, to May 19, 2015. He was the chairman of the East German Christian Democratic Union (CDU) from 1966 to 1989. Göttig was the president of the People's Chamber (Volkskammer) from 1969 to 1976. He was also a deputy chairman of the State Council of East Germany from 1960 to 1989.

In economics, a free market is a system where prices for goods and services are decided by the market and consumers. In a free market, the government and other authorities don't interfere, and there are no special economic advantages, monopolies, or artificial scarcity. Those who support free markets say it's different from a regulated market where the government uses methods like tariffs to protect local businesses. In a free-market economy, prices are set by supply and demand, without government help. Scholars study free markets in fields like political economy, new institutional economics, economic sociology, and political science. These fields note that rules outside of supply and demand are important in current market systems, providing space for these forces to work. While free markets are linked to capitalism, they are also supported by anarchists, socialists, and some who favor cooperatives and profit sharing. Critics argue that free markets might not be truly free if there is significant market power, unequal bargaining power, or information imbalances. They think regulation is needed to correct these issues and improve market efficiency and social outcomes.

Lipscomb County is in Texas, United States. In 2010, it had 3,302 people. The county seat is Lipscomb. It was created in 1876 and organized in 1887. The county is named after Judge Abner Smith Lipscomb, who was a secretary of state of the Republic of Texas.
Didier Bezace was a French actor. He was born on February 10, 1946, and passed away on March 11, 2020.

Nadap is a village in Fejér County, central Hungary. It has 460 people living there. Nestled among low hills, Nadap is a starting point for countryside tours. There is an obelisk nearby called "Ancient Mark of Nadap." It is used as a reference point at 173.8 meters above sea level. Mihály Vörösmarty was baptized in the Catholic Church of Saint Rosalia in Nadap, and the baptismal basin is still in the church.

Surya Bahadur Thapa, born on March 21, 1928, and died on April 15, 2015, was a Nepali politician who served as prime minister five times. He worked under three different kings for over 50 years. Thapa began his career as an acting prime minister for only four days in 1955 but soon became well-respected. In 1959, he was elected to the upper house. From 1963 to 1964, he became the chair of the council of ministers. He went on to serve four more terms as prime minister: 1965 to 1969, 1979 to 1983, 1997 to 1998, and 2003. He left his Rastriya Prajatantra Party in November 2004. Thapa was the first prime minister under Nepal's panchayat system. In his later years, he led the Rastriya Janashakti Party. He passed away from respiratory failure during surgery.

A mast cell, also called a mastocyte or a labrocyte, is a type of cell in connective tissue that has lots of granules filled with histamine and heparin. Specifically, it comes from a type of stem cell and is part of the immune and neuroimmune systems. Mast cells were found by Paul Ehrlich in 1877. They are best known for their role in allergies and severe reactions, but they also help in healing wounds, making new blood vessels, and protecting against infections. Mast cells look and work similarly to basophils, another kind of white blood cell. However, it has been shown that these cells develop differently and are not the same type of cell.

Amanda Michelle Seyfried, born on December 3, 1985, is an American actress, singer, and model. She grew up in Allentown, Pennsylvania. Seyfried started modeling when she was 11 and began acting at 15. She had roles in "As the World Turns" from 1999 to 2001 and in "All My Children" in 2003. She gained attention after appearing in "Mean Girls" (2004) and in the TV show "Veronica Mars" from 2004 to 2006. She appeared in some smaller movies like "Nine Lives" (2005) and "Alpha Dog" (2006) and was in the TV series "Big Love" from 2006 to 2011. Seyfried then starred in several popular movies, including "Mamma Mia!" (2008), "Solstice" (2008), "Jennifer's Body" (2009), "Chloe" (2009), "Dear John" (2010), "Letters to Juliet" (2010), "Red Riding Hood" (2011), "In Time" (2011), "Les Misérables" (2012), "Gone" (2012), "Lovelace" (2013), "The Big Wedding" (2013), "A Million Ways to Die in the West" (2014), "Ted 2" (2015), "Pan" (2015), "Fathers and Daughters" (2016), "First Reformed" (2017), "The Clapper" (2017), "Anon" (2018), "Gringo" (2018), "Mamma Mia! Here We Go Again" (2018), and "The Art of Racing in the Rain" (2019). She also did voice work for animated movies like "Epic" (2013) and "Scoob!" (2020).
Ellen Marie Elze Anthing Vogel was an actress. She was born on January 26, 1922, and died on August 5, 2015. She acted in films, on stages, and on television.

The question mark is a punctuation mark used to show a question. It is also called an interrogation point, query, or eroteme in journalism. This mark is used for direct questions, not indirect ones. In some cases, it can represent missing or unknown information. In Unicode, it is represented by a specific code.
In United States politics and government, the term "presidential nominee" has two different meanings.

Alois Hitler Sr., born Alois Schicklgruber on June 7, 1837, died on January 3, 1903. He was an Austrian civil servant and the father of Adolf Hitler, who later became the dictator of Nazi Germany. Alois was born without a father's name, and his father was never officially known. This caused people to think that his wife, Klara, who was also Adolf's mother, might be his cousin. Because his father was unknown, Adolf could not prove his "Aryan descent." When Alois got a better job, he changed his name to Hitler. People are not sure why he did this. Alois and Adolf did not get along well. Alois often punished Adolf severely.

Rock of Ages Corporation is a granite quarrying and finishing company in Graniteville, Vermont. It was founded in 1885. The company has about 230 workers. In 2009, they earned $800,000 in profit from sales of $21.6 million, improving from a loss of over $2 million in 2008. On October 19, 2010, Swenson Granite from Concord, New Hampshire, agreed to merge with Rock of Ages. Swenson paid Rock of Ages shareholders $39 million. On September 16, 2016, Polycor Inc. in Quebec City, Canada, bought Swenson Granite and Rock of Ages to become the biggest marble and granite producer in North America. They also acquired Rock of Ages' division in Stanstead, Quebec. Rock of Ages has the world's largest "deep hole" granite quarry, known as the "E. L. Smith Quarry." Devonian Barre granite is mined there. Initially, granite was extracted using simple methods like hand saws and explosions. Today, advanced tools like diamond-tipped wire saws and water jets are used. Visitors can watch the workers at the quarry cutting granite. The company was featured in a 2005 PBS documentary about cemetery-related businesses.

The Mighty Bosstones, often just called the Bosstones, is an American ska punk band from Boston, Massachusetts. They formed in 1983. Since then, Dicky Barrett (lead singer), Joe Gittleman (bassist), Tim Burton (tenor saxophonist), and Ben Carr (dancer) have always been part of the band. Other band members include Joe Sirois (drummer), Leon Silva (saxophonist), Lawrence Katz (guitarist), John Goetchius (keyboardist), and Chris Rhodes (trombonist). The Bosstones are known as one of the first bands to create ska punk and the subgenre ska-core. Their 1989 album "Devil's Night Out" started their big success. In the 1990s, they played and recorded a lot, helping make ska punk popular. They became famous with their 1997 album "Let's Face It" and the song "The Impression That I Get." By December 2003, they had seven studio albums, three EPs, and a live album before taking a break. In 2007, they came back and have since made three more studio albums. From 1994 to 2002, and since 2007, they host an annual music festival called the Hometown Throwdown in Boston.

The Regional Representative Council, or DPD, is one of two parts of Indonesia's parliament. It works together with the DPR, or People's Representative Council, to make up the Indonesian national legislative body, called MPR. According to Indonesia's constitution, the DPD can only suggest and advise on bills related to regional governments. It cannot make laws directly. Members of the DPD are usually called senators.
An antacid is a substance that makes your stomach less acidic. It helps with heartburn, indigestion, or an upset stomach, making you feel better.

Taiwan, officially known as the Republic of China (ROC), is a country in East Asia. It is next to China, Japan, and the Philippines. Taiwan's main island is large, with mountains in the east and plains in the west. Taipei is the capital and largest city, with other big cities like New Taipei, Kaohsiung, Taichung, Tainan, and Taoyuan. Taiwan has about 23.7 million people and is very crowded. It is the largest and most populous country not in the United Nations. Taiwanese people first lived on the island around 6,000 years ago. In the 17th century, Dutch colonizers came, bringing many Han Chinese immigrants. In 1683, the Qing Dynasty of China took control. Later, in 1895, Taiwan became part of Japan. After World War II, the ROC government, which had taken over from the Qing Dynasty, controlled Taiwan. In 1949, the ROC government moved to Taiwan after losing control of mainland China to the Communist Party. Since then, the ROC government has claimed to be the legitimate government of all of China but has controlled only Taiwan and some smaller islands. Taiwan has grown very quickly since the 1960s, known as the "Taiwan Miracle." It has a strong economy, with industries like steel, machinery, electronics, and chemicals. Taiwan is a developed country with a high GDP per capita. It ranks well in freedoms, education, health, and development. Taiwan’s status is unclear. It is not a member of the United Nations, replaced by China in 1971. China says Taiwan is part of China and does not allow countries to have official relations with Taiwan. Taiwan has official ties with 14 out of 193 UN member states and the Holy See. International organizations that China is part of either do not allow Taiwan membership or let it join as a non-state member. Taiwan is a member of the World Trade Organization, APEC, and the Asian Development Bank under different names. Neighboring countries and major economies maintain unofficial ties with Taiwan through representative offices. In Taiwan, the main political divide is between those who want eventual Chinese unification and those who support independence for Taiwan.
Aulnois-sous-Laon is a town in the Aisne department of Hauts-de-France in northern France. People from this town are called Aulnoisiens or Aulnoisiennes.

Jacques Houplain was a French painter and engraver. He was born on September 10, 1920, and passed away on February 22, 2020.

Mahākāla is a deity in Hinduism, Buddhism, and Sikhism. In Hinduism, Mahākāla is a form of Shiva and is the partner of Mahākālī. He is a main figure in Shaktism. In Buddhism, particularly in Tibetan traditions, Mahākāla is known as Citipati and is a protector deity. He is also a protector in Chinese and Shingon Buddhism. In Chinese and Cantonese, he is called "dàhēitiān" and "daaih'hāktīn". In Korean, he is "daeheukcheon". In Vietnamese, he is "đại hắc thiên". In Japanese, he is "daikokuten". In Sikhism, Mahākāla is known as Kal, who controls Maya.

The Gulf of Gonâve is a big part of the Caribbean Sea along Haiti's west coast. Haiti's capital, Port-au-Prince, is on this coast. Other cities include Gonaïves, Saint-Marc, Miragoâne, and Jérémie. Several islands are in the Gulf, with Gonâve Island being the largest, and the Cayemites being much smaller.

Fillmore is a small city in Ventura County, California. It is in the Santa Clara River Valley. Fillmore is in an agricultural area with rich, fertile soil. The city has an historic downtown. This downtown was built when the Southern Pacific railroad came through the valley in 1887. The railroad gave the town its name. J. A. Fillmore was a general superintendent for the company's Pacific system. The population of Fillmore was 15,002 in 2010, up from 13,643 in 2000.

Ivy Queen, born Martha Ivelisse Pesante Rodríguez on March 4, 1972, is a Puerto Rican singer, songwriter, rapper, actress, and record producer. She first gained attention as a member of the Noise in Puerto Rico. There, she performed her first song "Somos Raperos Pero No Delincuentes" ("We Are Rappers, Not Delinquents"). In 1996, she went solo and released her debut album "En Mi Imperio (In My Empire)," which Sony Discos started selling in 1997. Her second album, "The Original Rude Girl," with the hit single "In the Zone," was also with Sony. Ivy Queen gained more fame in 2003 when she released her third album, "Diva," with Sony. Her albums "Diva," "Flashback," and "Sentimiento" were all successful, earning gold and platinum records. In 2010, her album "Drama Queen" included the top ten hit "La Vida Es Así." In 2012, she released "Musa," which was nominated for a Grammy. Ivy Queen often sings about strong women, love, and relationships and is known as the Queen of Reggaeton. She has acted in plays and created a doll based on her image. In 2012, she started acting in Eve Ensler's play "The Vagina Monologues." Ivy Queen is one of the richest reggaeton artists, with a net worth of $10 million in 2017.

In math, a real number is a value that can show a distance on a line, or an infinite decimal. The term "real" was first used by René Descartes in the 17th century to distinguish between real and imaginary roots of polynomials. Real numbers include rational numbers like -5 and 4/3, and irrational numbers like the square root of 2, which is about 1.41421356, and pi (3.14159265). These numbers can measure things like time, mass, and speed. Real numbers are often thought of as points on a line, with integers equally spaced. Each real number can be written as an infinite decimal. Real numbers are part of the complex numbers. Defining real numbers rigorously was a significant 19th-century mathematical achievement. Current definitions say real numbers form the unique complete ordered field, and include equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences, Dedekind cuts, or infinite decimals. All these definitions are equivalent. The set of real numbers is uncountable, meaning there can't be a one-to-one match with natural numbers. The cardinality of real numbers is greater than that of natural numbers. The Continuum Hypothesis states that no set can have a cardinality between that of natural numbers and real numbers. This hypothesis can neither be proved nor disproved using ZFC set theory.

This list shows the presidents of Djibouti. Since 1977, there have been two presidents. The president is the leader of the country and in charge of the government. They also command the Djibouti armed forces. The current president is Ismaïl Omar Guelleh, since 1999.
