Calhoun County is a name used for several counties in the United States. This name honors U.S. Vice President John C. Calhoun.

Challakere Kareem Jaffer Sharief was an Indian politician born on November 3, 1933, and died on November 25, 2018. He was a senior leader of the Indian National Congress. He served as the Railways Minister in the Government of India from 1991 to 1995.

The Brooks Range (Athabaskan "gwazhał") is a mountain range in northern North America, stretching from west to east across northern Alaska into Canada's Yukon Territory. At its highest point, Mount Isto, it reaches an elevation of about 1,850 meters. It is believed to be around 126 million years old. In the United States, these mountains are part of the Rocky Mountains, while in Canada, they are seen as separate, with the northern border of the Rocky Mountains being the Liard River in British Columbia. Most of the range is not inhabited. However, there are some small communities such as Anaktuvuk and Arctic Village, as well as Coldfoot, Wiseman, Bettles, and Chandalar. The Dalton Highway and Trans-Alaska Pipeline System pass through the Atigun Pass (4,643 feet) on their way to Prudhoe Bay on Alaska's North Slope. To the west, near the Wulik River in the De Long Mountains, is the Red Dog Mine, the largest zinc mine in the world. The range was named by the United States Board on Geographic Names in 1925 after Alfred Hulse Brooks, who was the chief USGS geologist for Alaska from 1903 to 1924. Various names have been used for this range, including Arctic Mountains, Hooper Mountains, Meade Mountains, and Meade River Mountains. The Canadian part of the range is officially called the British Mountains. In Canada, the British Mountains include Ivavik National Park.

The monk parakeet, also called the quaker parrot, is a kind of true parrot in the psittacidae family. It is a small, bright-green bird with a grayish breast and greenish-yellow belly. On average, it lives for 20 to 30 years. This parrot is originally from areas in Argentina and nearby South American countries. Now, it can be found in many places as wild parakeets, mostly in North America and Europe.

Greifswald, officially called the University and Hanseatic City of Greifswald, is a city in northeastern Germany. It is in the state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Greifswald is about the same distance from Germany's two largest cities, Berlin and Hamburg, and is about 80 km (50 miles) from the Polish border. The city is part of Western Pomerania and is next to the Baltic Sea. A small river called the Ryck flows through it. Greifswald is near Germany's two largest islands, Rügen and Usedom, and close to three of Germany's national parks. Since September 2011, it has been the capital of the new district of Vorpommern-Greifswald. Together with Stralsund, Greifswald is one of the four main cities in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. In 2013, the city had about 55,659 people, including many students and employees of the University of Greifswald. Greifswald is known for its university, the Biocon Valley around it, the Nord Stream gas pipeline, and the Wendelstein 7-X nuclear fusion project.

Balkrishna Vithaldas Doshi, born on August 26, 1927, is an Indian architect. He is an important figure in Indian architecture and is known for his work in developing architectural discussions in India. He worked with famous architects Le Corbusier and Louis Kahn. Doshi is a pioneer of modernist and brutalist architecture in India. Some of his notable designs are the IIM Bangalore, IIM Udaipur, NIFT Delhi, Amdavad ni Gufa, CEPT University, and the Aranya low-cost housing development in Indore. This development won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture. In 2018, he became the first Indian architect to receive the Pritzker Architecture Prize, one of the most prestigious awards in the field. He has also been given the Padma Shri and the Padma Bhushan awards.

Kraftwerk is a German band formed in Düsseldorf in 1970 by Ralf Hütter and Florian Schneider. They are known as pioneers of electronic music and among the first to make it popular. The group started as part of West Germany's experimental music scene in the early 1970s. They used synthesizers, drum machines, and vocoders. Albums like "Autobahn" (1974), "Trans-Europe Express" (1977), "The Man-Machine" (1978), and "Computer World" (1981) were successful. Their style combined electronic music with pop melodies and repetitive rhythms. They wore matching suits. After "Electric Café" (1986), Wolfgang Flür left in 1987, followed by Karl Bartos in 1990. Florian Schneider left in 2008. Kraftwerk's work has influenced many artists and genres, including synth-pop, hip hop, post-punk, techno, ambient, and club music. They won a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2014 and another for best dance/electronic album in 2018. As of 2020, the band continues to tour.

Putnam County is in New York, U.S. In 2010, it had 99,710 people. The main town is called Carmel. Putnam County was created in 1812 from Dutchess County and is named after Israel Putnam, a hero in the French and Indian War and a general in the American Revolutionary War. It's part of the New York-Newark-Jersey City, NY-NJ-Pennsylvania big area. Putnam County is in the Lower Hudson River Valley. It's about an hour's drive from midtown Manhattan, and a 1-hour, 20-minute train ride away. Putnam County is one of the richest counties in America. It was ranked 21st by median household income and 43rd by per-capita income in the 2012 and 2009-2013 American Community Surveys.

Lee Hyo-ri, born on May 10, 1979, is a singer from South Korea. She also works as a record producer, activist, actress, and TV host. Known as "the nation's fairy" when she performed with her family, she later joined the girl group Fin.K.L. and then became a solo artist. In 2003, she released her first solo album called "Stylist," winning "artist of the year" awards. In 2006, she became the highest-paid female singer in South Korea after signing with Mnet Media.

Violet Brown (née Mosse; born March 10, 1900, died September 15, 2017) was a Jamaican supercentenarian. She became the oldest verified living person in the world after Emma Morano died on April 15, 2017. Violet Brown died on September 15, 2017. At the time of her death, she was the fifth-oldest person in history. She and Nabi Tajima from Japan were among the last two people known to have been born in the 19th century.

Here is a list of the 67 counties in Pennsylvania. The city of Philadelphia is the same as Philadelphia County. In 1854, the cities became one. After a vote in 1951, Philadelphia took over all county government jobs. Eight of the ten most people-living counties are in the southeast. Four of the top five counties are there. Eight out of the top ten most people-living counties are in either the Philadelphia or Pittsburgh areas.

João Ubaldinho Ribeiro was born on January 23, 1941, and died on July 18, 2014. He was a Brazilian writer, journalist, screenwriter, and teacher. Some of his books and short stories were made into movies and TV shows in Brazil. Ribeiro became a member of the Brazilian Academy of Letters in 1994. At the time of his death, many people thought he was Brazil's best living novelist.

Zvečan is a town and municipality in the Mitrovica district of Kosovo. As of 2015, it has 16,650 people living there. The town covers an area and includes the town itself and 35 villages. Zvečan is in North Kosovo, an area with many Serb people. This region works mostly separately from the rest of Kosovo, which has many Albanian people. After the 2013 Brussels Agreement, the municipality joined a group of Serb-controlled areas.

Neopterygii comes from the Greek words "neos," meaning new, and "pteryx," meaning fin. It's a subclass of ray-finned fish (actinopterygii). Only a few changes happened as neopterygians evolved from earlier actinopterygians. They appeared in the late Permian period, before the time of dinosaurs. Neopterygians could move faster than their ancestors. During their evolution, their scales and skeletons became lighter, and their jaws got stronger and more efficient. Unlike other fish, neopterygians lost the ability to sense electric fields, even though some types like gymnotiformes and catfish later redeveloped this sense. A big step in the evolution of ray-finned fishes was the appearance of neopterygians. They gained better control over their dorsal and anal fins, which improved their swimming. They also developed new features in their skulls, allowing them to eat differently and live in new environments. All these changes were very important, making neopterygii the most common group of fish, and thus the most common type of vertebrate. Neopterygii includes teleosts, which are almost all living fish.

Numidia (202 BC – 40 BC, Berber: Inumiden) was an ancient kingdom of the Numidians in what is now Algeria, a small part of Tunisia, and a tiny part of Libya. At first, it was split into two regions: Massylii in the east and Masaesyli in the west. During the Second Punic War (218–201 BC), King Masinissa of the Massylii defeated Syphax of the Masaesyli. This led to the unification of Numidia into one kingdom. Numidia was originally an independent kingdom. It would sometimes be a Roman province and other times a Roman client state. At its largest, Numidia was bordered by the kingdom of Mauretania to the west, the Moulouya River, Africa Proconsularis (now part of Tunisia) to the east, the Mediterranean Sea to the north, and the Sahara to the south. Numidia is considered one of the first major states in Algerian and Berber history.
A country is an area where people live together, often considered a sovereign state. Sometimes, "country" can also mean multiple countries.
An anticyclonic storm is a weather storm where winds move in a clockwise direction around the storm. This is opposite to the winds in a low-pressure area, which move counterclockwise.

Usury is when someone makes loans in an unethical way, making the lender gain too much. It can be seen as wrong because it takes advantage of people's troubles. In some places, the law limits how much interest can be charged on loans. People who do usury are called usurers or loan sharks. In old societies, like ancient Christian, Jewish, and modern Islamic ones, charging any interest on loans was seen as wrong. In ancient India, there were laws stopping the highest castes from doing this. Religious texts from Buddhism, Judaism, Christianity, and Islam also condemn it. Some ancient societies, including Greece and Rome, banned loans with interest altogether. However, by the time of the Roman Empire, loans with carefully set interest rates were allowed. But during the Middle Ages in Europe, the Catholic Church and other churches said charging interest was sinful, just like taking a fee for using money. They believed that charging interest was wrong because it was a sin.

Wenatchee is a city in north-central Washington. It is the largest city and the county seat of Chelan County. In 2010, the city had 31,925 people. By 2019, it was estimated to have 34,360 people. Located where the Columbia and Wenatchee rivers meet, Wenatchee is on the western side of the Columbia River, near East Wenatchee. It borders Chelan and Douglas counties. Wenatchee is part of the Wenatchee–East Wenatchee metropolitan area, covering Chelan and Douglas counties with about 110,884 people. However, the "Wenatchee Valley" includes East Wenatchee, Rock Island, and Malaga. Named after the Wenatchi Indian tribe, the city's name means "river from canyons" or "rainbow robe" in Sahaptin. The "awenatchela" means "people at the source of a river." Wenatchee is known as the "apple capital of the world" because of its many orchards. The city is also called the "buckle of the power belt of the great northwest," referring to hydroelectric dams on the Columbia River. Rock Island Dam is in the middle of this "belt" and got the "buckle" name. This nickname appears at the top of Wenatchee's newspaper, the "Wenatchee World," but is not widely used elsewhere.

Charles Juste de Beauvau, Prince of Craon, was born on September 10, 1720, and died on May 21, 1793. He became the 2nd Prince of Craon in 1754 and was named Marshal of France in 1783. He was a French scholar, nobleman, and general. He was the son of Marc de Beauvau and the brother of Madame de Boufflers. He was also an uncle to the poet Stanislas de Boufflers.

Mikhail Nikolayevich Zadornov, born on July 21, 1948, in Jurmala, Latvia, Soviet Union, and died on November 10, 2017, in Moscow, Russia, was a Soviet and Russian comedian and writer. His father, Nikolai Zadornov, was a well-known writer from Riga. Zadornov's mother, Elena Matusevich (1909-1992), came from an old noble family, connected to the Polish King Stephen Bathory. As a child, Zadornov listened to his father read classic adventure and suspense stories and poems to him before bedtime. Zadornov's parents wanted him to become an engineer and sent him to an engineering institute. Mikhail Zadornov graduated from Moscow Aviation Institute. However, in the early 1980s, he began his career as a humorist, later joking about his engineering studies.

Samuel Willenberg, known as Igo, was born on February 16, 1923, and died on February 19, 2016. He was a Polish Holocaust survivor and an artist and writer. Willenberg was part of a special group, called the "Sonderkommando," at the Treblinka extermination camp in 1943. He took part in a planned revolt that month, and 300 people escaped. About 79 people survived the war. After the war, Willenberg went to Warsaw and joined the Warsaw Uprising. When he died, he was the last known survivor of the Treblinka prisoners' revolt. Like many other survivors, Willenberg moved to Israel. He received high honors from Poland, including the "Virtuti Militari" and the Commander's Cross of the Order of Merit, awarded by President Lech Kaczyński. His book "Revolt in Treblinka" was published in Hebrew, Polish, and English between 1986 and 1991. Willenberg also created sculptures and paintings.

Richmond is a town in Washington County, Rhode Island. The population was 7, 708 in 2010. It includes villages like Alton, Arcadia, Barberville, Carolina, Hillsdale, Kenyon, Shannock, Tug Hollow, Usquepaug, Wood River Junction, Woodville, and Wyoming. Students in Richmond go to school in the Chariho Regional School District.
Saint-Jean-sur-Verey is a village in Ain, which is in eastern France.

Adobe Dreamweaver is a web development tool made by Adobe Inc. It was created by Macromedia in 1997 and continued to be developed by them until 2005 when Macromedia was bought by Adobe. Dreamweaver works on both Mac and Windows. After Adobe bought Macromedia, newer versions of Dreamweaver followed web standards more closely. The latest versions support web technologies like CSS, JavaScript, and server-side languages such as ASP, ColdFusion, PHP, and others.

Zalmoxes is an extinct type of dinosaur from Romania. It belongs to a group called rhabdodontid ornithopod dinosaurs. The first known name for this dinosaur was "Rhabdodon robustum" in 1899, given by Franz Nopcsa. In 1915, Nopcsa changed it to "Rhabdodon robustus." In 1990, the name was fixed as "Rhabdodon robustus." In 2003, the species was renamed "Zalmoxes robustus." This name comes from the Dacian god Zalmoxis and refers to the strong bones. Another species, "Zalmoxes shqiperorum," was named in 2003. This name honors the Albanian people.
Jalal Dabagh, born in 1939, is a Kurdish politician and writer/journalist.

Golf Mill Shopping Center, also called Golf Mill Center, is a mall in Niles, Illinois. It is at 239 Golf Mill Center. The mall has about 100 specialty stores. There are also four big stores: JC Penney, Target, Kohl's, and Ross Dress for Less. The mall includes an AMC theater, two grocery stores, an XSport fitness gym, and a nine-story office building. It is near where Golf Road (Illinois Route 58), Milwaukee Avenue (Illinois Route 21), and Greenwood Avenue meet.

Wikimania is the official yearly conference of the Wikimedia Foundation. At the conference, people talk about and discuss Wikimedia projects like Wikipedia, other wikis, open-source software, free knowledge, and free content. They also discuss social and technical aspects related to these projects. Since 2011, the "Wikimedian of the Year" award winner is announced at Wikimania. The award was previously called "Wikipedian of the Year" until 2017. The next Wikimania will be in Bangkok, Thailand, in 2021. The planned event for August 2020 was delayed because of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Saint-Trivier-de-Courtes is a town in Ain, which is in eastern France.

Giuseppe Zamberletti was born on December 17, 1933, and died on January 26, 2019. He was an Italian politician. Zamberletti helped start Italy's Civil Protection organization. He became the first minister of Italy's Civil Protection in 1981.

Alanis Nadine Morissette, born on June 1, 1974, is a singer, songwriter, record producer, and actress from Canada and the United States. Known for her emotional mezzo-soprano voice, she started her career in Canada in the early 1990s with two dance-pop albums that didn't do very well. Later, under a recording deal, she moved to Holmby Hills in Los Angeles. In 1995, she released "Jagged Little Pill," a rock-oriented album that sold over 33 million copies worldwide and is her most famous work. Her next album, "Supposed Former Infatuation Junkie," came out in 1998. After that, she took more control of her music and became the producer for her albums "Under Rug Swept" (2002), "So-Called Chaos" (2004), "Flavors of Entanglement" (2008), and "Havoc and Bright Lights" (2012). Her ninth album, "Such Pretty Forks in the Road," was released in 2020. Morissette has sold more than 75 million records worldwide and is called the "queen of alt-rock angst" by Rolling Stone.

Shah Azizur Rahman was a politician from Bangladesh. He served as the prime minister. However, he faced a lot of controversy for working with the Pakistan army during the time Bangladesh was trying to become its own country.

A parameter is a characteristic that helps define or classify a system, like an event, project, or object. It is useful for identifying or evaluating the system's status or performance. In general, a parameter is something that is important when studying or working with a particular system. The word "parameter" is used in various fields such as math, computer programming, engineering, statistics, logic, and linguistics. Sometimes, people use "parameter" incorrectly, as a fancy word for "limit" or "boundary," which can be confusing. This might happen because "parameter" is sometimes confused with "perimeter."

A mirage is a natural optical effect where light bends, making distant objects or the sky seem displaced. The word "mirage" comes from the Latin "mirari," meaning "to look at" or "to wonder at." There are three main types: inferior, superior, and fata morgana. Fata morgana is a special kind of superior mirage that shows many stacked images, changing quickly. Unlike a hallucination, a mirage is a real phenomenon that can be photographed, as light rays actually bend to create the false image. However, what we see depends on how we interpret it. For example, on land, inferior mirages can easily be mistaken for small bodies of water.

Tom Pevsner was born on October 2, 1926, and died on August 18, 2014. He was a British film assistant director and producer. He was the second of three children. His father, Sir Nikolaus Pevsner, was an architectural historian of Russian-Jewish background. The family moved to the UK from Germany in 1933 to avoid the Nazis. After serving in the British army from 1944 to 1948, Tom studied languages at Cambridge University. He was part of the St John's College Film Society and edited "The Cambridge Review." After graduation, he worked at the Film Finance Corporation. Tom Pevsner worked on several notable films. He was an assistant director for "The Ladykillers" (1955), "The Longest Day" (1962), and "The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes" (1970). He also produced "Dracula." He worked as an associate and then executive producer on every James Bond film from "For Your Eyes Only" to "GoldenEye." His work on the Bond series is mentioned in "Spectre," where character Q refers to a hotel named Pevsner. Tom Pevsner died at the age of 87. He was honored during the 87th Academy Awards in February 2015.

Richard Church Thompson was an American illustrator and cartoonist. He was born on October 8, 1957, and passed away on July 27, 2016. He is famous for his comic strip called "Cul de sac" and an illustrated poem titled "Make the Pie Higher." In 2010, he received a special award called the Reuben Award for being the best cartoonist that year.

Nelson Mandela Bridge is in Johannesburg, South Africa. It is the fourth bridge over the railway lines west of Johannesburg Park Station. The first bridge is the Johan Rissik Bridge next to the station. The bridge was finished in 2003 and cost 38 million rand to build. It was meant to connect two important business areas, Braamfontein and Newtown, and help improve the city center. The bridge is part of Johannesburg's M27 route.

The Hateful Eight is a 2015 American western movie by Quentin Tarantino. It stars Samuel L. Jackson, Kurt Russell, Jennifer Jason Leigh, Walton Goggins, Demián Bichir, Tim Roth, Michael Madsen, and Bruce Dern. They are eight strangers who seek shelter from a snowstorm in a stagecoach stop after the American Civil War. Tarantino announced the film in November 2013. He planned it as a novel and a sequel to Django Unchained (2012), but later decided to make it a standalone film. The script leaked in January 2014, but Tarantino directed a live reading. After that, he restarted the project. Filming began on December 8, 2014, near Telluride, Colorado. Italian composer Ennio Morricone wrote the original score for the film, his first and only score for a Tarantino movie, and his first complete western score in 34 years. The Weinstein Company distributed the film in the United States. It was released on December 25, 2015, in a limited roadshow release on 70 mm film, then expanded widely on December 30, 2015. Critics praised Leigh's performance and Morricone's score, and the film earned positive reviews. It grossed $155.8 million. Tarantino's budget estimates ranged from $44 million to $62 million. Morricone won his first Academy Award for best original score and a Golden Globe. The film also received Oscar nominations for best supporting actress (Leigh) and best cinematography (Robert Richardson). Tarantino re-released the film on Netflix as a four-episode miniseries in 2019 with the subtitle "Extended Version." This was Tarantino's last film with the Weinstein Company, as he ended his partnership after allegations of sexual abuse against Harvey Weinstein in October 2017.

Mason is a city in Michigan, the U.S. It is named after the state's first governor, Stevens T. Mason. According to the 2010 census, the city has 8, 252 people. Mason is the county seat of Ingham County. It is special because it is the only city in the U.S. that serves as a county seat but is not the state capital. The state capital, Lansing, is also in Ingham County. Even though Mason is the county seat, many county offices and courtrooms are in Lansing.
Ambleny is a commune in the Aisne department, which is in the Hauts-de-France region of northern France. People from Ambleny are called Amblenois or Amblenoises.

Natural Steps is a small town in Pulaski County, Arkansas, United States. It is 18 miles northwest of Little Rock and sits on the southern bank of the Arkansas River. According to the 2010 census, the town has 426 people. Today, Natural Steps is a small farming community with some businesses. The Natural Steps, a rock formation, still exist and are used as a marker for river runners. However, the formation is not open for public viewing.

The cochlea is part of the inner ear and helps us hear. It is a spiral-shaped space in the bony labyrinth, making 2.75 turns in humans. At the center is the modiolus. Inside the cochlea, there is a key part called the organ of Corti, which helps us hear. It is found along the wall separating the fluid-filled chambers in the coiled tube. The word "cochlea" comes from this name.

Myrtle "Kay" Thompson Cagle (June 3, 1925 – December 22, 2019) was an American pilot. She was also part of the Mercury 13, a group of female astronauts. Cagle taught people to fly planes as a flight instructor and wrote about aviation in North Carolina.

In American history, the fire-eaters were pro-slavery Democrats in the south before the Civil War. They wanted the southern states to break away and form a new country. This new country became known as the Confederate States of America. Robert Barnwell Rhett from South Carolina was a leader in this group. Some fire-eaters wanted to restart America's involvement in the slave trade, which had been illegal since 1808.

Daniel Michael Devito Jr., born on November 17, 1944, is an American actor, comedian, director, producer, and screenwriter. He is famous for playing Louie De Palma, a taxi dispatcher, in the TV show "Taxi" from 1978 to 1983. This role earned him a Golden Globe and an Emmy award. He also plays Frank Reynolds in the TV sitcom "It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia" since 2006. In films, he appeared in movies like "One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest" (1975), "Terms of Endearment" (1983), "Twins" (1988), "Matilda" (1996), and "Dumbo" (2019). He has also voiced characters in animated films such as "Space Jam" (1996) and "The Lorax" (2012). Devito and Michael Shamberg started Jersey Films. Stacey Sher later joined them as a partner. This company produced films like "Pulp Fiction," "Garden State," and "Freedom Writers." He also owned Jersey Television, which made shows like "Reno 911!" with his wife Rhea Perlman. Devito starred with Perlman in the 1996 film "Matilda," based on Roald Dahl's book. He was also a producer for "Erin Brockovich," which was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Picture. Devito's short height is due to a rare genetic condition called multiple epiphyseal dysplasia.
The Division of Reid is an Australian electoral district in New South Wales.
Auguste Chabaud was a French painter and sculptor. He lived from October 3, 1882, to May 23, 1955.

The 1978 FIFA World Cup, the 11th tournament, took place in Argentina from June 1 to June 25. Argentina won the cup by defeating the Netherlands 3-1 in extra time. The final match was played at Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires, the capital of Argentina. This victory was Argentina's first World Cup title. They became the fifth country, after Uruguay, Italy, England, and West Germany, to both host and win the World Cup. Argentina, the Netherlands, and Brazil were awarded gold, silver, and bronze medals, respectively. Iran and Tunisia made their debut in the tournament. This World Cup featured 16 teams, which was the original number. Only 15 teams (plus the host, who qualified automatically) could participate from 1930 to 2002, except that the defending champions were automatically qualified from 1934 to 2002. For the next World Cup in Spain, FIFA increased the number of teams to 24. The official ball was the Adidas Tango.

Healesville Sanctuary, formerly called Sir Colin Mackenzie Sanctuary, is a zoo that focuses on Australian animals. It is in Healesville, a rural area of Victoria, Australia. The zoo has a history of breeding native animals. It is one of only two places that have successfully bred a platypus, the other being Sydney's Taronga Zoo. It also helps protect the helmeted honeyeater, an endangered bird. The zoo is set in a natural bushland. Paths wind through different areas where visitors can see wallabies, wombats, dingoes, kangaroos, and over 200 bird species. Guided tours, bird shows, and information areas are available for visitors.
Pré-en-pail was a former commune in the Mayenne department in northwestern France. On January 1, 2016, it became part of a new commune called Pré-en-pail-Saint-Samson.

The French National Aeronautical and Astronautical Association, known as 3AF or AAAF, is based in Paris. It was formed in 1971 from two earlier groups: AFITAE, which started in 1945, and SFA, which began in 1955. 3AF brings together people interested in aerospace, whether for work or personal reasons. Their goal is to share opinions and advance scientific and technological knowledge related to aerospace and its history. Members are mostly technicians, engineers, and researchers. Industrial partners include major companies like Alcatel Space, EADS, and Arianespace. 3AF is part of the Confederation of European Aerospace Societies, along with similar associations from Germany, Britain, and Italy.

Fermentation is a process where chemical changes happen in organic materials due to enzymes. In biochemistry, it means using enzymes to get energy from carbohydrates without oxygen. In food making, it refers to how tiny living things change food or drinks in a good way. This field is called zymology. Fermentation is how microorganisms produce energy by breaking down nutrients in the absence of oxygen. People have used fermentation since ancient times to make foods and drinks. For example, fermentation makes lactic acid in pickles, kombucha, kimchi, and yogurt. It also helps make alcohol in wine and beer. Inside animals, including humans, fermentation happens in the gut.

Arif-Ur-Rehman Alvi was born on August 29, 1949. He is a Pakistani politician. Alvi became the 13th president of Pakistan on September 9, 2018. He served in the National Assembly of Pakistan from June 2013 to May 2018, and again from August to September 2018. Alvi was a founder of Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) and was chosen as Pakistan's president in a presidential election on September 4, 2018.

Maynard Elliott Solomon, born on January 5, 1930, co-founded Vanguard Records and was a music producer. Later, he wrote biographies about Viennese classical composers. He wrote an influential biography about Beethoven and an award-winning book of essays. He also wrote a biography about Mozart. Solomon was the first to openly suggest that Schubert was homosexual in a scholarly setting.
Lancaster can mean: A city A county

Potsdam is the biggest city in Brandenburg, a state in Germany. It's next to Berlin, the capital of Germany, and part of the Berlin-Brandenburg area. Potsdam is near the Havel River, southwest of Berlin. Potsdam used to be where Prussian and German kings lived until 1918. The city's design showed ideas from the Enlightenment era. It combined buildings and nature to make it look like a "pretty, countryside dream" to remind people of their connection to nature and reason. The city is known for its lakes and cultural landmarks, especially the Sanssouci parks and palaces, the largest UNESCO World Heritage site in Germany. The 1945 Potsdam Conference was held at Cecilienhof Palace. In the 1930s, Babelsberg, a place southeast of Potsdam, became a major film studio. Since the fall of the Berlin Wall, it has been important for European film production. Filmstudio Babelsberg is the oldest large film studio in the world. Potsdam became a science center in the 19th century. Today, it has three colleges, the University of Potsdam, and over 30 research institutes.

Ray Milton Dolby was an American engineer and inventor. He was born on January 18, 1933, and passed away on September 12, 2013. Dolby invented a noise reduction system called Dolby NR. He also helped develop the video tape recorder while working at Ampex. Additionally, he founded Dolby Laboratories.

Michael Gregory Rowe, born on March 18, 1962, is an American TV host and narrator who used to sing opera. He is famous for hosting "Dirty Jobs" on the Discovery Channel and "Somebody's Got to Do It" for CNN. Currently, he hosts a series called "Returning the Favor" on Facebook, where he finds people doing good deeds and returns the favor. He also hosts a podcast named "The Way I Heard It with Mike Rowe," which tells short stories for curious people with short attention spans. Mike Rowe has narrated shows like "Deadliest Catch," "How the Universe Works," and "Shark Week" on channels such as the Discovery Channel, the Science Channel, and National Geographic. He has also appeared in commercials for Ford Motor Company. In June 2020, the Discovery Channel announced "Dirty Jobs: Rowe'd Trip," which will air four episodes in mid-July 2020. The series is described as a mix of a reunion, a road trip, and a look-back-special.

Joe Osborn was born on August 28, 1937, and died on December 14, 2018. He was an American bass guitar player. He worked as a session musician in Los Angeles with a group called the Wrecking Crew in the 1960s and 1970s. He also worked in Nashville with a group called the A-Team of studio musicians during the same time period.
Buhler is a city in Reno County, Kansas, United States. In 2010, the city had 1,327 people.

Screaming Trees was an American rock band formed in Ellensburg, Washington in 1985. The band members were Mark Lanegan (vocals), Gary Lee Conner (guitar), Van Conner (bass), and Mark Pickerel (drums). Barrett Martin replaced Pickerel later. Screaming Trees are known for their grunge music, but their sound included hard rock and psychedelic elements. They made seven studio albums, five EPs, and three compilations. Screaming Trees were one of the pioneers of grunge music, alongside bands like Alice in Chains, Pearl Jam, Nirvana, and Soundgarden. They became famous during the early 1990s grunge movement. The band had a top ten hit on the modern rock tracks charts. They faced problems making a follow-up to their album "Dust," leading to their official breakup in 2000.

Hedemora is a town in Dalarna County, Sweden. It had 7,273 people living there in 2010. Although it is not very big, Hedemora is called a "city" because of its history. It is the oldest city in the county. Some people from Hedemora include Jonas Nilsson, Kerstin Thorborg, Martin Matsbo, Bertil Norman, and Ulf Stenlund. Hedemora makes diesel engines for ships. Their engines are used in submarines, like those built by Kockums. The Collins class submarines are for the Royal Australian Navy, and the Archer class submarines are for the Republic of Singapore Navy. Hedemora is also the home of Clifftop Games, an independent game developer that created games like Kathy Rain and Whispers of a Machine.

The Indian roller (Coracias benghalensis) is a bird in the roller family. It is found in west Asia and the Indian subcontinent. It is not considered endangered. The Indochinese roller used to be considered a subspecies. The male birds show off by flying in exciting ways during breeding time. You often see them perched on trees or wires near roads. They like to live in open grasslands and scrub forests. The Indian roller is most common in India. Some Indian states have picked it as their state bird.

The 1963 Atlantic hurricane season included one of the deadliest tropical cyclones: Hurricane Flora. The season ran from June 15 to November 15. Nine named storms formed, which was close to average. The first storm, Hurricane Arlene, developed between Cape Verde and the Lesser Antilles on July 31. It caused damage worth about $300,000 in Bermuda. Other storms like Beulah, Debora, and an unnamed one did not hit land. In September, Hurricane Cindy damaged Texas, causing three deaths and around $12.5 million in damage. Hurricane Edith hit the Lesser Antilles and eastern Greater Antilles, leading to 10 deaths and about $43 million in damage, mostly on Martinique. The most serious storm was Hurricane Flora, a Category 4 hurricane. It caused heavy rain and floods, leaving at least 7,193 deaths and about $773.4 million in damage in the Greater Antilles, including Cuba. Hurricane Flora is among the deadliest Atlantic hurricanes. In October, Hurricane Ginny moved off the southeastern United States and struck Nova Scotia, causing at least three deaths and $400,000 in damage in the U.S. The last storm, Tropical Storm Helena, hit Guadeloupe, causing five deaths and over $500,000 in damage. The storms overall caused at least 7,214 deaths and about $830.1 million in damage.

Vicente Trueba Pérez was born on October 16, 1905, in Sierra Pando, Torrelavega, Cantabria. He died on November 10, 1986. He was a professional cyclist who raced on roads. He is best known for winning the King of the Mountains award in the Tour de France. This was for being the overall winner in the mountains classification. He also came in sixth place in the general ranking of the Tour de France.
Septèmes-les-Vallons is a town in the Bouches-du-Rhône area of southern France. It is about 10. 7 kilometers or 6. 5 miles north of Marseille's center.

In a musical composition, a chord progression is a sequence of chords. These progressions form the basis of harmony in Western music from classical to modern times. They are crucial in pop, rock, blues, jazz, and traditional music. In these genres, chord progressions determine the melody and rhythm. Chord progressions help establish or contradict the key of a song, known technically as tonality. In classical music theory, they are often written using roman numerals, like I–vi–ii–v. In popular and traditional music, chords are often named and described by their quality. For example, in the key of C major, the chord progression might be written as C major–A minor–D minor–G major. In rock and blues, musicians use roman numerals to easily transpose songs to different keys. For example, the 12-bar blues often uses I, IV, and V chords, like i–i–i–i, IV–IV–I–I, V–IV–I–I. Chord progressions can vary in complexity. Simple pop and rock songs from the 1980s to 2010s might use basic progressions. Funk focuses on rhythm and groove, so entire funk songs can use just one chord. Jazz-funk might use a two-, three-, or four-chord vamp. Punk songs often use just a few chords. On the other hand, bebop jazz songs can have 32-bar forms with one or two chord changes per bar.
Lorscheid is a town in the Trier-Saarburg district, in Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany.

The Denisovans were an extinct species of ancient humans who lived in Asia during the Paleolithic era, possibly until around 14,500 years ago in New Guinea. Not much is known about them because only a few remains have been found. Scientists learned a lot about them through DNA analysis. They are sometimes called "homo denisova," "h. altaiensis," or "h. sapiens denisova." The first Denisovan was identified in 2010 from a young girl's finger bone found in a cave in Siberia. The cave was also home to Neanderthals, but it’s not clear if Denisovans and Neanderthals ever lived together there. More Denisovan remains were found in Siberia and one in China. This shows they lived in different habitats, including forests, tundras, mountains, and jungles. From DNA, we know they had dark skin, eyes, and hair. They were similar to Neanderthals but had bigger molars, like some ancient humans and australopithecines. Denisovans mixed with modern humans. About 3 to 5 percent of the DNA of people from Melanesia and Aboriginal Australians comes from Denisovans, while Papuans have around 6 percent. There’s also evidence they interbred with local Neanderthals, with about 17 percent of the Denisovan DNA coming from them. A hybrid named "Denny" was found with a Denisovan father and a Neanderthal mother. About 4 percent of the Denisovan DNA comes from an unknown ancient human species that separated from modern humans over a million years ago.

Questacon, the national science and technology center, is in Canberra, Australia. It's on the southern side of Lake Burley Griffin. Questacon has over 200 interactive exhibits about science and technology. It also has science programs to inspire Australian children to love science.

Peter Neville Luard Pears, born on June 22, 1910, and died on April 3, 1986, was an English singer. He worked closely with composer Benjamin Britten for nearly forty years, both personally and professionally. Pears started his musical career slowly, unsure if he should play an instrument or sing. It wasn't until he met Britten in 1937 that he decided to focus on singing. After becoming partners, Britten wrote many songs and operas with Pears's voice in mind. Pears sang in over ten of Britten's operas. In concert halls, Pears and Britten were well-known for singing Schubert and Schumann's songs. They recorded many of Britten's works for Pears and also sang other composers' music. Pears sang music from the 16th to the 20th century. With Britten, Pears helped found the Aldeburgh Festival in 1947 and the Britten-Pears School in 1972. After Britten died in 1976, Pears continued to be active in the festival and the school, where he directed singing. His voice had a special sound, not everyone liked it, but he could sing in many different styles.

Edgar Lawrence Doctorow, born on January 6, 1931, and died on July 21, 2015, was an American novelist, editor, and professor. He is best known for his historical fiction. Doctorow was considered one of the most important American novelists of the 20th century. He wrote twelve novels and three volumes of short fiction, as well as a stage drama. Some of his famous novels include "Ragtime" (1975), "Billy Bathgate" (1989), and "The March" (2005). His works often featured fictional characters in real historical settings with well-known figures and used various narrative styles. Doctorow's stories were praised for their creativity, and he was admired for his bold imagination. Many of his novels and short stories were also turned into movies, such as "Welcome to Hard Times" (1967), "Daniel" (1983), "Billy Bathgate" (1991), and "Wakefield" (2016). His most famous adaptations were the film "Ragtime" (1981) and the Broadway musical of the same name (1998), which won four Tony Awards. Doctorow received several awards, including the National Book Critics Circle Award for "Ragtime," "Billy Bathgate," and "The March," and the American Academy of Arts and Letters gold medal for fiction. Former President Barack Obama called him one of America's greatest novelists.

Roger Mayweather was born on April 24, 1961, in Grand Rapids, Michigan. He was a boxer and a trainer. He fought professionally from 1981 to 1999. He was a champion in two weight categories: super featherweight and light welterweight. He also held titles in light welterweight and welterweight. Mayweather had a family in boxing; his brothers were Floyd Mayweather Sr. and Jeff Mayweather. His nephew, Floyd Mayweather Jr., became a famous boxer. Roger trained Floyd Jr. from 2000 to 2012, and Floyd Jr. became one of the greatest boxers of all time.

Beauty and the Beast: The Enchanted Christmas is a 1997 American animated Christmas musical fantasy film. It came out directly to video. The film is a sequel to the 1991 Disney animated movie, "Beauty and the Beast." In 1997, it sold 7.6 million VHS tapes. This film is the first of two sequels based on "Beauty and the Beast," with the second being "Belle's Magical World" in 1998.
Charmes-sur-Rhône is a village in the Ardèche region of France, in the south.

Aberdeen (in Lakota, "ablíla") is a city in Brown County, South Dakota, United States. It is about northeast of Pierre. According to the 2010 census, Aberdeen had 26,091 people, making it the third-largest city in the state after Sioux Falls and Rapid City. Aberdeen is part of the Aberdeen micropolitan area, which includes Brown and Edmunds counties and had 40,602 people in 2010. The city is known as a college town, as it is home to Northern State University and Presentation College.
Anicadu is a village that is about 4 km from Mallapally town. It is in the Pathanamthitta district.

Cranbrook is a city in southeast British Columbia, Canada. It is on the west side of the Kootenay River, where the Kootenay River meets the St. Mary's River. Cranbrook is the largest town in the area called East Kootenay. In 2016, Cranbrook had 19,259 people, and when you include nearby areas, the total was 26,083. The regional office of the East Kootenay Regional District is in Cranbrook. Also, Cranbrook has the Canadian Museum of Rail Travel. This museum shows old train cars, including some built in the 1920s for the Canadian Pacific Railway and some from the 1900s for the Spokane International Railway.

The Swedish Bandy Association is the governing body for bandy in Sweden. It organizes men's leagues like Elitserien and Allsvenskan, and women's league Damallsvenskan. It also manages the men's and women's national teams. The association was founded in Stockholm on April 5, 1925, and moved from Katrineholm to Stockholm. Bandy was introduced in Sweden in 1895 by Clarence von Rosen, who learned the game in Great Britain. He started the first Swedish Bandy club, Stockholm Hockeyklubb. Bandy was first organized within the Swedish Ballgame Association in 1906, then the Swedish Football Association in 1907. At a meeting on April 5, 1925, 49 clubs formed the Swedish Bandy Association. Since 1931, the association has run national leagues in Sweden. The Swedish Bandy Champions title is given to the winners of the final, played in March. The association used to have 23 district associations but in 2013, they changed to six larger districts: Central Sweden, North, Stockholm, Småland, South West, and Västergötland. The Swedish Bandy Association was one of the founding members of the Federation of International Bandy in 1955.
Launay-Villiers is a commune in the Mayenne department in northwest France.
Cher is a department in the Centre-Val de Loire region of France. The department is named after the Cher River.

kfum Örebro is a YMCA association in Örebro, Sweden, founded in 1890. In 1990, the club won the Swedish women's juniors national volleyball championship. From 1996 to 2001, the club won the Swedish women's volleyball championship for six years in a row. The men's floorball team played in the Swedish top division during the 1990s.

Nuclear weapons testing, uranium mining, and nuclear power have often been topics for discussion in Australia. The anti-nuclear movement has a long history in the country, starting with debates about French nuclear testing in the Pacific in 1972-73 and uranium mining in Australia from 1976-77. In the mid-1970s, several groups focused on nuclear issues were formed, such as the Movement Against Uranium Mining and Campaign Against Nuclear Energy (CANE), working with groups like Friends of the Earth and the Australian Conservation Foundation. The movement faced a setback in 1983 when the new Labor government did not stop uranium mining as promised. By the late 1980s, uranium prices fell, nuclear power became more expensive, and the anti-nuclear movement seemed to succeed. CANE was disbanded in 1988. Around 2003, people supporting nuclear power suggested it could help with global warming, and the Australian government showed more interest. However, campaigners and some scientists argued that nuclear power could not replace other energy sources, and uranium mining could lead to greenhouse gas emissions. As of 2015, Australia had no nuclear power plants but five uranium mines, with four in South Australia and one in the Northern Territory. Most of the uranium mined in Australia is exported. Australia does not have nuclear weapons or nuclear-powered vessels.

Glasgow Central is one of two main train stations in Glasgow, Scotland. It opened on August 1, 1879, by the Caledonian Railway. Managed by Network Rail, it is the northern end of the West Coast Main Line, serving inter-city trains between Glasgow and England. The other main station in Glasgow's city center is not mentioned here. In 2017-2018, about 33 million people used Glasgow Central. It is the twelfth-busiest railway station in Britain and the busiest in Scotland. Network Rail says over 38 million people use it yearly, with most being passengers. Glasgow Central is a Category A listed building. In Simon Jenkins' "Britain's 100 Best Railway Stations," it received five stars, ranking among the top ten. In 2017, customer satisfaction was very high, with a score of 95.2%, the highest in the UK.

Aerogel is a very light material made by replacing the liquid in a gel with a gas. It is so light that it has very low density and does not conduct heat well. People often call it "frozen smoke," "solid smoke," "solid air," or "blue smoke" because it looks translucent and scatters light. Some aerogels feel like foam, while others feel like expanded polystyrene. They can be made from different materials. In 1931, Samuel Kistler created the first aerogel by drying a gel without losing its structure. Later, Kistler worked with other materials like alumina, chromia, and tin dioxide. Carbon aerogels were developed in the late 1980s. Aerogels are not a single material with a fixed formula but a group of materials with a similar structure.

James Albert Smith Leach, born on October 15, 1942, is an American academic and former politician. He was the ninth chair of the National Endowment for the Humanities from 2009 to 2013. Leach also worked as a member of the U.S. House of Representatives from Iowa from 1977 to 2007. He taught at Princeton University and was the interim director of the Institute of Politics at the John F. Kennedy School of Government at Harvard University from September 17, 2007, to September 1, 2008. Leach was a Republican in the U.S. House of Representatives for 30 years, representing Iowa's 1st district until 2003. In Congress, he led the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services from 1995 to 2001. He also led the Asian and Pacific Affairs subcommittee of the House Committee on International Relations from 2001 to 2006. Leach helped start and co-chaired the Congressional Humanities Caucus. He lost his 2006 re-election bid to Dave Loebsack, who was from the Democratic Party. Leach was also known for sponsoring the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act in 1999, a significant piece of banking legislation.

edinburgh trams is a tramway in edinburgh, scotland. It is operated by a company called edinburgh trams ltd. The tramway runs between york place in the new town and edinburgh airport, with 16 stops. Construction started in june 2008 and opened on may 31, 2014. The project cost £375 million in 2003, but the cost increased to £521 million by may 2008. After delays, the final cost was £776 million. The tramway was profitable in just two years and more people used it than expected. In march 2019, the council agreed to extend the line to newhaven. The new line will be ready by early 2023.

Quarten is a municipality in the constituency of Sarganserland, in the canton of St. Gallen, Switzerland. It is located above Lake Walensee. The municipality includes Quarten itself, as well as Oberterzen, Unterterzen, Quinten, Mols, Murg, and parts of Tannenbodenalp.

In aesthetics, the uncanny valley describes how people feel about objects that look almost human. When objects look too human-like but are not perfect, people might feel strange or uncomfortable. The term "valley" refers to a dip in how much people like these objects, as they become more human-like. Examples can be seen in robots, 3D animations, and realistic dolls. As we get better at making things look real, like in virtual reality and augmented reality, people might have eerie feelings when something is almost, but not quite, human-like.

Andre Kirk Agassi, born on April 29, 1970, is an American retired tennis player who used to be the world's top player. He won eight Grand Slam titles in singles and got a gold medal in the 1996 Olympics. He was the first male player to win four Australian Open titles, a record later broken by Novak Djokovic and Roger Federer. Agassi is the second of five male players to win a career Grand Slam, and the first to achieve a career Golden Slam (a Grand Slam and an Olympic gold medal). He is also the only man to win the ATP Tour World Championships. Agassi was the first male to win Grand Slam titles on three different surfaces: hard, clay, and grass. He won 17 ATP Masters Series titles and helped the U.S. Davis Cup team win in 1990, 1992, and 1995. His career peaked in 1995 when he first reached the world No. 1 ranking, but he faced personal issues in the mid-to-late 1990s and dropped to No. 141 in 1997. He regained the No. 1 ranking in 1999 and had his best years until 2003. Agassi had back problems due to bulging discs and a bone spur, which led to his retirement on September 3, 2006, after losing in the US Open. He founded the Andre Agassi Charitable Foundation, raising over $60 million for at-risk children in southern Nevada. In 2001, he opened the Andre Agassi College Preparatory Academy in Las Vegas, a public school for at-risk children. He has been married to tennis player Steffi Graf since 2001.

Lothar Herbert Matthäus, born on March 21, 1961, is a German football manager and former player. He led West Germany to win the 1990 FIFA World Cup and lifted the trophy. He was named European Footballer of the Year and was the first to receive the FIFA World Player of the Year award, making him the only German to win it. Matthäus played in five FIFA World Cups (1982, 1986, 1990, 1994, 1998), a record held by no other outfield player in men's football until 2018, when Rafael Márquez from Mexico tied it. He played in 25 World Cup games, the most by any single player. Matthäus was the captain of the West German team that won the 1990 World Cup in Italy and the German squad in the 1994 World Cup in the United States. He also won the UEFA Euro 1980 and played in the 1984, 1988, and 2000 UEFA European Championships. In 1999, at age 38, he was voted German Footballer of the Year for the second time, having previously won it in 1990. Matthäus is the player with the most appearances for Germany, retiring with 150 total appearances (83 for West Germany) over 20 years, and scoring 23 goals. He is a member of the FIFA 100 list, chosen by Pelé as one of the greatest living football players. Diego Maradona praised him, saying, "He is the best rival I've ever had. I guess that's enough to define him." Matthäus was a versatile player known as one of the greatest midfielders of all time. He was famous for his smart passes, good position sense, timely tackles, and strong shots. During his career, he mostly played as a box-to-box midfielder but later played as a sweeper.
Karl-Josef Rauber, born on April 11, 1934, is a cardinal in the Catholic Church. He worked as a papal nuncio from 1982 until he retired in 2009.

Dwight Lyman Moody, known as D. L. Moody, lived from February 5, 1837, to December 22, 1899. He was an American preacher and publisher connected with the holiness movement. He started the Moody Church and schools in Massachusetts, now called Northfield Mount Hermon School. He also founded Moody Bible Institute and Moody Publishers. One of his famous sayings was, "Faith makes everything possible... Love makes everything easy." Moody left his successful shoe business to focus on spreading his religious message. He worked with the YMCA during the Civil War, helping Union soldiers. In Chicago, he created a major evangelical center that is still active today. He worked with singer Ira Sankey. Together, they toured the United States and the British Isles. Moody spoke passionately about God's love and friendship, kindness, and forgiveness. He did not focus on preaching about hellfire and condemnation.

Stephanie Murphy was born as Đặng Thị Ngọc Dung on September 16, 1978. She is an American politician from Florida. She belongs to the Democratic Party and represents Florida's 7th congressional district in the United States House of Representatives. She won this seat in 2016 by defeating the previous representative, John Mica. The district includes parts of downtown and northern Orlando, as well as Winter Park, Maitland, Sanford, and Altamonte Springs. Murphy is the first Vietnamese-American woman and the second Vietnamese-American overall to be elected to Congress, following Republican Joseph Cao from Louisiana.

Patrick Head, born on June 5, 1946, helped start Williams Formula One team. He worked as a technical director at Williams Grand Prix Engineering for 27 years. During this time, he created many new ideas for the race cars. Head was in charge of designing and building Williams cars until May 2004, when his duties were passed to Sam Michael.

Jizya, or jizyah, is a yearly tax historically collected from permanent non-Muslim subjects, known as dhimmis, in states governed by Islamic law. Muslim jurists required adult, free, and sane males among the dhimmis to pay the jizya, while women, children, elders, the sick, the disabled, monks, hermits, slaves, and foreigners temporarily living in Muslim lands were exempt. Those joining the military or unable to afford it were also exempt. The Quran and hadiths mention jizya but do not specify its rate. Early Muslim rulers adapted existing taxation systems from previous rulers, such as the Byzantine and Sasanian empires. Jizya varied in application throughout Islamic history. It was one of the main sources of revenue for some Islamic polities, like the Ottoman Empire and Indian Muslim sultanates. The tax rate was usually a fixed annual amount based on the payer's financial capability. Historically, jizya was seen as a fee for protection, exemption from military service, permission to practice a non-Muslim faith, and proof of submission to the Muslim state. Some saw it as a symbol of non-Muslims' inferiority for not converting to Islam, or as a significant source of revenue. Monks and the clergy were exempt. The term jizya appears in the Quran, referring to a tax from "People of the Book," specifically Jews and Christians. It later applied to other religions like Zoroastrians and Hindus. In the Indian subcontinent, the practice was abolished by the 18th century, and it nearly vanished during the 20th century with the decline of Islamic states and increased religious tolerance. Today, no nation state in the Islamic world imposes jizya, though there have been reports of groups like the Pakistani Taliban and ISIS attempting to revive it. Some modern Islamic scholars argue jizya should be paid by non-Muslims in an Islamic state. For example, Sayyid Qutb saw it as punishment for polytheism, while Abdul Rahman Doi viewed it as a counterpart to zakat paid by Muslims. Khaled Abou El Fadl, a moderate Muslim, rejects the dhimma system, including jizya, as inappropriate for modern nation-states and democracies.

Saint-Sauveur-en-Puisaye is a village in the Yonne department, which is in Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, in central France. In the early 1970s, the Château de la Folie, located north of the village (between Saint-Sauveur-en-Puisaye and Mézilles), was part of a "Maharishi's Science of Creative Intelligence" project. People from all over the world came here to learn transcendental meditation and help renovate the buildings to turn the château into a meditation center. There were plans to build a meditation campus in the fields between the château and the Etang de la Folie, right next to the D7 road. However, the project was abandoned in the mid-1970s for unknown reasons.

Rodney Stephen Steiger, born on April 14, 1925, and died on July 9, 2002, was an American actor. He was known for playing unusual, often angry and crazy characters. Steiger was called "one of Hollywood's most charismatic and dynamic stars." He was closely linked to method acting, fully becoming his roles, which sometimes led to disagreements with directors and co-stars. In 1954, he acted as Marlon Brando's mobster brother, Charley, in "On the Waterfront." In 1964, he played the title character, Sol Nazerman, in "The Pawnbroker," which won him an Academy Award for Best Actor. Steiger was born in Westhampton, New York, to a vaudevillian father. He had a tough childhood and ran away from his alcoholic mother when he was 16. During World War II, he served in the South Pacific. After the war, he started acting on TV in 1947 and got praised for his role in the TV play "Marty" in 1953. He began his stage career in 1946 with "Curse You, Jack Dalton!" and appeared in plays like "An Enemy of the People," "Night Music," "Seagulls Over Sorrento," and "Rashomon." Steiger first appeared in a movie in 1951, in "Teresa." He starred in films such as "The Big Knife," "Oklahoma!," "Across the Bridge," and "Al Capone." His role as a bitter Jewish Holocaust survivor in "The Pawnbroker" (1964) earned him critical acclaim. In "The Heat of the Night" (1967), he played a police chief in Mississippi who learns to respect an African-American officer, Sidney Poitier. That movie won him another Academy Award. In 1968, he acted as a serial killer in "No Way to Treat a Lady." During the 1970s, Steiger focused on European productions to find more challenging roles. He portrayed Napoleon Bonaparte in "Waterloo" (1970), a Mexican bandit in "Duck, You Sucker!" (1971), Benito Mussolini in "The Last Days of Mussolini" (1975), and a troubled priest in "The Amityville Horror" (1979). In the 1980s, his health issues made it hard for him to find roles, and he appeared in low-budget B-movies. His last role was as Judge H. Lee Sarokin in "The Hurricane" (1999), with Norman Jewison, his director from "The Heat of the Night." Steiger was married five times and had a daughter, opera singer Anna Steiger, and a son, Michael Steiger. He died of pneumonia and kidney failure on July 9, 2002, aged 77, in Los Angeles, and was survived by his fifth wife, Joan Benedict Steiger.

Suddi, in the Sardinian language, is a "comune" (municipality) in the province of South Sardinia, in Italy. It is near Cagliari. On December 31, 2004, Suddi had 1,179 people living there. It covers an area of. Suddi shares borders with the following municipalities: Gesico, Mandas, Selegas, Senorbì, and Siurgus Donigala.
remetschwil is a municipality in the baden district of the aargau canton in switzerland.

Suseok, also known as viewing stones or scholar's stones, is a term in Korean for naturally occurring or shaped small rocks that are traditionally valued. These stones are similar to Chinese gongshi and Japanese suiseki. Suseok can be any color. They come in different sizes, from less than one kilogram to hundreds of kilograms. The term also includes rocks placed in traditional Korean gardens.

Glynis Johns, born on October 5, 1923, is a retired British actress, dancer, pianist, and singer. She was born in Pretoria, South Africa, while her parents were performing there. Glynis is famous for creating the role of Desirée Armfeldt in the Broadway show "A Little Night Music," where she won a Tony Award. She also played Winifred Banks in the Disney musical film "Mary Poppins." In these roles, she sang special songs, like "Send in the Clowns" and "Sister Suffragette." Glynis was nominated for an Oscar for her work in the 1960 film "The Sundowners." She is known for her husky, breathy voice and cheerful personality.
Manuele Blasi, born on August 17, 1980, is an Italian former football player who played as a midfielder.

Ketchikan is a city in Alaska's southeastern part. It is the largest town in the Ketchikan Gateway Borough and has 8,050 people living there, according to the 2010 census. Ketchikan is the fifth-biggest city in Alaska, and the tenth-biggest place when we count smaller areas too. The whole Ketchikan Borough, which includes nearby towns and villages, had 13,477 people in 2010. In 2017, Ketchikan had about 13,754 people. The city was first officially formed in 1900, making it the oldest incorporated city in Alaska. Ketchikan is on an island called Revillagigedo, named in 1793 by Captain George Vancouver. The city is near Ketchikan Creek, which gives it its name. The meaning of "Ketchikan" is not clear; it could mean "the river belonging to kitschk" or "thundering wings of an eagle."

Teulada, also called "tegula" in Latin, is a municipality in the province of South Sardinia, in Italy. It is near Cagliari. Sant'Isidoro di Teulada, a part of Teulada, might be where the ancient Roman city Bithia, also known as Biotha or Biora, was located. During World War II, there was a naval battle on November 27, 1940. British ships, including HMS Newcastle and three other cruisers, fought against Italian Navy ships near a place called Cape Spartivento.

Joe Perry, born on September 10, 1950, is an American musician and songwriter. He is the lead guitarist and a founding member of the rock band Aerosmith. Aerosmith is very famous and has sold more than 150 million albums worldwide and 70 million in the United States. Perry has his own band called the Joe Perry Project. He also plays in a band called Hollywood Vampires with Alice Cooper and Johnny Depp. Perry is known as one of the greatest guitarists of all time, ranked 84th by Rolling Stone. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with Aerosmith in 2001. In 2013, Perry and his songwriting partner Steven Tyler received the ASCAP Founders Award and were inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame. In October 2014, a book about his life called "Rocks: My Life in and Out of Aerosmith" was published.

The Torres Strait is a waterway between Australia and the island of New Guinea. It is about 30 kilometers wide at its narrowest part. To the south is Cape York Peninsula, which is the northern tip of the Australian mainland. To the north is the Western Province of Papua New Guinea. The strait is named after navigator Luis Vaz de Torres, who sailed through it in 1606.

George Washington was inaugurated as the first president of the United States on Thursday, April 30, 1789. This event took place on the balcony of Federal Hall in New York City. He became the first president, starting his four-year term. Robert Livingston, who was the Chancellor of New York, gave Washington his oath of office. This inauguration started the executive branch of the U.S. government under the new Constitution, which was written in 1787. John Adams became the first vice president on April 21, 1789. He began his duties as the Senate's presiding officer on that day.

Landshut is a town in Bavaria, located in the southeast of Germany. Situated on the banks of the River Isar, Landshut is the capital of Lower Bavaria, one of seven administrative regions in Bavaria. It is also the main city in the surrounding district and has over 70,000 people living there. Landshut is the largest city in Lower Bavaria, followed by Passau and Straubing. It is also the second biggest city in Eastern Bavaria. Landshut is often called "City of the Three Helmets" because of its special coat of arms. It is famous for the Landshuter Hochzeit, a big medieval festival. Landshut is close to Munich and the Franz Josef Strauss International Airport, making it an important place for investments. It is one of the wealthiest industrial towns in Bavaria and has the lowest unemployment rate in East Bavaria.

Leon Jackson, born on December 30, 1988, is a Scottish singer. He won the fourth series of the British talent show "The X Factor" in 2007. After winning, he was the main star of a web series called "Leon's Life," which was on from 2007 to 2008. His first album, "Right Now," came out in 2008 and was the 75th best-selling album in the UK that year. It had songs like "Don't Call This Love," "Creative," and "Stargazing." His first single, "When You Believe," was a cover of a song by Whitney Houston and Mariah Carey. It sold over 400,000 copies and was the 92nd best-selling single of the 2000s and the third best-selling single of 2007. Jackson's single was the best-selling single by a British male artist in 2007, beating other artists like Mika, Take That, and Mark Ronson. It came in third place, behind Leona Lewis's "Bleeding Love" and Rihanna's "Umbrella." By 2016, Jackson had one UK number one single and two UK top ten singles. His debut album was in the UK top fifty for nine weeks. His winning single, "When You Believe," was the seventh best-selling single from an "X Factor" winner, outperforming Little Mix, Sam Bailey, and Louisa Johnson. His debut album was the eighth best-selling debut album from an "X Factor" winner, beating Ben Haenow and Joe McElory.

Dara Singh Randhawa, born Dedar Singh Randhawa, was born on November 19, 1928, and died on July 12, 2012. He was an Indian wrestler, actor, and politician. He began acting in 1952 and was the first athlete to be nominated to India's Rajya Sabha, the upper house. He worked as a Hindi and Punjabi film producer, director, and writer, and appeared in films and on TV. He is famous for his undefeated wrestling record and later becoming a successful movie star. His role as Hanuman in the 1976 film "Bajrangbali" and in Ramanand Sagar's "Ramayan" made him well-known. In 2018, WWE inducted him into the Hall of Fame.

Todor Stoyanov Burmov (14 January 1834 – 7 November 1906) was a leading Bulgarian conservative politician and the first prime minister of an independent Bulgaria. Burmov studied theology and taught in Gabrovo and worked as a newspaper editor. During Ottoman rule, he and Gavril Krastevich supported a moderate group that wanted an independent Bulgarian Orthodox church linked to the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople, against more radical nationalists who pushed for a complete split. Burmov was close to Alexander of Bulgaria and was chosen as the prime minister of the newly independent country on July 17, 1879, despite the conservatives' weak position. His government focused on stabilizing the country, including declaring martial law in Varna and areas with Muslim rebellions. The government failed due to lack of support from the conservatives in the assembly and fell that same year. After his time as prime minister, Burmov remained a key political figure. He served as finance minister in the governments of Leonid Sobolev and Archbishop Kliment Turnovski. Later, he returned to journalism and left the conservatives to join Dragomir Tsankov's Progressive Liberal Party.

Pinhais is a municipality in Paraná state, Brazil. In 2018, it had 130, 789 people. Pinhais became a separate municipality in 1992, splitting from Piraquara. It is part of the Curitiba metropolitan region. Pinhais is the smallest municipality in Paraná by size. It has the Autódromo Internacional de Curitiba and the Expotrade Arena within its area.
Ganbareh" is a song by the German group Sash! It came out on June 24, 2002, through Virgin Records. This was the first single from their fourth album, called "S4! Sash!

A parody mass is a musical setting of the mass, often from the 16th century, that uses parts of another pre-existing piece of music, like a motet or a secular song, as part of its melody. It's different from the other main types of Renaissance mass composition: the cantus firmus and the paraphrase mass. The term "parody" doesn't mean humor here; it refers to using parts of other music, which could be either sacred or secular. Sometimes, non-liturgical sacred music, like motets, was used. Instead of calling it a "parody mass," the term "imitation mass" has been suggested, as "parody" is based on a misreading of a late 16th-century text. During the Renaissance, the parody mass was very popular, with Palestrina writing about 50 examples. By the first half of the 16th century, this style was the main form. In 1562, the Council of Trent banned the use of secular material in church music, stating that nothing profane should be used. The reforms were strictly followed only in Italy; in France, changes in taste had already brought about many of the council's wishes, and in Germany, they were largely ignored. In a typical parody mass, a polyphonic fragment from another piece is used. If only one voice from the source is used, elaborated and moving between parts, it's called a paraphrase mass. Parody techniques include adding or removing voices, adding new fragments, or using the fragment at the beginning of each part of the mass. Italian music theorist Pietro Cerone, in his 22-volume work "El Melopeo y Maestro," provided guidelines: each main section should start with the source's beginning, the Kyrie's interior section should use a secondary motive, and some parts, like the second and third Agnus Dei, should be freely composed. He also advised using many musical ideas from the model. Examples of early parody masses include "Missa malheur me bat," "Missa mater patris," and "Missa fortuna desperata" by Josquin des Prez, and "Missa de Dringhs" by Antoine Brumel. By the middle of the 16th century, most masses used the parody technique.

Zifeng Tower, also known as Greenland Center-Zifeng Tower or Greenland Square Zifeng Tower, used to be called Nanjing Greenland Financial Center. This very tall building in Nanjing, Jiangsu, has 89 floors and was finished in 2010. The first 41 floors have shops and offices. Floors 49 to 71 have a hotel, many restaurants, and a public viewing area on the 72nd floor. Its shape helps separate these different sections. Zifeng Tower is currently the tallest building in Nanjing and Jiangsu Province. It is the eleventh tallest in China and the twentieth tallest in the world. The building was designed by the architectural firm Skidmore, Owings and Merrill, led by Adrian Smith. The tower covers an area of 18,721 square meters, and the Nanjing Greenland Intercontinental Hotel is inside it.

Jealousy is feeling insecure, afraid, or worried about not having something others have or feeling unsafe. It can include feelings like anger, resentment, or feeling inferior. Originally, "jealousy" meant something different from "envy," but these words are often used the same way now. Jealousy is common in relationships and can be seen in babies as young as five months old. Some think jealousy is found in all cultures, while others think it depends on the culture. Jealousy can be suspicion or reaction. It often involves a mix of strong emotions. Psychologists study why people feel jealous and what makes them jealous. Sociologists say cultural beliefs influence what causes jealousy and how to show it. Biologists look at unconscious factors that affect how people feel jealous. Jealousy has been a theme in art, from paintings and plays to songs and books, and religious leaders have talked about it in their teachings.

The Foucault pendulum is a simple device named after French physicist Léon Foucault. It was created to show that the Earth is rotating. This pendulum was first shown in 1851 and was the first experiment to provide clear evidence of the Earth's rotation. Today, Foucault pendulums can be found as popular displays in science museums and universities.

John Singer Sargent, born on January 12, 1856, and died on April 14, 1925, was an American artist living in Europe. He is known as the top portrait painter of his time, famous for his paintings of luxurious Edwardian era. He painted about 900 oil paintings and over 2,000 watercolors, along with many sketches and drawings. His works show his travels around the world, including places like Venice, the Tyrol, Corfu, the Middle East, Montana, Maine, and Florida. Sargent was born in Florence to American parents. He learned art in Paris and later moved to London, spending most of his life in Europe. He was well-known for painting portraits of important people. His first important painting, "Madame X," shown in the Paris Salon in the 1880s, was meant to make him popular among society painters. However, it caused a scandal instead. After the scandal, Sargent went to England, where he continued to paint successful portraits. His early paintings showed great skill, especially in drawing with a brush. In later years, this skill was admired but also criticized for seeming too simple. His official portraits followed the grand style, but his other works, like landscapes, showed influence from the Impressionist movement. In his later years, Sargent sometimes disliked the restrictions of official portrait work and focused more on large wall paintings and outdoor painting. Art historians didn't pay much attention to artists like Sargent, who painted royalty and high society, until the late 20th century.

Proposition 64, also known as the Adult Use of Marijuana Act (AUMA), was a 2016 vote that made cannabis legal in California. Its full name is the Control, Regulate and Tax Adult Use of Marijuana Act. The voters approved it with 57% support. It became law on November 9, 2016. Recreational cannabis sales started in California by January 2018.

David Wayne Parks was an American football player who played as a wide receiver and end. He was born on December 25, 1941, and died on August 8, 2019. Parks was chosen first overall in the 1964 NFL draft from Texas Technological College (now Texas Tech University). He was selected to three Pro Bowls and was named All-Pro twice. In 1965, he won the "triple crown" by leading the NFL in receptions, receiving yards, and receiving touchdowns. In 2008, he was chosen to be in the College Football Hall of Fame.
