Alain Émile Louis Marie Poher was a French politician born on April 17, 1909, and died on December 9, 1996. He was a centrist politician, first associated with the Popular Republican Movement and later with the Democratic Centre. Poher was a senator for Val-de-Marne from 1946 until 1995. He served as the president of the Senate from October 3, 1968, to October 1, 1992. In this role, he became the interim president of the country twice. In the 1969 presidential election, he was a main candidate but lost to Georges Pompidou in the second round.

Cipriano de Rore, sometimes called Cypriano, was born in 1515 or 1516 and died between September 11 and 20, 1565. He was a composer from France or Flanders who lived during the Renaissance period. He worked in Italy. He was one of the main composers who moved from France or Flanders to Italy. He was also one of the most famous madrigal composers in the mid-16th century. His music was experimental, used many notes, and was very expressive. His style of music had a big impact on the future of madrigals.

Luis Maldonado Venegas was a Mexican politician and lawyer. He was born on November 19, 1956, and died on April 30, 2019. Maldonado was part of the Party of the Democratic Revolution. He worked as a federal deputy in the Mexican Congress, representing Mexico City and the fourth electoral region during the 63rd legislature. Additionally, he was the national president of the Convergencia political party and served in both houses of Congress.

Abigail Kathleen Breslin, born on April 14, 1996, is an American actress and singer. She grew up in New York City. Breslin started acting in commercials when she was three years old. She first appeared in a movie called "Signs" in 2002, when she was five. For her role, she was nominated for a Young Artist Award. She got more famous for her part in "Little Miss Sunshine" in 2006, where she played Olive Hoover. For this, she was nominated for Screen Actors Guild, BAFTA, and Academy Awards. She won the Screen Actors Guild award for best cast and Critics' Choice Movie Award for best young performer. Breslin has been in many other movies, like "No Reservations," "Rango," and "Ender's Game." She also starred in the TV show "Scream Queens" from 2015 to 2016.

Boyd County is in Nebraska. In 2010, it had 2,099 people. The main town is called Butte. The county was created in 1891 and named after James E. Boyd, who was Nebraska's governor at that time. In the Nebraska license plate system, Boyd County uses the number 63. When the system began in 1922, Boyd County had the 63rd-most cars. In 2010, three small towns in Boyd County had very few people: Anoka had 6, Gross had 2, and Monowi had just 1. Monowi was the only town in the United States with only one person living there in 2010.
Kurt Paul Schmitt was born on October 7, 1886, in Heidelberg and died on November 2, 1950, in Heidelberg. He was a German economic leader and also served as the Reich economy minister.

Plymouth County is in Massachusetts, U.S. In 2010, it had 494, 919 people. The county seats are Plymouth and Brockton. The Spanish treasure fleet, also known as the West Indies fleet, silver fleet, or plate fleet, was a group of ships organized by the Spanish Empire from 1566 to 1790. These ships sailed between Spain and its territories in the Americas across the Atlantic Ocean. They carried many different goods, such as food, wood, metals like silver and gold, gems, pearls, spices, sugar, tobacco, silk, and other special items from Spain's American territories to Spain. In return, Spanish goods like oil, wine, cloth, books, and tools were sent to the Americas. The West Indies fleet was the first steady trade route across the Atlantic. Similarly, the Manila galleons were the first steady trade route across the Pacific.

Mclaren Racing Limited is a British racing team based in Woking, Surrey, England. They are famous for racing in Formula One and also competed in American open wheel racing. They won the Canadian-American Challenge Cup (Can-Am) sports car racing championship. The team is the second oldest and second most successful Formula One team after Ferrari. They have won 12 drivers' championships and eight constructors' championships. Mclaren is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Mclaren Group. Founded by Bruce Mclaren in 1963, the team won its first grand prix in 1968. Bruce Mclaren died in 1970, and Teddy Mayer took over, leading the team to their first Formula One constructors' championship in 1974 with Emerson Fittipaldi and James Hunt winning the drivers' championship. They began a long sponsorship with Marlboro in 1974. In 1981, Mclaren merged with Project Four Racing. Ron Dennis took over as team principal and bought out the original Mclaren shareholders. With Porsche and Honda engines, Niki Lauda, Alain Prost, and Ayrton Senna won seven drivers' championships, and Mclaren won six constructors' championships. The Prost and Senna partnership was particularly successful, but later they had a rivalry, and Prost left for Ferrari. English team Williams challenged Mclaren during this period. By the mid-1990s, Honda withdrew from Formula One, Senna moved to Williams, and Mclaren went three seasons without a win. With Mercedes-Benz engines, sponsorship, and Adrian Newey, they won more championships with Mika Häkkinen. In the 2000s, driver Lewis Hamilton made them consistent front-runners and won their latest title in 2008. Ron Dennis retired in 2009, handing over to Martin Whitmarsh. However, in 2013, after their worst season since 2004, Whitmarsh was replaced. Mclaren announced they would use Honda engines from 2015, replacing Mercedes-Benz. They raced as Mclaren Honda for the first time since 1992 at the 2015 Australian Grand Prix. In 2017, Mclaren agreed to use Renault engines from 2018 to 2020. Mclaren will return to use Mercedes-Benz engines from 2021 until at least 2024. Mclaren returned to the Indianapolis 500 in 2017 with Andretti Autosport. In 2019, they announced they would run the full IndyCar series with Arrow Schmidt Peterson Motorsports, under the name Arrow McLaren SP.

Flushing is a neighborhood in the middle part of Queens, New York City. It's the fourth-largest business area in the city. The main shopping and business area, downtown Flushing, is very busy. It's the third-busiest intersection in New York City, after Times Square and Herald Square. Flushing was first settled in 1645, when New Netherland was created. It was called Vlissingen, after a Dutch city. When the English took over in 1664, and Queens County was formed in 1683, Flushing became one of the main towns. In 1898, Flushing joined New York City. Flushing grew in the early 1900s because of new bridges and transportation. In the late 1900s, many immigrants, mainly Chinese and Korean, moved there. The area has many different neighborhoods and lots of different people live there. People can get to Flushing by train from Long Island, or by subway. It's in Queens Community District 7, and has postcodes 11354, 11355, and 11358. The area is watched over by the NYPD's 109th Precinct.

Return to Never Land is a 2002 movie about Peter Pan. It is a sequel to the 1953 Disney film and is based on J. M. Barrie's 1911 novel Peter and Wendy. The movie was released on February 15, 2002. It was produced by Walt Disney Television Animation and released by Walt Disney Pictures, with distribution by Buena Vista Pictures. The movie made $115 million worldwide. Some critics thought the songs were forgettable and the story was not very good. The story focuses on Wendy's daughter. During the bombing in London, she doesn't believe her mother's Peter Pan story. She is accidentally brought to Neverland by pirates. To go back home, she meets Peter Pan, Tinker Bell, and the Lost Boys. They help her learn to fly and believe in the story.

Elizabeth I, born on September 7, 1533, and died on March 24, 1603, was queen of England and Ireland from November 17, 1558, until her death. She was sometimes called the Virgin Queen, Gloriana, or Good Queen Bess. Elizabeth was the last ruler of the Tudor dynasty. She was the daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, his second wife, who was executed when Elizabeth was two and a half years old. Henry VIII declared Anne's marriage invalid and declared Elizabeth illegitimate. Her half-brother, Edward VI, ruled until 1553. He ignored the claims of his two half-sisters, Mary, a Roman Catholic, and Elizabeth. Edward's will was set aside, and Mary became queen, removing Lady Jane Grey. During Mary's reign, Elizabeth was imprisoned for about a year because people thought she supported Protestant rebels. Upon Mary's death in 1558, Elizabeth became queen. She ruled by good advice and trusted her advisors, like William Cecil, who became Lord Burghley. Elizabeth established the Church of England, of which she was the head. Elizabeth never married or had children. After her cousin, James VI of Scotland, became her heir, he eventually became King James I of England, leading to the formation of Great Britain. During Elizabeth's reign, she was involved in imprisoning and executing Mary, Queen of Scots. Elizabeth was cautious in her foreign affairs, balancing between France and Spain. She supported a few unsuccessful military campaigns in the Netherlands, France, and Ireland. In the 1580s, England went to war with Spain, and the English navy defeated the Spanish Armada in 1588, making Elizabeth famous. Elizabeth's rule was celebrated for its cultural achievements, including the plays of William Shakespeare and Christopher Marlowe, and the maritime exploration led by Francis Drake. Some saw her as patient and lucky, while others thought she was often quick-tempered and indecisive. At the end of her reign, economic and military issues reduced her popularity. Still, her 44 years on the throne brought stability to England and helped create a national identity.

Silicon is a chemical element with the symbol Si and atomic number 14. It is a hard, brittle solid that looks shiny, like a metal. It is a tetravalent metalloid and a semiconductor. On the periodic table, it is in group 14, between carbon and elements like germanium, tin, and lead. It is not very reactive. In 1823, Jöns Jakob Berzelius first prepared and identified pure silicon. Silicon oxides form silicate anions. It has the second-highest melting and boiling points among metalloids and nonmetals, after boron. Silicon is the eighth most common element in the universe by mass. On Earth, it is mostly found in minerals like silica and silicates. About 28% of the Earth's crust is made of silicon. It is used in construction and to make cement, concrete, ceramics, and glass. Silicon compounds are also used for abrasives and strong ceramics. Silicon was crucial for the digital age, as it is used in semiconductor electronics. Most of the silicon used is not purified much. It is essential for making transistors and integrated circuits, like those in computers and phones. Free silicon is used in steel making, aluminum casting, and making chemicals. Silicon is important for some living things. Some sea sponges and microorganisms make their skeletons from silica. Plants also contain silica in their tissues.

Princeton, originally called Vermilion Forks, is a town in the Similkameen region of southern British Columbia, Canada. It is located east of the Cascade Mountains, which extend south into Washington, Oregon, and California. The Tulameen and Similkameen rivers meet in Princeton. In 2016, the town had 2,828 people. Princeton has businesses on seven blocks of Bridge Street and five blocks of Vermilion Avenue. There are also businesses along Highway 3. Historically, mining has been the main industry. Princeton's biggest employers are the Copper Mountain Mine, a sawmill owned by Weyerhaeuser, and some smaller timber companies, including Princeton Wood Preservers and Princeton Post and Rail.

Ingvar Axel Harald Ericsson was born on August 31, 1927, and died on May 14, 2020. He was a Swedish middle-distance runner who focused on the 1500 meters race. Ericsson participated in the 1952 and 1956 Summer Olympics. In 1952, he finished eighth. At the European Championships, he was seventh in 1950 and fourth in 1954. Ericsson won the national 1500 meters title three times— in 1952, 1954, and 1955—and set a new national record in 1956. His job was a firefighter.

A medical school teaches medicine and gives professional degrees to doctors and surgeons. These degrees include the bachelor of medicine and surgery (MBBS, MBCHB, MBBCh, BMBS) and the doctor of medicine (MD). Some schools also offer master's degrees (M.Sc.), a physician assistant program, or other advanced studies. Medical schools do research and run teaching hospitals. Medical schools differ in their rules, teaching methods, and programs around the world. They are usually very competitive, using exams, grades, and leadership roles to choose students. In most countries, studying medicine is done as an undergraduate degree without needing extra classes first. But more and more schools now take students who have completed an undergraduate degree. In the U.S. and Canada, almost all medical schools require a previous university degree. Medical degrees are given after a 5-year or longer undergraduate program, or a 4-year graduate program. Many modern schools teach basic sciences and clinical skills together. Traditional programs have separate preclinical and clinical parts. Students in preclinical sciences learn about biochemistry, genetics, pharmacology, and other subjects. Clinical rotations include internal medicine, surgery, pediatrics, psychiatry, and more. Doctors get their degree from medical schools, but they need to be licensed by the local government to practice. Licensing requires passing tests, background checks, and years of postgraduate training. Medical schools are managed by each country and listed in a directory called the World Directory of Medical Schools.

Freedom riders were activists who rode buses into the southern United States in 1961 and later to challenge segregation. In 1961, the first freedom ride started in Washington, D.C., and was planned to end in New Orleans. The Supreme Court had ruled in "Morgan v. Virginia" (1946) and "Boynton v. Virginia" (1960) that segregated buses were against the law. However, states in the South ignored these rulings, and the federal government did not enforce them. "Boynton" said that restaurants and waiting rooms in bus stations serving interstate buses could not be segregated. In 1955, the Interstate Commerce Commission had ruled in "Sarah Keys v. Carolina Coach Company" that the "Plessy v. Ferguson" "separate but equal" doctrine did not apply to interstate bus travel. But they did not enforce this ruling, and segregation laws remained in the South. The freedom riders mixed races on buses to fight segregation. This challenged local laws and customs. The freedom rides and the violent reactions drew attention to the problem. Police arrested the riders for breaking local laws, but sometimes they did not stop white mobs from attacking them. Most freedom rides were organized by the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE), but some were by the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC). The rides began in 1960, after students had used sit-ins and boycotts to challenge segregation in lunch counters and stores. The Supreme Court's "Boynton" decision supported travelers ignoring local segregation rules. Southern police thought the freedom riders were breaking the law and arrested them. In some places, like Birmingham, Alabama, police worked with hate groups to attack the riders.

Christian Science is a belief system connected to members of the Church of Christ, Scientist. People who follow this belief are often called Christian Scientists. The church is sometimes known as the Christian Science Church. It started in New England in the 19th century with Mary Baker Eddy. In her 1875 book "Science and Health," she said sickness could be cured through prayer. This book became the main text of Christian Science, along with the Bible. By 2001, it had sold over nine million copies. Eddy and 26 followers got permission in 1879 to create the Church of Christ, Scientist. The first church was built in Boston, Massachusetts, in 1894. Christian Science grew quickly in the United States, reaching nearly 270,000 members by 1936. By 1990, the number had dropped to about 100,000, and by 2009, there were fewer than 50,000 members. The church publishes a newspaper called "The Christian Science Monitor," which won seven Pulitzer Prizes between 1950 and 2002. They also have reading rooms worldwide. Eddy said Christian Science returned to the original Christianity and its healing aspects. It has key differences from traditional Christianity, especially in thinking the world is mostly spiritual, not physical. They believe diseases are caused by wrong thoughts, not physical problems. They think sick people should be prayed for instead of treated with medicine. While Christian Scientists don't avoid all medical care, they prefer prayer over medicine. Critics say this can be dangerous, as several deaths occurred between the 1880s and 1990s because of it.

Cócorvado National Park is in the Osa Peninsula, southwestern Costa Rica. It was created on October 24, 1975. The park is the largest in Costa Rica and covers about one-third of the Osa Peninsula. It is considered one of the most biodiverse places on Earth. National Geographic calls it "the most biologically intense place on earth." It has a lot of wildlife and is popular among tropical ecologists. The park has the biggest primary forest on the American Pacific coast and some of the last big areas of lowland tropical forests in the world. Historically, logging took place in lowland areas because they were more accessible and had the biggest valuable trees. However, these areas are also rich in biodiversity. Most tropical forests remain, but lowland forests are usually too small to support natural biodiversity. Larger animals need a big, undisturbed habitat. Unfortunately, even tourism, which helps preserve parks like Cócorvado economically, can threaten the long-term biodiversity. The park’s waters are calm and rich in biodiversity. Cano Island Biological Reserve is one of the parks along the coast. Humpback whales visit Drake Bay to winter and breed. Ballena National Marine Park is specially designed for humpback whales. Bryde's whales and other baleen whales also migrate through the area. Spinner dolphins, rough-toothed dolphins, and false killer whales and killer whales are seasonal residents. Whale watching tours are available. Manatees were hunted in Costa Rica, leaving only a few today, which can sometimes be seen at Manzanillo Beach, Talamanca, and Limón.

Syed Mir Jafar Ali Khan Bahadur (– 5 February 1765) was a military general who became the first dependent ruler of Bengal for the British East India Company. He began ruling in 1757 after betraying Siraj ud-Daulah, the previous Nawab of Bengal, during the Battle of Plassey. Mir Jafar was supported by the British until 1760 but failed to meet their demands. In 1758, Robert Clive found out that Mir Jafar had made a treaty with the Dutch. This led to a battle. A British official suggested Mir Qasim, Mir Jafar’s son-in-law, should be the deputy subahdar. In October 1760, the company forced Mir Jafar to give up his position to Mir Qasim. However, Mir Qasim tried to make the company leave his territory, which led to his removal. Mir Jafar was then reinstated as Nawab in 1763 with company support. Mir Qasim refused to accept this and went to war with the company. Mir Jafar ruled until his death on 5 February 1765 and is buried at the Jafarganj cemetery in Murshidabad, West Bengal. Mir Jafar is seen as a controversial figure in Indian history, often viewed as a traitor by Bengalis.

This led to her working on television as the host of a children's show called "Junior Magazine" in Wellington. Over her long career, she acted in comedy and drama in theater, film, and TV.

Aquarius is a constellation in the zodiac, between Capricorn and Pisces. Its name means "water-carrier" or "cup-carrier" in Latin, and its symbol is (Unicode ♒), which looks like water. Aquarius is one of the oldest recognized constellations in the zodiac. It was included in the 48 constellations listed by the astronomer Ptolemy in the 2nd century, and it remains one of the 88 modern constellations. This constellation is in a region often called the sea because many constellations with watery names can be found there, like Cetus the whale, Pisces the fish, and Eridanus the river. Beta Aquarii is the brightest star in the constellation, with an apparent magnitude of 2.9.

Kareby is a small place in Kungälv municipality, Västra Götaland county, Sweden. It had 292 people living there in 2010. Kareby has four sports teams. The women's bandy team won the Swedish championship in 2016.

A lifeguard watches over swimmers, surfers, and people doing water sports. They work in places like swimming pools, water parks, beaches, spas, rivers, and lakes. Lifeguards know how to swim and can give first aid, especially CPR and using AEDs. They use different tools and equipment to rescue people in water. In some places, lifeguards help during emergencies, and in some communities, they are the main first responders.

Nuclear espionage means giving state secrets about nuclear weapons to other countries without permission. This has happened in many cases both known and suspected. Since nuclear weapons are very important secrets, countries that have them have strict rules about sharing information on their design, how many they have, how they are delivered, and where they are deployed. Countries are also limited in sharing information about their nuclear weapons because of non-proliferation agreements.

The word seneschal can mean different things, all related to supervising or managing in history. Most often, a seneschal was a high-ranking position in a royal, ducal, or noble household during the Middle Ages and early modern period. This role was like a steward or majordomo in a big medieval house. In a royal household, a seneschal managed domestic affairs and servants. This meant overseeing many workers and servants and having a lot of power in the community. In the Middle Ages, much of the local economy came from such households. Another meaning refers to late medieval and early modern France, where a seneschal was a royal officer in charge of justice and administration of certain southern provinces called seneschalties. This role was similar to a northern French bailiff. In the United Kingdom, seneschal is a church term, referring to an official in a cathedral.
Lütschental is a village and municipality in the Interlaken-Oberhasli region, which is in the canton of Bern, Switzerland.

The battle took place on September 24, 1877, in Kagoshima, Japan. It was the last battle of the Satsuma rebellion. Saigō Takamori's samurai, who were heavily outnumbered, fought against the imperial Japanese army led by generals Yamagata Aritomo and Kawamura Sumiyoshi. Saigō's army was destroyed, and he died. This battle ended the Satsuma rebellion. The imperial army won and strengthened their control. There were no more internal rebellions.

Jenna Bush Hager, born on November 25, 1981, is an American news personality, author, and journalist. She currently co-hosts "Today with Hoda & Jenna," which is the fourth hour of NBC's morning news program. Jenna and her twin sister, Barbara, are the daughters of George W. Bush, the 43rd U.S. president, and Laura Bush. They are the first twin children of a U.S. president. After her father finished being president, Jenna became an author, worked as an editor for "Southern Living" magazine, and appeared on NBC as a correspondent, contributor, and co-host.

Fakenham is a market town and civil parish in Norfolk, England. It is near Norwich, about northwest of the city. The town is where several local roads meet, including roads to King's Lynn, Cromer, Norwich, and Swaffham. In 2001, the town had 7,357 people living in 3,292 homes, and this number grew to 7,617 in 2011. Fakenham is part of North Norfolk for local government. The town has been a market town since 1250, especially known for trading corn, barley, and wheat. In the 19th century, it became famous for its printing. Fakenham Racecourse, a horse racing venue south of the town, is supported by the Prince of Wales. The town's long name, Fakenham Lancaster, comes from the manor being owned by John of Gaunt, the Duke of Lancaster, in 1377. This name is still used today, appearing on history trail plaques and in town wards named Lancaster North and Lancaster South.

Hartselle is the second largest city in Morgan County, Alabama, United States. It is located south of Decatur. Hartselle is part of the Decatur metropolitan area and the Huntsville-Decatur combined statistical area. As of the 2010 U.S. Census, the city's population was 14,255. Hartselle was founded in 1870 when the South and North Alabama Railroad arrived. The city is named after George Hartsell, one of the railroad's owners. The post office opened in 1873, and the city was officially incorporated on March 1, 1875. Many of the oldest buildings were destroyed in a fire in 1916.

Western romance languages are part of a group that includes Gallo-Romance and Iberian-Romance branches, as well as Northern Italian. These languages use "s" for plurals, soften some sounds, and pronounce "c" softly, like /t͡s/ or /s/. However, Italian and French dialects are very similar, while French and Spanish are more different. Based on how well people can understand each other, about 12 languages are grouped together: Portuguese, Spanish, Asturian-Leonese, Aragonese, Catalan, Galician, Gascon, Provencal, Gallo-Wallon, French, Franco-Provençal, Romansh, and Ladin. This classification is tricky because italo-romance and Iberian languages are more alike than italo-romance and Gallo-Romance. Some groupings also include italo-dalmatian as part of Western or Eastern Romance. Today, the four most widely spoken standardized Western romance languages are Spanish (about 410 million native speakers and 125 million second-language speakers), Portuguese (around 220 million native and 45 million second-language speakers, mainly in Africa), French (about 80 million native and 70 million second-language speakers, mostly in Africa), and Catalan (about 7.2 million native speakers). Many people also speak these languages, especially French, as a second language in West Africa.

Cleaner shrimp are a type of swimming crab that helps other sea creatures by removing parasites. They belong to three families: Hippolytidae, Palaemonidae, and Stenopodidae. Cleaner shrimp, especially those in the Hippolytidae family and the Lysmata genus, are often called cleaner shrimp. These shrimp help fish by eating parasites, mucus, and small wounds on their bodies, which can reduce infections and help fish heal. Cleaner shrimp gather at specific areas called cleaning stations in coral reefs, where they perform a dance to attract fish. Some cleaner shrimp, like Urocaridella, live in caves and are less active. These shrimp increase their dance movements when they are hungry, showing they compete for fish. Cleaner shrimp are popular in saltwater aquariums because they keep the fish clean and look colorful.

Mount Vernon is a city in Posey County, Indiana, United States. It is the westernmost city in the state. The southernmost city is Rockport, located about southeast of Mount Vernon along the Ohio River. Mount Vernon's population was 6,687 in the 2010 census. It is in Black Township and part of the Evansville, Indiana, metropolitan area, which had a population of 358,676 in 2010.

Runa Laila, born on November 17, 1952, is a Bangladeshi playback singer and composer. She is very well-known in South Asia. She began her career in the Pakistani film industry in the late 1960s. Her singing style was inspired by Pakistani singer Ahmed Rushdi. She replaced another singer named Mala and paired with Rushdi. Runa's voice was heard in films like "The Rain" (1976), "Jadur Banshi" (1977), "Accident" (1989), "Ontore Ontore" (1994), "Devdas" (2013), and "Priya Tumi Shukhi Hou" (2014). For her work in these films, she won seven Bangladesh National Film Awards for best female playback singer. She also won the best music composer award for the film "Ekti Cinemar Golpo" (2018).

Cebuano, also called Bisaya or Binisaya, is an Austronesian language spoken in southern Philippines, mainly in central Visayas, parts of Eastern Visayas, and most of Mindanao. It comes from the island of Cebu and is primarily used by Visayan groups, like the Cebuanos. From the 1950s to the 1980s, Cebuano had the most native speakers among Philippine languages, even though Filipino (Tagalog) is spoken by more people now. It is the most widely spoken Visayan language. Cebuano is also called the "lingua franca" in central Visayas, parts of Eastern Visayas, some parts of Palawan, and most of Mindanao. Its name comes from Cebu, where it originated. In some places, like Ormoc, people call it by local names like Ormocanon or Albuerahanon. Cebuano is known by the three-letter code CEB, but not by a two-letter code. The Komisyon ng Wikang Filipino, which oversees Philippine languages, writes the name as Sebwano. Cebuano and related dialects, including Boholano, are also known as Cebuan in linguistics, and they make up one of the main groups of Visayan languages.

ʿilm al-kalām, often shortened to kalām, is a type of Islamic theology. It focuses on studying Islamic beliefs and doctrines. This field was created to explain, argue about, and defend these beliefs against doubt. People who study kalām are called mutakallimūn. This role is different from that of Islamic philosophers, jurists, and scientists. The word "kalām" in Arabic means "speech" or "word," and in Islamic theology, it relates to the "word of God" found in the Quran. Murtada Mutahhari describes kalām as a discipline that discusses and defends the main beliefs a Muslim must believe in. People wonder why it's called kalām, with one idea being that it deals with whether the Quran, God's word, is part of God's essence or a created speech.

Eden Riegel, born on January 1, 1981, is an American actress and dialogue director. She played the character Bianca Montgomery in the TV show "All My Children." Bianca became famous as a gay icon and a popular character. Eden was nominated for an Emmy Award for her performance in 2005 and won it that year. Besides "All My Children," she appeared in other TV shows and films. She also acted as Eden in the web series "Imaginary Bitches." Eden worked as the voice director for Disney's animated TV series "Amphibia" and "The Owl House." From April 2010 to November 2011, she played the character Heather Stevens in "The Young and the Restless."

Dhayam is a 2017 Indian Tamil thriller film. It was written and directed by Kannan Rangaswamy and produced by A. R. S. Sunder. The entire film was shot in one room. The main actors are Santhosh Prathap, Jayakumar, Aanchal Singh, Sandhu Samaira, and Iria Agarwal. The music was composed by Sathish Selvam. The film's cinematography was done by A. Packiaraj, and it was edited by R. Sudharsan. It was first shown in theaters on March 24, 2017.

Mystery Science Theater 3000, or MST3K, is an American comedy TV show. It was created by Joel Hodgson and is made by Alternaversal Productions. The show first aired on November 24, 1988, on KTMA-TV in Minneapolis, Minnesota. It ran for seven seasons on Comedy Central until 1996 and then three more seasons on the Sci-Fi Channel until 1999. In 1993, 60 episodes were produced and shown later. In 2015, Hodgson started a new series with 14 episodes, which first appeared on Netflix in 2017, followed by another six-episode season in 2018. Total episodes produced are 217, and two live tours have been done. The show stars Joel Robinson, played by Hodgson, who is trapped on a satellite with two mad scientists, "the Mads." Joel watches bad movies and creates robots to keep him company and comment on the movies. The movie is shown on a screen, and Joel, his robot friends, and the Mads are seen in silhouettes from below. Sketches, called "host segments," separate the "theater segments." Hodgson was the original Joel Robinson, but halfway through the fifth season, Mike Nelson replaced him. Other actors include Trace Beaulieu, Josh Weinstein, Jim Mallon, Kevin Murphy, Frank Conniff, Mary Jo Pehl, Bill Corbett, Paul Chaplin, and Bridget Jones Nelson. The 2017 revival has a new cast, including Jonah Ray as the new Joel, Felicia Day and Patton Oswalt as the Mads, and Baron Vaughn, Hampton Yount, and Rebecca Hanson voicing Tom Servo, Crow T. Robot, and Gypsy. The original show didn't get many viewers, but fans called "MSTies" spread the show through online word-of-mouth, repeats, and home media. The show won a Peabody Award in 1993 and was nominated for two Emmy Awards in 1994 and 1995. It was also nominated for the CableACE Award from 1992 to 1997. MST3K influenced social TV and inspired similar projects. The show helped bring attention to many poorly made movies.

Sir David Wing-cheung Tang was a businessman, philanthropist, and socialite from Hong Kong. He was born on August 2, 1954, and passed away on August 29, 2017. Sir David is famous for starting the Shanghai Tang fashion chain in 1994. He sold this company to Richemont in 1998.

Seminole County is in Oklahoma, a state in the U.S. According to the 2010 census, the population was 25,482. The county seat is Wewoka. Most of the county is part of the Seminole Nation reservation, with a small part in the east belonging to the Muscogee (Creek) Nation. The county is known for the Greater Seminole Field, one of the most important oil fields, which is still producing. It extends into nearby counties. During the early oil boom, many workers and adventurers came to the county, making the population triple quickly. As oil production later went down, jobs and people left.

Granzymes are enzymes that help kill cells, especially those that are cancerous or infected. They are found in cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells. These cells release granzymes along with another substance called perforin into the target cell. Granzymes can also be found in parts of the cell called the rough endoplasmic reticulum, the Golgi complex, and the trans-Golgi network. Granzyme B is a specific type of granzyme that starts a process called apoptosis, which is a form of programmed cell death. It does this by activating caspases, especially caspase-3, which break down other parts of the cell. Granzyme B also cuts proteins that change the cell's membrane, leading to the release of substances that trigger apoptosis. Granzymes can kill both cells and bacteria. They break down parts of the bacteria's electron transport chain, causing damage. Granzyme B also cuts viral proteins to stop the virus from replicating. These enzymes can directly bind to DNA and RNA, which helps them break down DNA and RNA-binding proteins. They are not just found in T cells and natural killer cells. They are also present in other immune cells like dendritic cells, B cells, and mast cells. Some non-immune cells like keratinocytes, pneumocytes, and chondrocytes can also make granzymes. Granzymes B can be released outside the cell, especially in cells that don't normally release perforin or form immune synapses. This external granzyme B can build up in conditions with chronic inflammation, breaking down proteins in the extracellular matrix and interfering with tissue healing. It has been linked to diseases like atherosclerosis, aneurysms, and skin aging.

The East Midlands is one of nine official regions in England. It includes Derbyshire, Leicestershire, Lincolnshire (excluding North and North East Lincolnshire), Northamptonshire, Nottinghamshire, and Rutland. The region has an area and a population over 4.5 million as of 2011. Six main cities are Derby, Leicester, Lincoln, Mansfield, Northampton, and Nottingham. Other important towns are Boston, Chesterfield, Corby, Grantham, Hinckley, Kettering, Loughborough, Newark-on-Trent, Skegness, Wellingborough, and Worksop. Its closeness to London and its location on major roads help the East Midlands to do well economically. Nottingham and Leicester are recognized as sufficient-level world cities. The main airport serving the region is East Midlands Airport, located between Derby, Loughborough, and Nottingham.

Muskmelon, also known as "cucumis melo," is a type of melon that has been grown into many different kinds. Some common ones are honeydew, crenshaw, and casaba, which have smooth skin. Others, like cantaloupe, persian melon, and Christmas melon, have a netted surface. There are many cultivated varieties of muskmelons, similar to the number of types of wild cabbage, but their physical differences are not as great. Muskmelons belong to a fruit type called pepo. The origin of muskmelons is not clear. Research suggests that seeds and rootstocks were traded along ancient world routes. Some scientists think muskmelons came from the Levant and Egypt. Others believe they originated in India or central Asia. Some say Africa could be the original home. Today, wild muskmelons can still be found in some African countries.
Elitserien is the top division for men's volleyball in Sweden. In late February or early March, it is followed by the Swedish national championship playoff.

John Walton, born in 1952 in St. Ives, Sydney, Australia, was an actor. He acted on stage, television, and in films. He was famous for his role in the TV show "The Young Doctors." He passed away on July 17, 2014.

Northern California, often called NorCal, is the top part of California. It includes the northern 48 counties. Main cities are in the San Francisco Bay Area (with San Jose, San Francisco, and Oakland), the Sacramento Area (with Sacramento as its capital), and the Fresno Area (with Fresno). This region has redwood forests, the Sierra Nevada mountains including Yosemite Valley and part of Lake Tahoe, Mount Shasta (the second-tallest peak in the Cascade Range after Mount Rainier), and much of the Central Valley, a very productive farming area. The 48-county definition doesn't apply to the Northern California megaregion, which includes from Fresno to Sacramento, and east to the Nevada border, including Lake Tahoe and Reno. People lived in this area for at least 19,000 years. Europeans started settling here in the 1770s with the founding of the Monterey mission, followed by more missions along the coast as far north as Sonoma County.

M'sila is a province in northern Algeria. It has about 1 million people and covers 18,718 square kilometers. The capital city, also named M'sila, has around 100,000 people and is home to M'sila University. Some areas in this province include Bou Saada and Maadid. There is also a salt lake called Chott el Hodna near M'sila. However, most of the area is dry and not developed. M'sila is famous for farming. Additionally, it was where the first village was built as part of a government plan to help nomadic Algerians settle down and use local materials. This village, called Maader, has houses, public spaces, and a mosque.

Dominique Baudis was a French defender of rights, also known as an ombudsman. He was born on April 14, 1947, and passed away on April 10, 2014. Before this role, he was a journalist and a politician. He also served as the mayor of Toulouse. Later, he became a member of the DL party and then joined the main center-right group called Union for a Popular Movement.

The Hawthorn football club, known as the Hawks, is a professional Australian rules football team in the Australian Football League (AFL). Founded in 1902, it's the youngest Victorian-based team in the AFL and has won thirteen premierships. It's the only club to have won premierships in each decade from the 1960s to the 2010s. The team wears brown and gold striped shirts. Their Latin motto means "let us be judged by our actions." The Hawks started in Hawthorn, an inner-eastern suburb of Melbourne, and used to train and have an office at Glenferrie Oval. They haven't played there since 1973. In 2006, the club moved their training and office to Waverly Park, about 21 km from the city center and near their main supporters in Melbourne's outer-eastern area. Their mascot is a hawk. Since 2007, they've played four games annually at York Park in Launceston, Tasmania, with other games at the Melbourne Cricket Ground. Hawthorn's current VFL team is the Box Hill Hawks.
